nodes.title: Momentum Strategies in Futures Markets

nodes.name: trend continuation from price momentum
nodes.description: Past price movements in futures contracts persist into the future due to incomplete price discovery or slow incorporation of information, allowing momentum strategies to profit from continuation of established trends.

nodes.name: cross-contract momentum spillover
nodes.description: Price trends in one futures contract spill over to related contracts due to correlated underlying fundamentals or hedging flows, allowing momentum signals to be exploited across multiple related instruments.

nodes.title: 20 for Twenty
Order Book Price Impact

nodes.name: order flow imbalance price pressure
nodes.description: Price changes occur at rates dependent on the imbalance between bid and ask limit order volumes near the mid-price. Excess buy orders relative to sell orders increase the probability of upward price movement, and vice versa.

nodes.name: order book depth depletion
nodes.description: Spreads exhibit long memory (Hurst index H > 0.5) because large market orders deplete limit-order book depth at best prices, and the book rebuilds slowly, creating persistent spread widening that decays as a power law.

nodes.name: short-horizon order flow predictability
nodes.description: Order flow imbalances contain predictive information about near-term price movements, allowing short-horizon trading signals to exploit the lag between order arrival and full price adjustment.

nodes.title: A Stochastic Model for Order Book Dynamics

nodes.name: queue imbalance pressure on mid-price
nodes.description: Asymmetries in the sizes of limit order queues at bid and ask levels directly push the mid-price; larger queues on one side create execution pressure that moves prices toward that side.

nodes.name: order arrival intensity asymmetry
nodes.description: Imbalances in the rate at which buy and sell orders arrive at the limit order book drive transient mid-price movements; higher arrival intensity on one side creates directional pressure.

nodes.title: Volatility is Rough

nodes.name: rough volatility mean reversion
nodes.description: Spot volatility exhibits rough (fractional Brownian motion) dynamics with Hurst parameter H < 0.5, meaning volatility shocks have long memory and mean-revert more slowly than standard models predict, causing persistent deviations from equilibrium volatility levels.

nodes.name: volatility clustering with long memory
nodes.description: The rough volatility structure implies that volatility shocks have long-range dependence and clustering properties distinct from standard GARCH or Heston models. Past volatility levels influence future volatility in a way consistent with fractional Brownian motion rather than Markovian processes.

nodes.title: Jump Process Modelling in Finance

nodes.name: jump arrival signal extraction
nodes.description: Asset prices exhibit discontinuous jumps driven by discrete information arrivals (earnings, macro announcements, shocks). Extracting the timing and magnitude of these jumps from price data allows inference of latent information events and their market impact.

nodes.name: jump-diffusion decomposition
nodes.description: Asset returns can be decomposed into continuous diffusion (Brownian motion) and discontinuous jump components. The jump component captures tail risk and sudden repricing, while diffusion captures normal market microstructure and gradual information incorporation.

nodes.name: tail risk premium from jump risk
nodes.description: Investors demand compensation for exposure to jump risk (sudden large price movements) that cannot be hedged through continuous trading. This jump risk premium manifests in option prices and expected returns, particularly for assets with higher jump intensity or magnitude.

nodes.title: Rough Paths in Finance
E2EAI: End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Active Investing

nodes.name: nonlinear factor exposure predictiveness
nodes.description: Original factors may have nonlinear relationships with future returns that linear IC/ICIR thresholds fail to capture. A gated attention mechanism dynamically selects factors based on their actual contribution to portfolio returns rather than static correlation thresholds.

nodes.name: cross-sectional factor return accumulation
nodes.description: Deep factors learned from multiple original factors can accumulate predictive power through their cross-sectional regression coefficients (factor returns). The direction and magnitude of these accumulated returns determine the factor's ability to explain future stock returns.

nodes.name: stock relationship neutralization
nodes.description: Industry and cross-industry relationships between stocks create systematic biases in factor exposures. Removing these relationship effects via graph attention networks isolates the true idiosyncratic factor signal from confounding peer influences.

nodes.title: Optimal Investment in Equity and Credit Default Swaps in the Presence of Default

nodes.name: default risk hedging via CDS
nodes.description: Investors dynamically trade credit default swaps to hedge against equity losses from default events. By purchasing CDS protection, investors offset the direct loss of equity value upon default, reducing portfolio volatility and improving utility.

nodes.name: opportunity cost hedging via CDS
nodes.description: Beyond hedging direct default losses, investors use CDS to hedge against restrictions on future trading opportunities that occur after a default event. This forward-looking hedge protects against the loss of investment flexibility and rebalancing ability.

nodes.title: A multi-factor market-neutral investment strategy for New York Stock Exchange equities

nodes.name: trend-chasing behavioral bias
nodes.description: Investors exhibit reduced cognitive load and increased trend-following behavior when price trends are clear and visually apparent, leading to predictable momentum patterns that can be exploited by measuring both trend strength and clarity.

nodes.name: overbought/oversold mean reversion
nodes.description: Extreme relative strength conditions (overbought or oversold) in a security signal subsequent price reversals as markets correct overextended positions, identifiable through momentum oscillators.

nodes.name: fundamental value mean reversion
nodes.description: Stocks with valuations (price-to-sales, book-to-market) or profitability metrics (ROA, gross margins) that deviate from recent historical norms tend to revert toward their typical levels, creating predictable return patterns.

nodes.name: analyst sentiment revision drift
nodes.description: Changes in analyst recommendation consensus signal shifts in institutional attention and information diffusion, with stocks experiencing recommendation upgrades or downgrades exhibiting subsequent drift in the direction of the revision.

nodes.title: Equity Factors: To Short Or Not To Short, That Is The Question

nodes.name: asymmetric factor predictability between long and short legs
nodes.description: Long and short positions in classical equity factors exhibit different degrees of predictability, with the short leg often being more predictable than the long leg. Exploiting this asymmetry through a long-short portfolio construction generates alpha that cannot be captured by hedging only the long leg.

nodes.name: short-leg cost-benefit tradeoff in factor implementation
nodes.description: While shorting incurs specific costs (borrowing, fees, execution friction), the superior predictability of the short leg can overcome these costs and deliver better risk-adjusted returns than long-only hedged implementations, particularly for smaller asset bases where per-unit costs are less prohibitive.

nodes.title: Factor Models for Alpha Streams

nodes.name: covariance matrix singularity from limited observations
nodes.description: When the number of alpha streams (N) far exceeds historical observations (M), the sample covariance matrix becomes singular or near-singular, making direct optimization and weight allocation intractable. This motivates the need for factor model dimensionality reduction.

nodes.name: factor model dimensionality reduction via principal components
nodes.description: Alpha covariance structure can be decomposed into a small number (M) of principal component factors capturing large eigenvalues, with remaining small eigenvalues treated as noise. This reduces the effective dimensionality from N alphas to M factors while preserving the dominant correlation structure.

nodes.name: regularization via underlying tradables as risk factors
nodes.description: Instead of relying on unstable alpha correlations, use the underlying stocks themselves as risk factors. The factor covariance matrix (stock variances and covariances) can be computed from longer historical windows and existing multi-factor stock models, avoiding the need to correlate alphas with each other.

nodes.name: alpha taxonomy clustering for correlation stability
nodes.description: Alphas constructed similarly tend to be correlated; grouping them into clusters based on construction methodology (taxonomy) and treating clusters as risk factors improves out-of-sample stability compared to computing correlations directly from limited time series.

nodes.title: Stochastic Price Dynamics Implied By the Limit Order Book

nodes.name: limit order book volatility smile mispricing
nodes.description: The limit order book structure implies a volatility smile that reflects market expectations of price jumps and fat tails. Traders can exploit discrepancies between this implied volatility smile and actual realized market behavior to identify mispriced options and predict future price movements.

nodes.name: jump-diffusion process inference from order book
nodes.description: The distribution and spacing of limit orders in the order book reveals information about the market's expectation of jump risk and tail events. This allows explicit inference of a jump-diffusion process that accounts for the observed volatility smile and fat tails in returns.

nodes.title: Price Jump Prediction in Limit Order Book

nodes.name: bid-ask liquidity imbalance predicts trade direction
nodes.description: When bid-side limit order volume exceeds ask-side volume at the best level, the next market order is more likely to be a buy order (and vice versa). This imbalance signals which side has more aggressive demand, making the direction of the next trade predictable from order book depth.

nodes.name: market order size predicts price jumps
nodes.description: Larger market orders are more likely to exhaust available liquidity at the best bid/ask and trigger an inter-trade price jump (execution at a worse price than the best quote). Market order size is consistently informative for predicting whether the next trade will jump price levels.

nodes.name: trade-through signals future price jumps
nodes.description: When a market order consumes multiple price levels (a trade-through), it indicates strong directional pressure and depleted liquidity, making subsequent inter-trade price jumps more likely as the order book must rebuild at wider spreads.

nodes.title: Directional Price Forecasting in the Continuous Intraday Market under Consideration of Neighboring Products and Limit Order Books

nodes.name: limit order book information content
nodes.description: The order flow dynamics embedded in the limit order book contain predictive information about future volatility and price movements that is not captured by classical models. Hawkes-based models extract this information through the self-exciting structure of order arrivals.

nodes.name: neighboring product price spillover
nodes.description: Prices of related products (especially quarter-hourly products whose delivery periods overlap with the target hourly product's trading window) contain predictive signals for the target product's price direction, reflecting cross-product dependencies and arbitrage dynamics.

nodes.name: short-term price momentum from recent transactions
nodes.description: The volume-weighted average price (VWAP) of the most recent transactions has strong predictive power for near-term price direction, suggesting that market participants underreact to or gradually incorporate recent trade information.

nodes.title: Hidden Order in Trades Predicts the Size of Price Moves

nodes.name: informed trading detection via order flow entropy
nodes.description: Informed traders with private information generate persistent, non-random order flow that reduces entropy in the state-transition sequence. This structural departure from randomness can be detected information-theoretically without revealing the sign of the private information, because entropy is invariant under buy/sell label permutation.

nodes.name: volatility magnitude prediction without directional information
nodes.description: Low order-flow entropy signals imminent large price moves (high volatility) by detecting informed trading activity, but cannot predict direction because the same entropy signature arises from informed buyers and informed sellers. This decoupling allows magnitude forecasting consistent with weak-form market efficiency.

nodes.title: Correlation of coming limit price with order book in stock markets

nodes.name: order book clustering attraction
nodes.description: Traders place limit orders preferentially at price levels that already contain large cumulative volumes of unexecuted orders, creating self-reinforcing clustering. This non-random selection of limit prices based on existing order book density amplifies price fluctuations.

nodes.name: price gap amplification
nodes.description: Large gaps between occupied price levels on the order book lead to large price changes in subsequent transactions. The unequal attractive power of prices with high order concentration creates sparse regions that, when crossed, produce outsized returns.

nodes.name: fat-tail price fluctuation generation
nodes.description: The power-law distribution of limit price placement (exponent ~-1.5) combined with order book clustering creates fat tails in price changes. Traders' mimetic preference for high-volume price levels generates the observed heavy-tailed return distribution rather than random order placement.

nodes.title: Investigating Limit Order Book Characteristics for Short Term Price Prediction: a Machine Learning Approach

nodes.name: limit order book imbalance pressure
nodes.description: Asymmetries in the depth and volume of buy versus sell orders in the LOB create predictable short-term price pressure, as the market moves to rebalance the order book or as informed traders exploit the imbalance.

nodes.name: order book microstructure predictability
nodes.description: Limit order book dynamics contain stationary patterns that reveal information about future mid-price movements. By extracting these patterns through stationarity transformations, deep learning models can predict price direction more accurately than raw non-stationary price data alone.

nodes.title: One-level limit order book models with memory and variable spread

nodes.name: order flow imbalance pressure on mid-price
nodes.description: The arrival of new orders within the spread and the standing orders at the opposite side of the book create directional pressure on the mid-price. Imbalances between buy and sell order flow cause predictable mid-price movements that can be anticipated by analyzing the current state of the order book.

nodes.name: standing order depletion effect
nodes.description: After a price change, the standing orders at the opposite side of the book are depleted or reduced. This depletion state affects the probability and timing of subsequent price movements, as fewer orders are available to absorb new flow, making consecutive price increments more likely.

nodes.name: spread-conditional price dynamics
nodes.description: The variable spread width at any point in time conditions the distribution of time until the next price change and the probability of directional price movements. Wider spreads indicate different order book states that predict different price dynamics than narrow spreads.

nodes.title: Two Price Regimes in Limit Order Books: Liquidity Cushion and Fragmented Distant Field

nodes.name: liquidity cushion depth adaptation
nodes.description: The densely-filled regime around the midpoint price (liquidity cushion) adjusts its width in response to trading activity and stock characteristics. Stocks with higher trading frequency, more quote changes, and greater trading volume maintain wider liquidity cushions, reflecting market makers' provision of tighter spreads and deeper near-quote liquidity in response to demand.

nodes.name: order lifetime stratification
nodes.description: The limit order book is filled by orders of vastly different lifetimes that serve distinct functions: short-lived orders (< 10s, 76% of orders) provide minimal volume; medium-lived orders (10s-10min) fill the liquidity cushion near quotes; long-lived orders (≥ 10min, <1% of orders) provide depth far from quotes. This stratification means marginal distributions of order properties are misleading without conditioning on lifetime.

nodes.name: fragmented distant field accumulation
nodes.description: Long-lived limit orders accumulate far from the quotes in a sparse, fragmented regime that persists across the trading day. These orders are inserted at particular times and are prone to flash crashes, suggesting they represent strategic positioning (possibly to exploit or depress price movements) rather than continuous liquidity provision.

nodes.title: Effects of a Price limit Change on Market Stability at the Intraday Horizon in the Korean Stock Market

nodes.name: low-frequency price swing amplification
nodes.description: Widening price limits increase the amplitude of low-frequency price components (slow-moving trends and reversals), making intraday price paths more volatile at longer timescales without affecting high-frequency microstructure noise.

nodes.name: inventory risk increase for liquidity providers
nodes.description: Market makers and retail liquidity providers face greater adverse selection risk when low-frequency price swings amplify, as they must hold larger inventory positions exposed to slower but larger price movements, reducing their willingness to provide liquidity.

nodes.title: A Functional Limit Theorem for Limit Order Books with State Dependent Price Dynamics

nodes.name: state-dependent order flow impact on price dynamics
nodes.description: The probability and magnitude of price changes depend on the standing volume at the top of the book (bid/ask imbalance). Active orders (market orders and spread placements) trigger price movements with intensities that vary with the volume state, creating a feedback between order book depth and price volatility.

nodes.name: volume-dependent price diffusion
nodes.description: In the scaling limit, the bid and ask price processes follow diffusion processes (SDEs) whose drift and volatility coefficients are functions of standing volumes. This couples price dynamics to the full order book state rather than treating prices as independent.

nodes.name: two-timescale order arrival heterogeneity
nodes.description: Active orders (market orders and spread placements) that move prices arrive on a slow timescale, while passive orders (cancellations and placements outside the spread) arrive on a fast timescale. This separation explains why most order flow events do not trigger price changes, with empirical evidence showing only 0.2–2% of orders move prices.

nodes.title: Anomalous diffusion and price impact in the fluid-limit of an order book

nodes.name: order imbalance price discovery
nodes.description: The difference between bid and ask order densities (order imbalance) drives price discovery and trading volume. The mid-price is determined as the point where order imbalance equals zero, and the gradient of imbalance determines trading flow via a financial Ohm's law.

nodes.name: anomalous diffusion of order flow
nodes.description: Orders diffuse through the price space with anomalous (non-standard) diffusion dynamics characterized by long-memory waiting times, rather than classical Brownian motion. This produces power-law or non-Gaussian price impact curves depending on the diffusion parameter.

nodes.name: information-driven order arrival
nodes.description: New information triggers a stochastic forcing function that biases order diffusion and generates correlated buy/sell order flow. The market's price response to information shocks depends on how traders collectively condition liquidity provision on past order flow.

nodes.name: discretization-dependent price impact shape
nodes.description: The functional form of price impact (logarithmic vs. power-law) depends critically on the numerical discretization scheme and sampling frequency used to simulate order book dynamics, not solely on underlying model parameters. Non-uniform sampling can produce artificial kinks in price impact curves.

nodes.title: Jump diffusion approximation for the price dynamics of a fully state dependent limit order book model

nodes.name: order imbalance price pressure
nodes.description: The state of the limit order book, particularly order imbalance at the top of the book (relative volumes on bid vs ask sides), directly influences the arrival rates and types of incoming orders, which in turn drives price dynamics. Imbalanced order books attract orders that move prices toward equilibrium.

nodes.name: standing volume feedback on order arrival
nodes.description: The density and distribution of standing limit orders at different price levels (captured by relative volume density functions) causally affects the conditional distribution of where new limit orders are placed and the intensity of market order arrivals, creating endogenous feedback in price dynamics.

nodes.name: exogenous news jump arrival
nodes.description: Large, unexpected exogenous news events (or endogenous shocks) trigger price jumps that do not scale with tick size, creating discontinuities in price paths that cannot be captured by continuous diffusion models alone. These jumps occur independently of the microstructure state.

nodes.title: Simulating and analyzing a sparse order book: an application to intraday electricity markets

nodes.name: Samuelson effect (volatility acceleration near maturity)
nodes.description: Order book activity and price change intensity increase exponentially as time to maturity decreases, driven by convergence of forward prices to spot prices and increased urgency of position settlement.

nodes.name: Sparse liquidity constraint on price formation
nodes.description: In illiquid markets with large gaps between price levels, the scarcity of limit orders at adjacent ticks prevents continuous price discovery and forces larger price movements when orders arrive, as the order book cannot absorb volume smoothly.

nodes.name: Spread compression with increasing liquidity
nodes.description: As trading volume and order book activity increase toward session end, the bid-ask spread narrows due to denser order placement and more competitive pricing, reducing transaction costs.

nodes.title: Machine Learning for Forecasting Mid Price Movement using Limit Order Book Data

nodes.name: order book imbalance predictability
nodes.description: The sign of the next price movement can be predicted by the current imbalance between bid and ask sides of the limit order book. This creates a mechanical price resistance that depends on the relative queue depths across sides.

nodes.name: microstructure noise reduction via mid-price smoothing
nodes.description: Transaction prices exhibit high-frequency noise due to bid-ask bounce and market microstructure effects. Using mid-prices (average of best bid and ask) and applying temporal smoothing filters reduces noise and reveals true directional price movements that are predictable from order book state.

nodes.name: temporal order flow persistence
nodes.description: Order book dynamics exhibit temporal dependencies where recent order flow imbalances and queue changes predict near-term price direction. The transformer's temporal attention captures these short-lived but exploitable patterns in market microstructure.

nodes.title: Limit Order Book Dynamics in Matching Markets: Microstructure, Spread, and Execution Slippage

nodes.name: structural spread immunity to compensation
nodes.description: A rigid bid-ask spread (ΔV) between an agent's internal reservation price and the best available market bid persists despite linear monetary compensation, because compensation only shifts the bid side while the ask price (based on ordinal categorization) remains invariant. Execution requires compensation to exceed a regime-switching threshold C*, at which point the partner effectively changes categorical identity.

nodes.name: threshold decay execution
nodes.description: Execution occurs not when the spread closes via price improvement, but when a time-decaying liquidity threshold T(t) falls sufficiently low due to inventory costs (age, social pressure). The market-to-book ratio θ = Vreach/Vuncond only needs to exceed this declining threshold, allowing agents to 'settle' for below-target prices as urgency increases.

nodes.name: persistent execution slippage
nodes.description: After execution at a price below the internal ask (θ < 1), the structural spread ΔV remains encoded in the system because the internal reference price Vuncond persists as a psychological anchor. This creates permanent dissatisfaction or regret, mathematically equivalent to a trader executing at an unfavorable price to clear inventory.

nodes.name: reference-dependent spread rigidity
nodes.description: The bid-ask spread derives from ordinal preference rankings rather than continuous utility, making it immune to additive price improvements within the same asset class. Regional differences in absolute compensation levels do not reorder the preference structure; compensation functions as a participation fee rather than a utility substitute.

nodes.title: Continuous-time Modeling of Bid-Ask Spread and Price Dynamics in Limit Order Books

nodes.name: order book queue depletion price impact
nodes.description: Price jumps occur when market orders arrive and deplete the queues of limit orders at best prices. The size of price jumps is determined by how many price levels must be cleared to fulfill the incoming market order, which depends on the stationary distribution of limit orders across price levels in the order book.

nodes.name: cancellation-adjusted order distribution coupling
nodes.description: The distribution of price returns is directly coupled to the distribution of incoming limit orders, mediated by order cancellation rates. Orders placed closer to the spread have higher cancellation rates, while orders deeper in the book have lower cancellation rates, such that the execution probability is roughly uniform across price levels. This creates a one-to-one correspondence between the tail of the order distribution and the tail of price returns.

nodes.name: fleeting order noise filtering
nodes.description: High-frequency cancellations of limit orders (especially those placed inside the spread by algorithmic traders) create noise in best bid-ask prices. Observing prices only at trade times (when market orders arrive) rather than at every quote update filters out this noise and reveals the true price process driven by fundamental order book dynamics.

nodes.name: power-law tail transmission from order book to returns
nodes.description: Power-law distributed tails in the volume of orders at various price levels in the limit order book are transmitted to power-law tails in the distribution of price returns through the queue depletion mechanism and cancellation dynamics, explaining the empirically observed fat tails in return distributions.

nodes.title: Intraday Limit Order Price Change Transition Dynamics Across Market Capitalizations Through Markov Analysis

nodes.name: price inertia by market capitalization
nodes.description: High-capitalization stocks exhibit stronger self-transition probabilities (price inertia) due to dense order books and intense competition among liquidity providers engaging in fine price shading, while low-capitalization stocks show lower stability and larger price revisions due to sparse order books and wider spreads.

nodes.name: intraday temporal regime switching
nodes.description: Limit order price change dynamics exhibit distinct regimes across the trading day—opening and closing hours show elevated price inertia while midday shows stabilized lower inertia—driven by time-varying liquidity conditions, information arrival patterns, and strategic positioning behavior that differs between market open, midday, and close phases.

nodes.name: bid-ask asymmetry in positioning timing
nodes.description: Sellers initiate end-of-day positioning strategies earlier than buyers, creating an additional pre-close phase on the ask side (four temporal phases) versus the bid side (three phases), reflecting asymmetric inventory management and liquidation urgency between buy and sell limit order submitters.

nodes.title: Forecasting high-frequency financial time series: an adaptive learning approach with the order book data

nodes.name: order imbalance pressure
nodes.description: Imbalances between bid and ask quantities create directional pressure on prices. When bid quantity is relatively high compared to ask quantity, it signals stronger demand and predicts upward price movement.

nodes.name: order flow imbalance pressure
nodes.description: The submission, cancellation, and execution of limit and market orders creates directional pressure on mid-price movements. The imbalance between buy and sell order flow at different price levels drives short-term price changes that can be forecasted from LOB state.

nodes.name: non-stationarity adaptation
nodes.description: Market microstructure parameters and price dynamics change over time due to regime shifts and volatility clustering. Adaptive window-based learning that adjusts model specification dynamically outperforms fixed models in non-stationary environments.

nodes.title: Early Detection of Latent Microstructure Regimes in Limit Order Books

nodes.name: Gradual depth erosion before stress
nodes.description: Informed traders accumulate positions gradually, consuming market depth over time in a latent build-up phase before stress becomes visible. This sustained depth decline precedes the sharp depth collapse observed during stress onset, creating a predictable lead window.

nodes.name: Order-flow toxicity accumulation
nodes.description: Order-flow toxicity builds gradually during the latent build-up regime before being reflected in prices and spreads. Persistent directional imbalance signals the accumulation of informed trading pressure that will eventually manifest as stress.

nodes.name: Inventory imbalance widening
nodes.description: Market-maker inventory imbalances widen bid-ask spreads with a delay relative to the underlying order-flow pressure. Mild spread widening in the build-up regime reflects accumulating inventory risk before the sharp spread collapse of stress.

nodes.title: Using Deep Learning for price prediction by exploiting stationary limit order book features
Optimal execution and price manipulations in time-varying limit order books

nodes.name: time-varying liquidity depth effect on price manipulation
nodes.description: When limit order book depth varies over time (λ(t) is non-constant), market makers can create price manipulation strategies by strategically posting or canceling orders. A time-varying depth interacts with order resilience to enable round-trip trades with negative expected cost, whereas constant depth prevents such manipulations.

nodes.name: price manipulation strategies (PMS), transaction-triggered price manipulations (TTPM)
order resilience and market maker order placement
nodes.description: Market makers control two dimensions of order book dynamics: resilience (ρ_t, the rate at which orders appear at better prices) and depth accumulation (η_t, the rate of piling orders at existing prices). The condition 2ρ_t + η_t ≥ 0 prevents price manipulations; violations occur when market makers cancel orders (reducing ρ_t) faster than they accumulate depth.

nodes.name: nonlinear price impact from order book shape
nodes.description: The density distribution of limit orders at different price levels (shape function f) creates nonlinear price impact: trading costs are not proportional to trade size but to a power of trade size. This nonlinearity arises from the cumulative cost of consuming orders across multiple price levels in the limit order book.

nodes.title: Forecasting of Jump Arrivals in Stock Prices: New Attention-based Network Architecture using Limit Order Book Data

nodes.name: adverse selection risk in limit order book
nodes.description: Market makers anticipate imminent price jumps from information arrivals and withdraw liquidity provision on the side of the book where they expect adverse movement, creating predictable asymmetric illiquidity patterns in the order book before jumps occur.

nodes.name: order book path-dependence
nodes.description: The historical sequence of limit order book states (prices, quantities, order flow intensity) contains predictive information about future jump arrivals, with the strength of this predictability varying by stock due to differences in market microstructure.

nodes.name: information arrival signaling through order book imbalance
nodes.description: Scheduled and non-scheduled news events that trigger price jumps are preceded by detectable changes in order book imbalance—such as asymmetric depth, spread widening, or intensity changes—that reflect market participants' anticipation of the information release.

nodes.title: Predicting intraday jumps in stock prices using liquidity measures and technical indicators

nodes.name: liquidity shock precursor to jumps
nodes.description: Abnormal patterns in liquidity measures (order imbalance, depth imbalance, trading volume, market depth) precede intraday price jumps, providing predictive signals before discontinuous price movements occur.

nodes.name: technical indicator momentum reversal
nodes.description: Price momentum and trend indicators (moving averages, stochastic oscillators, price rate of change) computed over recent intervals predict the direction and magnitude of imminent intraday jumps by capturing market microstructure dynamics.

nodes.title: Self-exciting price impact via negative resilience in stochastic order books

nodes.name: self-exciting price impact via negative resilience
nodes.description: When resilience is negative, a trader's own trades stimulate other market participants to trade in the same direction (via stop-loss cascades, front-running, or reduced counterparty availability), causing price deviations to amplify rather than revert, increasing subsequent execution costs.

nodes.name: order book recovery speed (resilience)
nodes.description: The speed at which the limit order book recovers from a trade determines whether price impact decays (positive resilience) or amplifies (negative resilience). Stochastic variation in this recovery rate affects optimal execution timing and strategy structure.

nodes.name: stochastic market depth pressure
nodes.description: Market depth (the quantity of orders available at various price levels) fluctuates stochastically over time. When depth contracts, the same execution volume creates larger price deviations; when it expands, impact is reduced. This forces traders to adapt execution schedules dynamically.

nodes.title: Studies of the limit order book around large price changes

nodes.name: liquidity depletion and slow recovery
nodes.description: Large price changes deplete the limit order book (disappearance of liquidity on one side), causing elevated bid-ask spreads and volatility that relax slowly via power law decay with exponent ~0.38, suggesting the market gradually rebuilds depth rather than snapping back immediately.

nodes.name: order flow imbalance persistence
nodes.description: After large price changes, the bid-ask imbalance (relative buy vs sell volume) shows strong deviations from equilibrium with slow power-law relaxation (~0.3-0.42), indicating that supply-demand pressure persists and gradually dissipates rather than reverting instantly.

nodes.name: mechanical order book rebalancing
nodes.description: Both limit order placement and cancellation activity spike after large price changes and decay via power law (~0.37-0.42), suggesting traders mechanically adjust their orders in response to the shock without strategic foresight; a zero-intelligence model reproduces this behavior, indicating it is not driven by sophisticated behavioral responses.

nodes.title: Order book dynamics in liquid markets: limit theorems and diffusion approximations

nodes.name: order flow imbalance pressure on price
nodes.description: Price moves occur when bid or ask queues are depleted by net order flow imbalance. The direction and timing of price changes are determined by which queue hits zero first, driven by the cumulative imbalance between limit orders (queue-increasing) and market orders/cancellations (queue-decreasing).

nodes.name: queue depletion boundary hitting
nodes.description: In the heavy-traffic limit, bid and ask queue sizes evolve as a two-dimensional Brownian motion in the positive orthant. Price changes occur at hitting times of the boundary axes (when either queue reaches zero), making price dynamics a piecewise constant process determined by boundary-hitting events of the diffusion.

nodes.name: order book depth replenishment after price move
nodes.description: When a price change occurs and a queue is depleted, the new queue sizes are drawn from a stationary distribution representing the depth of the order book at the next price level. This replenishment process, modeled as a sequence of random variables, captures how the order book 'reservoir' at deeper levels refills the best bid/ask queues after depletion.

nodes.title: The Price Impact of Order Book Events

nodes.name: market depth dampening effect
nodes.description: The price impact coefficient (sensitivity of prices to order flow imbalance) is inversely proportional to the depth of the order book. Greater depth at the best bid/ask reduces the price movement caused by the same order flow imbalance, as more shares are available to absorb the imbalance.

nodes.name: volume aggregation artifact
nodes.description: The empirically observed square-root relationship between price changes and trading volume is not a fundamental causal mechanism but rather a statistical artifact arising from temporal aggregation of the linear order flow imbalance model. When data is aggregated over time, the linear OFI-price relationship produces an apparent nonlinear volume-price relationship.

nodes.title: TLOB: A Novel Transformer Model with Dual Attention for Price Trend Prediction with Limit Order Book Data

nodes.name: microstructure information leakage
nodes.description: Price trends are predictable from the spatial structure of the limit order book because order placement patterns, bid-ask imbalances, and queue depths reveal informed trading intent before execution. The dual attention mechanism exploits these microstructure signals to forecast price movements.

nodes.name: horizon-dependent predictability decay
nodes.description: Price predictability is stronger at shorter horizons and deteriorates as prediction horizon lengthens, reflecting market efficiency. The paper's novel labeling technique removes horizon bias to enable more reliable longer-horizon predictions before market efficiency erodes the signal.

nodes.title: Quantifying bid-ask spreads in the Chinese stock market using limit-order book data: Intraday pattern, probability distribution, long memory, and multifractal nature

nodes.name: market opening liquidity shock
nodes.description: Bid-ask spreads widen sharply at market open and reopen after lunch break due to order accumulation during non-trading periods and uncertainty resolution at session start, creating an L-shaped intraday pattern.

nodes.name: tick size constraint on spread distribution
nodes.description: The minimum tick size (0.01 RMB) acts as a lower bound, causing the empirical spread distribution to decay faster for small spreads and drop abruptly at large spreads compared to markets without such constraints, following an inverse cubic law only for time-averaged spreads.

nodes.title: Tick Size Reduction and Price Clustering in a FX Order Book

nodes.name: price clustering from manual trader inertia
nodes.description: Manual traders remain set to the old price resolution after tick decimalization, creating persistent clusters at round numbers (old tick multiples). These clusters act as price barriers where best quotes congregate, reducing the effective price resolution used in the market.

nodes.name: algorithmic priority-taking via tick-ahead placement
nodes.description: Automatic traders exploit price clusters created by manual traders by submitting limit orders one tick ahead of clusters (e.g., orders ending in 1 or 9), easily gaining price priority and capturing liquidity at clustered prices.

nodes.name: round number attraction in order placement
nodes.description: Traders exhibit a natural preference for placing orders and executing trades at round numbers (prices ending in 0 or 5), independent of information content. This creates volume accumulation at these prices that persists even in liquid, mature markets.

nodes.title: Market Impact in a Latent Order Book

nodes.name: liquidity consumption and order book depletion
nodes.description: Large trades consume available liquidity at the best prices, forcing subsequent execution at worse prices. The visible order book density decreases near the market price as orders are matched, creating mechanical price pressure.

nodes.name: price mean-reversion via latent order replenishment
nodes.description: After a large trade moves prices away from fundamental value, agents reassess their limit order placements and drift back toward the reference price. This mean-reverting behavior provides resistance to sustained price moves and limits long-term impact, with strength determined by the mean-reversion intensity parameter κ.

nodes.name: diffusion-driven order book replenishment
nodes.description: Random fluctuations in agent price estimates (modeled as drift-diffusion with volatility σ) cause orders to spread away from the current market price. This mechanical diffusion replenishes liquidity far from the mid-price and counteracts the concentrated depletion caused by large trades.

nodes.title: Price impact without order book: A study of the OTC credit index market

nodes.name: information diffusion delay
nodes.description: Price impact increases gradually over 5-10 trades as information about a trade diffuses through the decentralized OTC market without a central order book, causing the propagator G(ℓ) to rise steeply before saturating rather than decaying immediately.

nodes.name: permanent impact from latent liquidity
nodes.description: Because OTC credit trades are not heavily split (clients request full liquidity needs in single deals), order sign autocorrelation is short-ranged, forcing the propagator to converge to a non-zero constant, meaning most price impact is permanent rather than transient and reflects underlying latent supply/demand.

nodes.name: information leakage from dealer competition
nodes.description: Trades advertised to more dealers (on-SEF venues requiring ≥3 competing brokers) experience higher price impact than off-SEF trades, because increased competition for quotes causes information leakage about client intentions despite lower instantaneous bid-ask costs.

nodes.name: order splitting and herding during stress
nodes.description: During late 2015 and early 2016 market stress, order sign autocorrelation and price response both increased sharply, indicating either increased real order splitting by clients or herding behavior, causing subsequent trades to have full price impact as dealers adjust inventory.

nodes.title: An Optimal Execution Problem with Market Impact

nodes.name: convex market impact avoidance
nodes.description: When market impact is a convex function of execution speed, traders optimally choose gradual liquidation over block liquidation to minimize the total price impact cost. The convexity of the impact function creates an incentive to spread trades over time rather than execute immediately.

nodes.name: execution speed optimization
nodes.description: Traders dynamically choose their execution speed (instantaneous sales rate) to balance the competing costs of market impact (which increases with speed) and price uncertainty (which increases with time). The optimal strategy depends on the strength of market impact relative to price volatility.

nodes.name: strong impact prevents instantaneous liquidation
nodes.description: When market impact grows sufficiently fast with trade size (h(∞) = ∞), the cost of immediate liquidation becomes prohibitively large, forcing traders to adopt a no-trading policy in infinitesimal time and instead execute gradually. This creates a discontinuity in the value function at time origin.

nodes.title: The price impact of order book events: market orders, limit orders and cancellations

nodes.name: order flow impact on price
nodes.description: Buy and sell market orders impact prices in their direction of trade (buys push price up, sells push down) through a time-decaying propagator function that reflects the cumulative effect of past order flow on current prices.

nodes.name: history-dependent impact fluctuation
nodes.description: The price impact of orders is not stationary but depends on the state of the order book and past order flow; impact functions vary based on historical order flow patterns, particularly through gaps in the order book that create non-linear effects.

nodes.name: limit order and cancellation impact
nodes.description: Limit orders and cancellations at the best bid/ask have measurable price impacts similar in magnitude to market orders; adding a buy limit order creates upward pressure while cancelling it reduces pressure, revealing that unobserved order book events 'dress' the observed impact of market orders.

nodes.name: bid-ask spread dynamics from order flow
nodes.description: The bid-ask spread and gaps in the order book fluctuate endogenously in response to order flow patterns; these spread dynamics create history-dependent variations in impact that can be modeled through autoregressive relationships with past order flow.

nodes.title: Understanding the Impacts of Dark Pools on Price Discovery

nodes.name: information risk mitigation via venue selection
nodes.description: Informed traders with noisy/weak signals prefer dark pools because they offer better prices, reducing expected losses from wrong information. This sorting effect—strong signals to exchanges, moderate signals to dark pools, weak signals to non-trading—arises from the tradeoff between execution certainty and price improvement.

nodes.name: informed-uninformed ratio amplification
nodes.description: Dark pools' impact on price discovery depends on information precision: when precision is high, most informed traders go to exchanges (leaving dark pools with more uninformed traders), improving exchange price discovery; when precision is low, most informed traders go to dark pools, reducing the informed-to-uninformed ratio on exchanges and impairing price discovery.

nodes.name: dark pool information content inverted-U relationship
nodes.description: Dark pool trades' ability to forecast price movements follows an inverted-U shape with liquidity (exchange spread): assets with moderate liquidity show highest information content in dark pool trades, while most liquid and illiquid assets show lowest information content.

nodes.title: Limit-order book resiliency after effective market orders: Spread, depth and intensity

nodes.name: liquidity-driven order submission
nodes.description: Traders strategically time market order submission when spreads are tight, same-side depth is high, and opposite-side depth is low, indicating they exploit favorable liquidity conditions to minimize execution costs.

nodes.name: order-book resiliency asymmetry
nodes.description: The limit order book exhibits different speed and pattern of recovery (resiliency vs. continuation) depending on market order aggressiveness: aggressive orders (Type-1/7) trigger price resiliency, while less-aggressive orders (Type-3/9) trigger price continuation, with asymmetrical limit order replenishment between buy and sell sides.

nodes.name: depth-intensity feedback
nodes.description: The resiliency behavior of bid-ask spread and order book depth is mechanically linked to the intensity of incoming limit orders, which replenish the book after liquidity shocks at different rates depending on order type and initial spread width.

nodes.title: Models for the impact of all order book events

nodes.name: liquidity refill dampening
nodes.description: Aggressive market orders in one direction trigger a counterbalancing flow of limit orders that arrive subsequently, reducing the price impact of further orders in the same direction while increasing impact of orders in the opposite direction. This dynamic liquidity adjustment prevents prices from becoming predictable despite persistent order flow.

nodes.name: order flow sign autocorrelation
nodes.description: Trade signs exhibit long-range positive autocorrelation (power-law decay with exponent γ < 1), which must be offset by time-decaying price impact (power-law decay with exponent β) to maintain price efficiency and prevent predictable returns.

nodes.name: gap-dependent impact modulation
nodes.description: For small-tick stocks, the bid-ask spread and gaps behind best quotes fluctuate in response to past order flow. These gaps modulate the instantaneous price impact of subsequent price-changing events: wider gaps (reduced liquidity) increase impact magnitude, while narrower gaps decrease it.

nodes.name: event-type heterogeneous impact
nodes.description: Different order book event types (market orders, limit orders, cancellations) have distinct and measurable price impacts that decay at different rates. Price-changing events have immediate impacts while non-price-changing events affect prices indirectly through their influence on subsequent events.

nodes.title: Market Impact: A Systematic Study of Limit Orders

nodes.name: order size information leakage
nodes.description: Large metaorders contain less information per share than smaller ones, causing a concave (power-law) relationship between order size and price impact rather than linear. The gradual execution and information revelation during the metaorder lifecycle drives the temporary price movement.

nodes.name: permanent impact stabilization
nodes.description: After a metaorder completes execution, prices relax partially but stabilize at approximately two-thirds of the maximum temporary impact. This permanent shift reflects fair pricing: the market has incorporated the information from the executed order and reaches a new equilibrium.

nodes.name: aggressive limit order execution pressure
nodes.description: Aggressive limit orders that cross the bid-ask spread create immediate temporary price pressure in the direction of the trade. The execution price is constrained to the best available limit, creating a mechanical price impact during the execution window.

nodes.title: Trading activity and price impact in parallel markets: SETS vs. off-book market at the London Stock Exchange

nodes.name: inventory balancing across market segments
nodes.description: Market members actively balance their inventory positions between on-book and off-book markets, showing strong anticorrelation between inventory changes from electronic trades and dealership trades. This allows members to manage risk and liquidity across parallel venues.

nodes.name: volume-dependent price impact in dealership markets
nodes.description: Off-book transactions exhibit strong volume-dependent price impact that varies significantly with trade size, whereas on-book electronic trades show minimal volume dependence. Larger off-book trades incur disproportionately larger price impacts due to the bilateral negotiation structure.

nodes.name: order flow persistence in institutional off-book trading
nodes.description: Non-member order flow in the off-book market exhibits slowly decaying autocorrelation in order signs, suggesting institutional traders execute large positions through multiple sequential trades rather than single block trades, creating predictable order flow patterns.

nodes.title: Non-average price impact in order-driven markets

nodes.name: order clustering impact
nodes.description: Temporal clustering of child orders in a metaorder execution causes larger price impact than the same total order size distributed evenly in time, because clustered orders create stronger directional pressure on the limit order book.

nodes.name: order size impact
nodes.description: Larger individual child orders that consume multiple levels of the limit order book cause greater price impact than smaller orders that only consume the first level, reflecting the cost of accessing deeper liquidity.

nodes.name: queue imbalance price pressure
nodes.description: Imbalance in the volume of limit orders on bid versus ask sides of the order book predicts and mechanically causes mid-price movements, as the market clears the imbalanced side.

nodes.title: Slow decay of impact in equity markets

nodes.name: autocorrelated order flow masking impact decay
nodes.description: Large trades are sliced over multiple days due to execution optimization, creating positively autocorrelated order flow. This autocorrelation artificially inflates measured impact persistence because subsequent trades in the same direction compound the price effect, obscuring the true decay of individual meta-order impact.

nodes.name: information content realization in price
nodes.description: Trades initiated by predictive signals contain information about future price movements. This information gradually reveals itself over the signal's prediction horizon (10-100 days), creating an apparent price plateau that is distinct from mechanical impact decay and must be deconvolved separately.

nodes.name: transient mechanical impact with power-law decay
nodes.description: After deconvolving correlated trades and information content, the mechanical price impact of an isolated meta-order decays to zero following a power-law (τ^-0.8) over a 10-day horizon. This decay reflects the market's gradual absorption of the liquidity demand, with no permanent price component attributable to the trade itself.

nodes.title: Market Price of Trading Liquidity Risk and Market Depth

nodes.name: order-flow price impact
nodes.description: Dealers set execution prices that adjust linearly for current order flow (Kyle's lambda effect), charging higher prices when large buy orders suggest the HFT is exploiting positive information. This creates a direct mechanical link between order flow and price that persists even as inventory aversion reduces HFT positions.

nodes.name: stochastic volatility from order flow
nodes.description: The randomness and mean reversion in order flow dynamics causes observed price volatility to become stochastic and state-dependent. Order flow volatility directly modulates the variance of traded prices, making volatility endogenous to trading activity rather than exogenous.

nodes.name: market depth encapsulation of liquidity risk
nodes.description: Market depth (the quantity of limit orders available at various price levels) aggregates and reflects the underlying market price of liquidity risk. Deeper markets indicate lower compensation required for bearing liquidity risk, while shallow markets indicate higher liquidity risk premiums.

nodes.title: Universal price impact functions of individual trades in an order-driven market

nodes.name: order aggressiveness price impact differential
nodes.description: Partially filled limit orders that remain on the book after partial execution create larger price impacts than fully filled orders, because the unexecuted portion sets a new best bid/ask price that is more aggressive than the price level that would result from complete execution.

nodes.name: trade size power-law impact
nodes.description: For fully executed trades, price impact follows a power-law relationship with trade size (r ~ ω^α where α ≈ 2/3), reflecting that larger trades move prices more but with diminishing marginal impact due to order book depth.

nodes.name: small trade negative correlation anomaly
nodes.description: For very small trades, price impact decreases with increasing trade size (negative correlation), caused by a compositional shift: smaller trades have higher proportions of partially filled orders (which have large impacts) while larger small trades have higher proportions of fully filled orders (which have small impacts).

nodes.title: Market Dynamics vs. Statistics: Limit Order Book Example

nodes.name: execution rate driven price impact
nodes.description: High trading execution rates (dv/dt) directly drive price movements and volatility. Market participants sense elevated trading rates and immediately adjust quotes, making execution rate the primary 'driving force' of price dynamics rather than news or other events.

nodes.name: liquidity deficit signaling
nodes.description: Periods of liquidity deficit (low time-in-book on best price levels combined with high execution rates) signal predictable price movements and represent optimal entry conditions. Conversely, liquidity excess signals exit conditions when future direction becomes uncertain.

nodes.name: ambiguous volume at best level
nodes.description: Large order book volume at best bid/ask levels has dual and context-dependent effects: it can act as 'price support' (causing reversals) or as 'liquidity attractor' (causing trend continuation), making volume disbalance metrics unreliable without understanding the underlying execution rate regime.

nodes.title: The Homogenous Properties of Automated Market Makers

nodes.name: non-linear price impact from pool depletion
nodes.description: As traders execute larger trades relative to pool size, the marginal price they face increases non-linearly due to the curvature of the constant product function. This creates slippage where the effective execution price diverges increasingly from the marginal price at the start of the trade.

nodes.name: impermanent loss from volatility
nodes.description: When external market prices move away from the AMM pool price, arbitrageurs rebalance the pool to track the true price. Liquidity providers suffer losses proportional to the magnitude of price movement because they are forced to sell the appreciating asset and buy the depreciating asset at unfavorable ratios determined by the constant product formula.

nodes.name: impermanent loss from shallow market depth
nodes.description: Liquidity providers suffer greater losses when pool reserves are shallow because the same trade size represents a larger fraction of available liquidity, causing larger price movements and forcing arbitrageurs to execute larger rebalancing trades that increase the loss magnitude.

nodes.title: Price impact asymmetry of institutional trading in Chinese stock market

nodes.name: order book depth asymmetry
nodes.description: Institutional sales encounter shallower order book depth (fewer buy orders at various price levels) than institutional purchases, causing larger price impact for sales. The paper proposes a new variable measuring order book structure (volumes and gaps at different price levels) that partially explains this asymmetry.

nodes.name: market condition dependence of price impact asymmetry
nodes.description: Price impact asymmetry between purchases and sales depends on market trend: in bear markets (drawdown periods), sales have larger impact; in bull markets (drawup periods), purchases have larger impact. This reflects different liquidity provision and demand patterns across market regimes.

nodes.name: pre-trade price momentum
nodes.description: Prices exhibit systematic momentum before institutional transactions: positive returns precede institutional purchases (run-up effect), while negative returns precede institutional sales. This suggests institutional trades are correlated with existing price trends rather than purely exogenous.

nodes.name: post-trade price reversal
nodes.description: Immediately after institutional transactions execute, prices reverse sharply (negative returns after purchases, positive returns after sales), indicating temporary price impact that partially reverts. This temporary component is larger for sales in bear markets.

nodes.title: Adaptive Optimal Market Making Strategies with Inventory Liquidation Cos

nodes.name: stochastic demand slope effect on inventory adjustment
nodes.description: The variance and correlation structure of the demand slope (sensitivity of order fill to spread distance) causes market makers to adjust inventory positioning differently than under deterministic demand. Higher demand variance reduces the strength of inventory adjustment, while correlation between demand slope and reservation price increases optimal spreads.

nodes.name: adaptive order placement based on price forecasts
nodes.description: Market makers should adjust bid-ask spread placement proportionally to expected future price changes: reducing ask spread and increasing bid spread when expecting price declines. This allows incorporation of time-series or machine learning price forecasts into intraday market-making decisions.

nodes.name: market order arrival intensity adaptation
nodes.description: Market makers should adapt their placement strategy online to track the current intensity and imbalance of buy versus sell market order arrivals, rather than assuming fixed or deterministic arrival rates. Recent history of market order arrivals predicts near-term intensity levels and should inform quote placement.

nodes.name: inventory liquidation cost penalty
nodes.description: End-of-period inventory must be liquidated via market order at a cost proportional to inventory size (modeled as λI_T where λ is a penalization parameter). This creates incentive for market makers to manage inventory levels throughout the trading period to minimize terminal liquidation impact.

nodes.title: Market depth and price dynamics: A note

nodes.name: nonlinear price impact from market depth
nodes.description: Trading volume causes larger price movements when market depth is low and smaller movements when depth is high, creating a nonlinear relationship between order flow and price changes. This nonlinearity can generate predictable, endogenous price fluctuations even when underlying trader behavior is linear.

nodes.title: Looking into informal currency markets as Limit Order Books: impact of market makers

nodes.name: illiquidity-driven wide spreads
nodes.description: In informal markets with low trader confidence and poor price discovery, market participants quote at large distances from the mid-price, resulting in wide bid-ask spreads that reflect uncertainty about the reference price rather than tight competition.

nodes.name: low-confidence price quoting
nodes.description: Traders in informal markets lack access to reliable reference prices and continuous market information, causing them to quote at large distances from the best bid/ask prices as a risk management strategy, leading to exponentially distributed quote distances.

nodes.name: order execution scarcity from order-book mismatch
nodes.description: The majority of posted buy and sell intentions remain unfulfilled (averaging ~10% execution ratio) because the informal market's LOB structure fails to efficiently match buyer and seller intentions, reflecting fundamental illiquidity and lack of market depth.

nodes.name: market maker liquidity provision improves microstructure
nodes.description: Introducing an optimally-priced market maker using the Avellaneda-Stoikov framework reduces bid-ask spreads and improves market depth, demonstrating that liquidity provision can substantially enhance informal market quality and execution rates.

nodes.title: Market Dynamics: On Directional Information Derived From (Time, Execution Price, Shares Traded) Transaction Sequences

nodes.name: execution flow dynamic impact
nodes.description: Asset prices are more sensitive to execution flow (dV/dt) than to traded volume (V). High execution flow spikes drive price movements, while high volume alone does not produce price singularities.

nodes.name: liquidity deficit trading asymmetry
nodes.description: Low-to-high execution flow transitions reliably predict directional price movement ('follow the market'), while high-to-low transitions produce uncertain reversals ('little bounce'). This asymmetry creates exploitable directional bias by filtering out high-flow reversals.

nodes.name: scalp-price trend detection
nodes.description: Price moves occurring during high execution flow periods (scalp-price) indicate genuine trend changes, while moves during low execution flow are noise. Filtering price changes by execution flow intensity isolates directional signals from reversals.

nodes.title: Price dynamics in a Markovian limit order market

nodes.name: queue depletion duration effect
nodes.description: The time until the next price change depends on current queue depths at the best bid and ask. Larger queue sizes increase the duration until depletion, creating predictable waiting times conditional on order book state. Duration has heavy tails when order flow is balanced.

nodes.name: volatility from order arrival intensity
nodes.description: Price volatility in limit order markets increases with the ratio of order arrival intensity to market depth. When orders arrive frequently relative to available liquidity, price changes become larger and more volatile.

nodes.title: Limit Order Book (LOB) shape modeling in presence of heterogeneously informed market participants

nodes.name: adverse selection from informed traders
nodes.description: Market makers widen bid-ask spreads to protect against losses from trading with informed traders who have superior information about future price movements. The spread emerges as compensation for the negative expected returns of limit orders placed too close to the efficient price when facing informed order flow.

nodes.name: informed market maker speed advantage
nodes.description: When informed market makers can cancel and reposition orders faster than informed traders can execute, they reduce adverse selection losses and increase liquidity provision. The race between informed traders and informed market makers determines LOB shape and spread width, with faster market makers able to quote tighter spreads.

nodes.name: noise trader toxicity
nodes.description: Uninformed noise traders create adverse selection risk for liquidity providers even though they trade for non-informational reasons. Market makers must widen spreads and reduce depth to compensate for losses incurred when their orders are picked off by informed traders following noise trader activity.

nodes.title: Price fluctuations from the order book perspective - empirical facts and a simple model

nodes.name: order book imbalance pressure
nodes.description: A significant imbalance between the total volume of limit orders to buy versus sell near the best bid/ask prices causes a deterministic short-term price change in the direction predicted by supply and demand—excess buy orders push price up, excess sell orders push price down.

nodes.name: nonlinear price impact function
nodes.description: The virtual price impact of a hypothetical market order is a nonlinear (convex) function of order size, with impact scaling approximately as N^δ where δ ≈ 1.7-2.2, rather than the linear relationship often assumed in models.

nodes.name: order book depth heterogeneity
nodes.description: Limit order sizes decrease systematically as one moves away from the best bid/ask prices (level 1), with average order size declining across deeper levels of the order book, creating non-uniform liquidity provision.

nodes.title: Dynamics of Order Positions and Related Queues in a Limit Order Book

nodes.name: queue position decay from market order impact
nodes.description: An order's position in the limit order book queue decays as market orders execute against the queue and as cancellations remove orders ahead of it. The rate of position decay is proportional to the intensity of market order arrivals and the average size of market orders hitting that queue level.

nodes.name: queue length mean reversion
nodes.description: Best bid and ask queue lengths exhibit mean-reverting dynamics driven by the net flow of limit orders minus market orders and cancellations. The speed of mean reversion is proportional to the order arrival intensity and cancellation rate, with the mean-reverting level determined by the order book net flow.

nodes.name: execution time distribution from queue dynamics
nodes.description: The expected time for an order to execute depends jointly on its position in the queue and the queue length. Orders in longer queues have lower execution probability per unit time, but being in front of a long queue is more valuable than being in front of a short queue, creating a trade-off between position and queue depth.

nodes.title: Waiting time asymptotics in the single server queue with service in random order
Trade arrival dynamics and quote imbalance in a limit order book

nodes.name: quote imbalance predictability of price direction
nodes.description: Asymmetric order book depth (more shares on bid vs ask) predicts the direction of the next price movement. When bid queue exceeds ask queue, prices tend to move up, and vice versa, because imbalance reflects aggregate market intention and order flow pressure.

nodes.name: queue depletion and trade flow interaction
nodes.description: When one side of the limit order book is depleted by aggressive trades and cancellations, the opposite side follows to maintain the bid-ask spread. This mechanical interaction between queue depletion and incoming order flow creates predictable price movements that are smaller than the full spread.

nodes.name: adverse selection in passive fills
nodes.description: Traders posting passively at the near side experience adverse price slippage because aggressive traders on the opposite side possess information advantages. The expected price move to a passive fill is biased unfavorably (upward for bid-side posts, downward for ask-side posts) relative to the midpoint at posting time.

nodes.title: Queue Imbalance as a One-Tick-Ahead Price Predictor in a Limit Order Book

nodes.name: queue imbalance price predictability
nodes.description: Imbalances in the number of limit orders queued at bid vs. ask prices contain information about the direction of the next mid-price tick. Traders with access to this queue depth information can predict price movements better than a random walk model, suggesting that queue positioning reflects latent demand/supply pressure not yet fully reflected in the current price.

nodes.title: Deep Learning Meets Queue-Reactive: A Framework for Realistic Limit Order Book Simulation

nodes.name: queue-level order flow correlation
nodes.description: Price levels in the limit order book are not independent; orders at different queue depths exhibit correlated arrival patterns that create predictable dependencies. Exploiting these cross-queue correlations allows identification of profitable trading opportunities that single-queue models miss.

nodes.name: market impact nonlinearity
nodes.description: Market impact follows a square-root law rather than linear relationship with order size. This nonlinearity arises from the interaction between order sizes and queue dynamics, allowing traders to exploit the convex structure of execution costs.

nodes.name: order size distribution adaptation
nodes.description: The distribution of incoming order sizes varies with market conditions and queue states. By modeling this conditional distribution rather than assuming fixed order sizes, the model captures realistic microstructure properties that enable better prediction of execution impact and queue depletion.

nodes.title: Convergence of tandem Brownian queues
A stochastic partial differential equation model for limit order book dynamics

nodes.name: order flow imbalance price impact
nodes.description: Trade imbalance (the signed ratio of buy versus sell market order volume) exhibits a nonlinear S-shaped relationship with mid-price changes on the meso-scale. This nonlinearity can be linearized by incorporating limit order flows as a weighted component, suggesting that passive liquidity provision modulates the price impact of aggressive order flow.

nodes.name: order book depth dynamics
nodes.description: Market depth at the best bid and ask prices evolves stochastically through order submissions, cancellations, and replacements. The depth at the top of the book determines the price impact coefficient—shallower depth amplifies price moves from the same order flow imbalance.

nodes.name: high-frequency trader inventory management
nodes.description: High-frequency traders submit and cancel large volumes of limit orders near the mid-price under tight inventory constraints, creating multiplicative noise in order book dynamics. Their net contribution to volume is zero over longer intervals but fluctuates at high frequency, destabilizing the order book.

nodes.name: order replacement toward mid-price
nodes.description: Market participants systematically replace cancelled orders with new orders closer to the mid-price (convection flow), creating a directional drift in order density toward the spread. This conservative flow shifts volume across price levels without changing total depth.

nodes.title: The order book as a queueing system: average depth and influence of the size of limit orders

nodes.name: order cancellation probability depth effect
nodes.description: The depth of the order book at any price level is determined by the fraction of arriving limit orders that will be cancelled rather than executed. Higher cancellation rates at distant prices create deeper order books, establishing a conservation law between order flows and book shape.

nodes.name: limit order size impact on book depth
nodes.description: For a given total volume of incoming limit orders, submitting fewer but larger individual limit orders results in a deeper order book around the spread, compared to submitting many small orders with the same total volume. Order size distribution directly shapes the cumulative depth profile.

nodes.name: market order execution pressure on shape
nodes.description: The arrival rate of market orders (relative to cancellation and limit order arrival rates) compresses the order book shape and reduces the probability that distant limit orders will be executed rather than cancelled, flattening the tail of the book.

nodes.title: Diffusive Limit of Hawkes Driven Order Book Dynamics With Liquidity Migration

nodes.name: self-exciting order flow clustering
nodes.description: Market events (orders, trades) cluster in time due to self-exciting dynamics—past events increase the intensity of future events. This clustering creates predictable patterns of correlated activity that precede price movements, allowing traders to exploit the lag before these patterns are fully reflected in prices.

nodes.name: cross-excitation between order types
nodes.description: Buy orders can trigger sell orders and vice versa through multivariate Hawkes kernels. The intensity of one order type depends on the history of other order types, creating feedback loops in the order flow that drive LOB dynamics.

nodes.name: liquidity migration across price levels
nodes.description: Order book depth exhibits spatial propagation as volume reallocates between neighboring price levels, with migration intensities themselves governed by Hawkes excitation. This creates a discrete Laplacian smoothing effect where liquidity spreads across adjacent queues in response to order flow history.

nodes.title: A Multi Agent Model for the Limit Order Book Dynamics

nodes.name: volatility-driven order cancellation
nodes.description: Traders cancel outstanding limit orders more frequently during high-volatility periods due to increased execution risk and herding behavior. This self-reinforcing effect is driven by agents' strategic response to perceived market volatility.

nodes.name: market sentiment aggregation
nodes.description: Trading decisions and order flow direction are determined by a composite signal combining private information (agent-specific signals), public information (volatility and liquidity), and risk aversion. Stronger sentiment signals increase trading probability and directional conviction.

nodes.name: liquidity risk aversion
nodes.description: Agents reduce their willingness to submit orders when the limit order book is sparse, as sparse books increase execution risk and potential adverse price impact. This creates a feedback loop where low liquidity discourages participation.

nodes.name: bid-ask bounce
nodes.description: Negative autocorrelation in returns emerges mechanically from limit order book matching dynamics, where execution at best bid/ask prices creates mean-reverting price movements at short time scales.

nodes.title: Adversarial blockchain queues and trading on a CFMM

nodes.name: sandwich attack price impact
nodes.description: Rational block producers inject transactions before and after a user's order to extract MEV, causing the user to execute at an artificially worse price. The scheduler's ability to reorder transactions creates incentives for this attack, which can force arbitrarily bad execution prices.

nodes.name: mempool queue position uncertainty
nodes.description: Users cannot know at order submission time how many transactions will execute before theirs due to adversarial scheduling and message injection by block producers. This uncertainty about relative position in the execution queue directly impacts final execution price on a CFMM.

nodes.name: MEV extraction via state machine ordering
nodes.description: Block producers strategically order messages to maximize their own utility by observing transaction payloads and injecting their own messages. The dependence of execution outcomes on both the number and contents of prior transactions enables profitable extraction strategies.

nodes.title: The position profiles of order cancellations in an emerging stock market

nodes.name: non-execution risk avoidance
nodes.description: Traders cancel orders placed far from the best price to avoid the opportunity cost of non-execution when prices move away from their submission price. This drives higher cancellation rates for less aggressive orders placed deeper in the limit order book.

nodes.name: free option risk avoidance
