nodes.description: Traders cancel stale orders when news arrives that moves the intrinsic value away from current market price, preventing execution at unfavorable prices. This mechanism causes cancellations to increase when market conditions change rapidly.

nodes.name: impatient trader order revision
nodes.description: Impatient traders place aggressive orders near the best price to increase execution probability, but when immediate execution fails, they cancel and resubmit at more aggressive prices. This creates a concentration of cancellations at the front of the limit order book despite the counterintuitive expectation that orders deeper in the book should be cancelled more.

nodes.title: A non-linear model of limit order book dynamics

nodes.name: order queue depletion and migration
nodes.description: Unmatched orders at a price level either quit the market with probability pQ, migrate to an adjacent price level (pM) based on side direction, or remain; this creates a flow of orders across price levels that depends on the depth imbalance, generating non-linear dynamics in the order book shape.

nodes.name: arrival rate asymmetry
nodes.description: New buy orders arrive at the best ask (lowest price level) and new sell orders arrive at the best bid (highest price level) with potentially different Poisson rates (λ_b vs λ_s); asymmetry in these arrival rates drives persistent imbalances in equilibrium order book depth across price levels.

nodes.title: Modelling intensities of order flows in a limit order book

nodes.name: spread-driven market order submission
nodes.description: Market order intensity decreases with wider spreads because traders can gain priority by submitting limit orders just above/below the best quote rather than paying the spread with a market order. Conversely, narrow spreads force immediate execution via market orders.

nodes.name: liquidity depletion rush
nodes.description: When volume at the best quote (first level) is small, traders rush to execute market orders to grab the last available shares at the current price before the quote vanishes, increasing market order intensity.

nodes.name: volatility-driven order submission
nodes.description: During periods of high volatility (indicated by unusually wide spreads), traders submit more orders overall as uncertainty increases, maintaining elevated market order intensity even at wide spreads.

nodes.title: Time Consistent Dynamic Limit Order Books Calibrated on Options

nodes.name: liquidity risk premium in limit order books
nodes.description: Prices for larger quantities exhibit convex (non-linear) ask curves and concave bid curves, reflecting that market makers demand higher per-unit prices for larger orders due to inventory and execution risk. This convexity captures the cost of liquidity provision absent in linear pricing models.

nodes.name: volatility smile incompleteness
nodes.description: Observed option bid-ask prices violate constant-volatility models (e.g., Black-Scholes), revealing that the underlying asset dynamics are incomplete. The market's option prices contain information about true volatility structure that static models cannot capture, forcing dynamic pricing to be calibrated on observed option limit order books rather than assumed dynamics.

nodes.title: A Scaling Limit for Limit Order Books Driven by Hawkes Processes

nodes.name: order clustering and self-excitation
nodes.description: Order arrivals and cancellations exhibit clustering behavior through Hawkes processes, where past order events increase the intensity of future orders at the same or nearby price levels. This self-exciting dynamic amplifies order flow volatility and price movements.

nodes.name: cross-order-type feedback
nodes.description: Cancellations and limit order placements at one price level trigger intensity changes in market orders or limit orders at different price levels, creating spatial dependencies. This models phenomena like peg orders that follow price changes and parent-child market order splitting.

nodes.name: volatility clustering from order dependencies
nodes.description: Cross-dependencies between different order types (market orders, limit orders, cancellations) generate positive correlation in squared price increments, producing volatility clustering. Higher order arrival and cancellation intensities increase both price and volume volatility.

nodes.name: order imbalance state-dependence
nodes.description: The arrival intensity of market orders and limit orders depends on the current state of the order book, particularly the volume distribution and imbalance at different price levels. This creates feedback where order book imbalance drives subsequent order arrivals.

nodes.title: From Glosten-Milgrom to the whole limit order book and applications to financial regulation

nodes.name: adverse selection cost from informed trading
nodes.description: Market makers widen the bid-ask spread to protect themselves from informed traders who exploit superior information about future price jumps. Limit orders placed too close to the efficient price face negative expected returns when executed against informed orders, forcing market makers to quote wider spreads.

nodes.name: queue position time priority value
nodes.description: Under price-time priority rules, limit orders submitted earlier at the same price level gain execution advantage. This creates a quantifiable value differential between queue positions, with early positions more likely to execute before adverse price moves occur, compensating for the adverse selection risk.

nodes.name: volume imbalance predictive power
nodes.description: The discrete tick grid combined with strategic order placement by informed and noise traders creates a relationship between order flow imbalance and future price movements. Volume imbalance predicts the direction and magnitude of efficient price jumps because informed traders consume liquidity in the direction of known price jumps.

nodes.name: tick-size constraint on spread
nodes.description: The minimum tick size creates a floor on bid-ask spreads for large-tick assets, forcing spreads to remain at 1 tick minimum regardless of liquidity conditions. For small-tick assets, spreads scale inversely with relative tick-size as a power law, reflecting the granularity constraint's reduced binding effect.

nodes.title: Integer Sequences from Queueing Theory
Hydrodynamic limit of order book dynamics

nodes.name: order flow intensity driven shape evolution
nodes.description: The density profile of limit orders at each price level evolves deterministically according to the arrival rates and cancellation rates of orders at that distance from the market price. Higher arrival rates increase order density; higher cancellation rates decrease it.

nodes.name: tick size compression price stabilization
nodes.description: As tick size approaches zero and order arrival rates increase proportionally, the best bid and ask prices converge to a constant midpoint in the fluid limit. This reflects how continuous order flow in liquid markets eliminates discrete price jumps.

nodes.name: order cancellation rate dependent mean reversion
nodes.description: The exponential decay rate of order density at each price level is determined by the local cancellation rate function. Higher cancellation rates cause faster mean reversion of the order book shape toward its steady state.

nodes.title: High frequency market microstructure noise estimates and liquidity measures

nodes.name: bid-ask bounce noise
nodes.description: Transaction prices deviate from fundamental values due to the mechanical bid-ask spread and discrete price changes, creating microstructure noise that is uncorrelated with the efficient price process. This noise component dominates observed returns at very high frequencies.

nodes.name: liquidity-noise covariation
nodes.description: More liquid stocks exhibit lower microstructure noise and lower noise-to-signal ratios in high-frequency returns because they have tighter spreads, larger trade sizes, and faster price discovery. Liquidity characteristics (spreads, depth, trading volume) mechanically reduce the magnitude of frictions captured in the noise component.

nodes.name: common liquidity factor pricing
nodes.description: A market-wide common factor in stock-level high-frequency microstructure noise is priced in asset returns, such that stocks with higher covariance to aggregate liquidity noise earn a liquidity risk premium. This suggests investors demand compensation for exposure to systematic liquidity deterioration.

nodes.title: The microstructure of high frequency markets

nodes.name: superior information advantage of high-frequency traders
nodes.description: High-frequency traders possess a distinct form of superior information (different from traditional insider information) that allows them to identify and exploit mispricings in the limit order book before other market participants can react, generating systematic profits.

nodes.name: limit order book clearing friction
nodes.description: Market frictions arising from the mechanics of limit order book clearing create persistent mispricings and wealth transfers between traders. These frictions can cause wealth exchange measurements to be misrepresented by up to 50% if not properly accounted for.

nodes.name: delta-hedging friction cost
nodes.description: Trading frictions in the market alter the execution and profitability of delta-hedging strategies by increasing transaction costs and slippage relative to the frictionless Black-Scholes model predictions.

nodes.title: A High Frequency Trade Execution Model for Supervised Learning

nodes.name: adverse price selection from order book depletion
nodes.description: Market makers suffer losses when large market orders consume entire price levels, causing sudden mid-price movements (price-flips) that leave the maker's resting orders stranded at stale prices. The maker is forced to unwind at worse prices than anticipated.

nodes.name: predictive price-flip detection
nodes.description: Limit order book depth and market order flow contain predictive information about imminent mid-price movements. By forecasting price-flips before they occur, market makers can preemptively adjust quotes to avoid adverse selection and capture additional spread.

nodes.name: order imbalance informativeness
nodes.description: Imbalances between demand and supply in the limit order book exhibit statistically significant relationships to short-term future returns, providing exploitable predictive signal for price direction beyond the inside market alone.

nodes.title: Optimal High Frequency Trading in a Pro-Rata Microstructure with Predictive Information

nodes.name: inventory risk premium
nodes.description: Market-makers widen spreads and adjust quote placement asymmetrically to compensate for the risk of holding unbalanced inventory positions. The inventory-risk-aversion parameter penalizes non-zero end-of-day positions, forcing market-makers to demand higher compensation (wider spreads or better execution prices) when inventory becomes imbalanced.

nodes.name: partial execution uncertainty
nodes.description: In pro-rata microstructures, limit order execution volumes are random and uncontrollable by the trader. This forces market makers to oversize their orders to achieve desired execution, creating inventory risk that cannot be precisely managed.

nodes.name: bid-ask spread capture
nodes.description: Market makers profit by executing limit orders at the bid-ask spread (δ/2 on each side). This spread capture is the primary source of market-making revenue and incentivizes continuous quoting despite inventory costs.

nodes.name: predictive information advantage
nodes.description: When a trader has superior information about future price direction (trend or momentum), they can adjust their limit order placement and market order timing to exploit this directional edge while managing inventory risk more efficiently.

nodes.title: Fill-Side Non-Retail Trading on Polymarket: An Empirical Study of Behavioral Tiers and Microstructure Signatures Under Quote-Attribution Constraints

nodes.name: market maker adverse selection from informed flow
nodes.description: Market makers on prediction markets face informed traders with informational advantage; the cost of providing liquidity is the informed-flow rents extracted by detectable trading patterns. Market makers must reprice aggressively in response to directional retail flow to protect against adverse selection losses.

nodes.name: volatility-driven market maker repricing
nodes.description: Market-maker repricing dynamics dominate the volatility signal that triggers margin reactions and liquidations. Market makers reprice in response to their own volatility assessments rather than purely in response to directional retail order flow, creating a feedback loop where repricing itself generates volatility.

nodes.name: boundary depth asymmetry in bounded-underlying markets
nodes.description: On binary event contracts with known terminal outcomes, market makers post quotes far from the prevailing mid price and concentrate depth at the boundaries rather than near mid, because the terminal collapse to {0,1} creates asymmetric payoff structure and inventory-adverse-selection trade-offs that differ qualitatively from continuous-underlying markets.

nodes.name: structurally absent near-mid liquidity
nodes.description: Binary event contracts exhibit persistent structural absence of liquidity near the mid price throughout the market lifecycle, a property of the supply side reflecting where non-retail participants choose to post limit orders and how those quotes evolve in response to bounded-underlying payoff structure.

nodes.title: The Anatomy of a Decentralized Prediction Market: Microstructure Evidence from the Polymarket Order Book

nodes.name: longshot spread premium
nodes.description: Market makers widen spreads on low-probability outcomes (longshots) relative to high-probability outcomes, reflecting either higher inventory risk, lower liquidity demand, or behavioral bias in pricing. This creates an asymmetric spread structure where the low-probability side trades at substantially wider quoted spreads than the high-probability side.

nodes.name: trade direction inference noise
nodes.description: The public order-book feed's change_side field marks which side of the book moved, not which side initiated the trade, making it impossible to reliably infer aggressor direction from feed data alone. This measurement error (∼59% accuracy vs. 81% on equity venues) causes direction-dependent microstructure measures like effective spread and Kyle's λ to flip sign on 60–67% of markets, rendering them unreliable without on-chain ground truth.

nodes.name: depth concentration by market fundamentals
nodes.description: Cross-sectional variation in limit-order-book depth is explained by market duration, price level, and trading volume, with no residual time-to-resolution effect. Markets with longer duration, mid-prices closer to 0.5, and higher volume attract deeper liquidity, suggesting that depth responds to fundamental market characteristics rather than temporal proximity to resolution.

nodes.name: self-counterparty wash trading
nodes.description: A non-trivial fraction of trades involve the same wallet on both sides of the transaction (median 1%, tail up to 22%), indicating either self-dealing, inventory management, or artificial volume creation. This is substantially lower than unregulated crypto token exchanges (25–70%) but higher than regulated equity markets (≈0%), reflecting Polymarket's intermediate regulatory environment and different wash-trading incentives.

nodes.title: High-Frequency Jump Tests: Which Test Should We Use?

nodes.name: jump detection alpha generation
nodes.description: Accurate identification of genuine price jumps amid noise and volatility allows traders to detect mispriced assets and exploit short-term market inefficiencies before prices revert.

nodes.name: microstructure noise filtering
nodes.description: Distinguishing true price jumps from microstructure noise requires robust test selection; failure to filter noise correctly leads to false jump detection and trading losses.

nodes.title: Short-term equity dynamics and endogenous market fluctuations

nodes.name: endogenous bifurcation-driven uncertainty
nodes.description: Phase-space bifurcations in the coupled price-volume dynamics create path-dependent sensitivity to small perturbations, generating endogenous randomness in price and volume determination that is independent of exogenous shocks. The system exhibits multiple equilibrium paths at critical points, making it impossible to uniquely determine price given volume or vice versa.

nodes.name: specialist inventory management constraint
nodes.description: NYSE specialists face a control problem balancing price regularity (minimizing bid-ask spread and price volatility) against profit maximization (proportional to volume) while minimizing interference with autonomous market evolution. This creates a tension between stabilizing prices and allowing natural market dynamics, generating suboptimal price paths.

nodes.name: price-volume coupling through supply-demand asymmetry
nodes.description: Supply shocks and demand shocks have asymmetric effects on price and volume due to second-order convexity conditions in the market microstructure. The coupling parameter β₁ determines whether supply or demand shocks produce larger price impacts relative to volume impacts, creating systematic co-movement patterns.

nodes.title: Neural Hidden Markov Model with Adaptive Granularity Attention for High-Frequency Order Flow Modeling

nodes.name: multi-scale order flow microstructure signal
nodes.description: Fine-grained tick-level order flow patterns (captured via dilated convolutions) contain predictive information about short-term price movements that coarse-grained models miss. Integration of these microstructure signals with liquidity trends enables more accurate forecasting of price dynamics.

nodes.name: adaptive regime-dependent liquidity shock prediction
nodes.description: Market regimes (latent states inferred by the Neural HMM) modulate the relationship between order flow and liquidity shocks. The model dynamically adjusts its temporal focus based on local volatility and transaction intensity, allowing it to predict liquidity disruptions more accurately during volatile periods when regime shifts are more frequent.

nodes.name: volatility-conditioned attention reallocation
nodes.description: The gating mechanism conditions on local volatility to dynamically reweight fine-grained versus coarse-grained temporal representations. During high-volatility regimes, the model shifts focus toward microstructure signals; during calm periods, it relies more on low-frequency liquidity trends. This adaptive allocation improves prediction accuracy across market conditions.

nodes.title: The Price of BitCoin: GARCH Evidence from High Frequency Data

nodes.name: transaction demand pressure on price
nodes.description: Bitcoin price increases with the size of the economy (transaction volume) because higher transaction demand requires more Bitcoin to be held as a medium of exchange, pushing prices up according to the money supply-demand equilibrium.

nodes.name: speculative demand pressure on price
nodes.description: Bitcoin price decreases when interest rates rise because investors shift from Bitcoin (store of value) to higher-yielding financial assets to avoid capital losses, reducing speculative demand for Bitcoin.

nodes.name: velocity pressure on price
nodes.description: Bitcoin price decreases with higher velocity of circulation because faster turnover of the same Bitcoin stock means less total Bitcoin needs to be held to facilitate the same transaction volume, reducing equilibrium price.

nodes.name: volatility clustering in immature markets
nodes.description: Bitcoin exhibits persistent volatility clustering where large price movements are followed by large movements and small by small, indicating an immature market with extreme price swings driven by conditional heteroscedasticity rather than fundamental shocks.

nodes.title: Sex and age determination in European lobsters using AI-Enhanced bioacoustics
Lobster: A GPU-Accelerated Framework for Neurosymbolic Programming
Model-Free Approaches to Discern Non-Stationary Microstructure Noise and Time-Varying Liquidity in High-Frequency Data

nodes.name: non-stationary microstructure noise distortion
nodes.description: Microstructure noise properties change over time in ways that standard volatility estimators assume away, causing them to misprice assets. Traders can exploit these mispricings by detecting when noise becomes non-stationary and adjusting their volatility estimates accordingly.

nodes.name: time-varying liquidity risk adjustment
nodes.description: Liquidity conditions vary systematically over time in ways measurable from high-frequency data. Traders who detect periods of elevated or depressed liquidity can adjust their position sizing and execution strategies to improve risk-adjusted returns.

nodes.title: The microstructural foundations of leverage effect and rough volatility

nodes.name: bid-ask liquidity asymmetry
nodes.description: Asymmetric liquidity between bid and ask sides of the order book (e.g., market makers adjust prices less after buy orders than sell orders due to inventory effects) generates negative correlation between price returns and volatility at longer timescales, producing leverage effect.

nodes.name: market endogeneity
nodes.description: High-frequency markets are dominated by endogenous algorithmic orders that react to other orders rather than exogenous economic signals. This self-exciting behavior (nearly unstable Hawkes process) is necessary to generate non-degenerate stochastic volatility at macroscopic scales.

nodes.name: metaorder fragmentation roughness
nodes.description: Large orders (metaorders) are split and executed over time by trading algorithms with heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions. This temporal fragmentation pattern induces rough (non-smooth) volatility dynamics with Hurst exponent around 0.1 at the macroscopic level.

nodes.title: Explainable Patterns in Cryptocurrency Microstructure

nodes.name: spread-driven adverse selection
nodes.description: Wider bid-ask spreads signal higher adverse selection risk, where informed traders are more likely to be present; this increases the cost of liquidity provision and predicts short-term returns as the market reprices for information asymmetry.

nodes.name: flash crash liquidity evaporation
nodes.description: During systemic market disruptions, algorithmic liquidity provision collapses asymmetrically: maker strategies suffer adverse selection losses while taker strategies benefit from capturing informed flow, revealing the fragility of microstructure-based strategies under stress.

nodes.title: A simple microstructure return model explaining microstructure noise and Epps effects

nodes.name: bid-ask bounce negative autocorrelation
nodes.description: Successive trades alternate between buy and sell sides with quasi-periodic structure, creating negative correlation between consecutive tick-by-tick returns. This sign-alternating pattern is the mechanical source of microstructure noise—the observed decrease in volatility estimates at higher frequencies.

nodes.name: long-memory price momentum
nodes.description: Tick-by-tick returns follow an ARFIMA process with fractional differencing, creating long-range correlations in absolute returns (volatility clustering) while short-range correlations in raw returns are suppressed by the bid-ask bounce. This long memory reflects genuine momentum in buy/sell pressure across time.

nodes.name: asynchronous cross-asset momentum overlap
nodes.description: When two assets have genuine correlated buy/sell pressure, their momentum is not perfectly synchronized due to trading delays and herding effects. At high frequencies, this asynchrony reduces measured cross-correlations; at lower frequencies, the long-memory process allows momentum to overlap more completely, increasing observed correlations.

nodes.name: non-Poissonian trade clustering
nodes.description: Inter-trade intervals follow non-exponential distributions (Weibull or generalized gamma) with clustering at short timescales and heavy tails, rather than Poisson arrivals. This clustering structure modulates how microstructure noise and cross-asset correlations manifest across different observation frequencies.

nodes.title: Solving the Equity Risk Premium Puzzle and Inching Towards a Theory of Everything

nodes.name: rare disaster risk premium
nodes.description: Investors demand a large equity premium because of low-probability, high-impact consumption crashes (disasters, market crashes, depressions). Equity returns fall sharply in these rare states, creating tail risk that standard models miss.

nodes.name: habit-driven time-varying risk aversion
nodes.description: Risk aversion fluctuates endogenously with consumption relative to habit levels. When consumption falls toward habit, investors become highly risk-averse and demand higher equity premiums; precautionary saving offsets borrowing pressure to keep interest rates stable.

nodes.name: long-run consumption uncertainty premium
nodes.description: Equity premium arises from time-varying economic uncertainty in long-run consumption growth. A small persistent predictable component in consumption and dividend growth, combined with fluctuating volatility, generates substantial risk compensation even with moderate risk aversion.

nodes.title: Estimation for high-frequency data under parametric market microstructure noise

nodes.name: bid-ask spread microstructure noise
nodes.description: Observed prices deviate from efficient prices due to the bid-ask spread and trade direction effects. The parametric noise function φ(Q_ti, θ_0) captures this deviation as a function of observable limit order book information (trade direction, volume, quoted spread), allowing estimation of the efficient price by removing this mechanical friction.

nodes.name: order flow imbalance noise
nodes.description: The microstructure noise in observed prices is driven by order flow imbalance and other limit order book state variables (quoted depth, duration between trades). These observable quantities can be used to parametrically model and remove the noise component, improving estimation of the true efficient price and volatility.

nodes.title: Modeling Price Clustering in High-Frequency Prices

nodes.name: trader type heterogeneity in tick size preferences
nodes.description: Different trader populations preferentially trade in different multiples of the tick size (cents, nickels, dimes), creating clustering at those price levels. This heterogeneity in trading conventions directly generates the observed non-uniform distribution of prices across tick multiples.

nodes.name: instantaneous volatility suppression of clustering
nodes.description: High instantaneous volatility reduces price clustering at ultra-high frequency by causing traders to deviate from their preferred tick multiples, whereas daily realized volatility increases clustering. The aggregation level determines whether volatility reinforces or weakens clustering behavior.

nodes.name: volume-driven clustering intensification
nodes.description: Higher trading volume increases the proportion of traders using round-number tick multiples, intensifying price clustering. Volume acts as a proxy for the prevalence of agents with tick-size preferences.

nodes.title: Data-Driven Multiscale Design of Cellular Composites with Multiclass Microstructures for Natural Frequency Maximization
A Deterministic Limit Order Book Simulator with Hawkes-Driven Order Flow

nodes.name: self-exciting order clustering
nodes.description: Past trade events increase the intensity of future trade events through a time-varying triggering kernel, creating predictable clustering patterns that can be exploited for alpha generation. The nonparametric estimation captures complex temporal dependencies missed by constant-kernel models.

nodes.name: long-memory order flow persistence
nodes.description: Order flow exhibits slow-decaying autocorrelation through power-law excitation kernels rather than exponential decay. This long memory arises from the heavy-tailed nature of the kernel, causing past events to influence future intensities over extended horizons.

nodes.title: TradeFM: A Generative Foundation Model for Trade-flow and Market Microstructure

nodes.name: order flow self-excitation
nodes.description: Past order arrivals increase the intensity of future orders of the same or related types through Hawkes self- and cross-excitation, creating clustering in order flow timing.

nodes.name: price formation from partial order flow
nodes.description: Market prices form efficiently from incomplete information—individual participants observing only their own trade stream can collectively discover true valuations through order flow dynamics. Universal price formation principles apply across heterogeneous assets without asset-specific calibration.

nodes.name: heavy-tailed order size distribution
nodes.description: Order volumes follow power-law distributions with extreme values far more frequent than Gaussian assumptions predict. This heavy-tailedness in order flow directly generates heavy-tailed returns through the aggregation of heterogeneous trade sizes.

nodes.title: PEARL: Private Equity Accessibility Reimagined with Liquidity

nodes.name: sale timing and valuation discretion
nodes.description: Private equity funds generate superior risk-adjusted returns by timing the sale of portfolio companies to avoid downturns and by employing discretionary valuation practices that smooth reported returns, particularly by dampening negative return periods.

nodes.name: management incentive alignment
nodes.description: PE funds create value by aligning management compensation with long-term performance through illiquid equity stakes, reducing short-term manipulation and encouraging sustained operational improvements.

nodes.name: operational improvement capture
nodes.description: PE funds systematically improve portfolio company cash flows and operational efficiency through sector-specific expertise and cost-cutting measures, generating alpha that is difficult to replicate with public market instruments alone.

nodes.name: leverage-enhanced returns with financial discipline
nodes.description: PE funds use optimized capital structures and debt leverage to enhance returns through tax shields and enforce financial discipline, though excessive leverage increases distress risk and reduces fund performance.

nodes.title: Uncertainty relations in models of market microstructure

nodes.name: price-volume uncertainty constraint exploitation
nodes.description: Price and trading volume are subject to a lower bound uncertainty relation in market microstructure; traders can exploit violations of this constraint to anticipate price movements, as the market has not yet adjusted to the underlying dynamics implied by volume fluctuations.

nodes.title: Understanding jumps in high frequency digital asset markets

nodes.name: event-driven jump clustering
nodes.description: Black swan events (regulatory announcements, influential tweets, market crashes, halving events) trigger concentrated price jumps that cluster in time and propagate across correlated cryptocurrencies. These jumps are not randomly distributed but concentrated around periods of high investor attention and notable incidents.

nodes.name: intraday jump momentum persistence
nodes.description: High-frequency intraday jumps significantly influence and predict the direction and magnitude of end-of-day returns on the same trading day. Positive intraday jumps are followed by positive end-of-day returns and vice versa, indicating that jump information is not fully incorporated into prices within the same day.

nodes.name: microstructure noise confounding in crypto markets
nodes.description: Cryptocurrency market microstructure differs fundamentally from traditional assets, causing standard high-frequency jump detection methods (developed for equities) to produce less accurate results. The specific noise characteristics of crypto exchanges require new econometric approaches for reliable jump identification.

nodes.name: intraday seasonality in jump frequency
nodes.description: Jump occurrence exhibits strong intraday and weekly seasonality patterns, with more jumps during mid-week trading hours (1pm-5pm UTC) and sharp drops during off-peak hours (1am-6am UTC). This seasonality mirrors volatility and volume seasonality, suggesting a common underlying driver related to trading activity concentration.

nodes.title: Inference on the intraday spot volatility from high-frequency order prices with irregular microstructure noise

nodes.name: bid-ask bounce microstructure noise
nodes.description: Observed limit order prices oscillate around an unobservable efficient price due to the bid-ask spread structure. Ask prices lie above the efficient price and bid prices below it, creating one-sided (lower-bounded) additive noise that must be disentangled from true price dynamics for accurate volatility estimation.

nodes.name: order book boundary estimation via local extrema
nodes.description: Local minima of observed ask prices reveal information about the underlying efficient price process because the noise has a lower bound. By tracking block-wise minima, one can extract the latent semimartingale boundary and estimate spot volatility at faster rates than under symmetric microstructure noise.

nodes.title: Interpretable Hypothesis-Driven Trading:A Rigorous Walk-Forward Validation Framework for Market Microstructure Signals

nodes.name: volume imbalance directional pressure
nodes.description: Buy-side volume imbalance relative to sell-side volume creates directional price pressure, with elevated imbalances signaling informed accumulation that predicts near-term returns.

nodes.name: order flow toxicity detection
nodes.description: High-frequency order flow toxicity (measured via volume-synchronized probability of informed trading adapted to daily data) predicts volatility spikes and adverse price moves, requiring elevated trading activity to generate reliable signals.

nodes.name: regime-dependent microstructure signal decay
nodes.description: Daily OHLCV-based microstructure signals function effectively only during high-volatility regimes with elevated information arrival; signals deteriorate or reverse during stable, low-volatility periods due to reduced information content and trading activity.

nodes.title: Isotropic Correlation Models for the Cross-Section of Equity Returns

nodes.name: non-diversifiable idiosyncratic risk premium
nodes.description: Under isotropic correlation structure, idiosyncratic risk cannot be fully eliminated through diversification even in large portfolios, creating a persistent risk premium that compensates investors for holding residual risk. This contradicts CAPM/APT assumptions and implies stock-picking generates non-zero returns.

nodes.name: limited effective degrees of freedom in large portfolios
nodes.description: When asset returns follow an isotropic correlation structure with typical pairwise correlations (~20%), the effective sample size of a portfolio converges to 1/ρ regardless of actual portfolio size, preventing asymptotic normality and limiting diversification benefits.

nodes.name: common market factor with residual spread-trade structure
nodes.description: The eigendecomposition of isotropic covariance reveals one dominant market factor (equal-weighted portfolio returns) and N-1 degenerate eigenvalues representing arbitrary spread trades, suggesting a single meaningful systematic risk source with substantial orthogonal idiosyncratic variation.

nodes.title: Networks of News and Cross-Sectional Returns

nodes.name: news-driven comovement
nodes.description: Stocks linked through news articles exhibit correlated returns because news about one firm creates attention spillovers and information diffusion to connected firms, particularly within the same sector.

nodes.name: news-attention-driven reversal
nodes.description: Lead stocks mentioned in news articles experience temporary price movements that reverse predictably in follower stocks one day ahead, as market participants gradually incorporate cross-firm news linkages and correct initial mispricings.

nodes.name: network-degree attention proxy
nodes.description: Stocks with higher news network degree (more frequent mentions in articles linking to other firms) receive disproportionate attention, creating predictable cross-sectional return patterns as investors gradually process the attention signal.

nodes.title: When Alpha Breaks: Two-Level Uncertainty for Safe Deployment of Cross-Sectional Stock Rankers

nodes.name: rank displacement under score extremity
nodes.description: Rank displacement (prediction error in ranking) is mechanically larger at extreme score percentiles because there is more 'room to move' in the ranking order. This creates a structural coupling where the learned error predictor internalizes this geometry, causing epistemic uncertainty to correlate with signal magnitude (median ρ = 0.616).

nodes.name: inverse-uncertainty sizing failure in ranking
nodes.description: Standard inverse-uncertainty weighting (reducing exposure proportionally to predicted error) systematically de-levers the strongest signals in cross-sectional ranking because uncertainty is structurally coupled to score magnitude. This causes continuous multiplicative sizing to reduce portfolio performance even when uncertainty estimates correctly rank stock-level failure risk.

nodes.name: model-specific regime failure under thematic shifts
nodes.description: Non-stationarity from thematic market rotations (e.g., AI sector rally in 2024) can break a historically profitable ranker's signal at longer horizons while weakening shorter-horizon performance, even when market stress proxies (VIX) show no extreme stress. Model failure is decoupled from market regime observables and requires direct monitoring of realized model efficacy.

nodes.name: tail-risk concentration in epistemic uncertainty
nodes.description: Stock-level epistemic uncertainty (predicted rank displacement error) is concentrated in the extreme tail of the distribution (P85+), allowing a discrete cap on only the most uncertain positions to provide robust risk control without penalizing the bulk of the portfolio or the score tails where strongest signals reside.

nodes.title: Quantum Temporal Convolutional Neural Networks for Cross-Sectional Equity Return Prediction: A Comparative Benchmark Study
Dissecting the explanatory power of ESG features on equity returns by sector, capitalization, and year with interpretable machine learning

nodes.name: ESG controversy signal on idiosyncratic returns
nodes.description: Companies with higher ESG controversy scores exhibit different idiosyncratic return patterns (returns not explained by market, size, and value factors). Controversy encoding appears to be the most material ESG feature for explaining return sign.

nodes.name: Market capitalization-dependent ESG valuation effect
nodes.description: The relationship between ESG scores and returns reverses by firm size: better ESG scores associate with higher returns for large-cap firms but lower returns for small-cap firms, suggesting differential investor demand or risk pricing by capitalization segment.

nodes.name: Temporal decay of ESG information content
nodes.description: The predictive and explanatory power of ESG features on returns diminishes over time as investor awareness increases and ESG information becomes incorporated into prices, consistent with efficient market hypothesis.

nodes.title: Spatio-Temporal Momentum: Jointly Learning Time-Series and Cross-Sectional Strategies

nodes.name: cross-sectional relative momentum ranking
nodes.description: Assets ranked by recent returns exhibit predictable relative performance; long positions in top-ranked assets and short positions in bottom-ranked assets capture a momentum premium. The paper argues that discrete decile allocation leaves intermediate-ranked assets unexploited.

nodes.name: time-series trend persistence
nodes.description: Individual assets exhibit continuation in the direction of returns over time; trading on the sign of past 12-month returns or trend indicators (MACD) captures a momentum risk premium by riding existing trends.

nodes.name: multi-asset momentum signal correlation
nodes.description: Momentum features across multiple assets in a portfolio contain shared predictive information about individual asset returns; jointly learning signals from the cross-sectional universe improves trend estimation and position sizing beyond single-asset momentum models.

nodes.title: Discovery of a 13-Sharpe OOS Factor: Drift Regimes Unlock Hidden Cross-Sectional Predictability

nodes.name: drift regime liquidity improvement
nodes.description: During periods when individual stocks exhibit sustained upward price drift (>60% positive days in 63-day windows), market microstructure improves with wider depth, tighter spreads, and higher volume. This reduces transaction costs and improves price discovery for cross-sectional signals, making value and reversal strategies more effective.

nodes.name: behavioral bias amplification in drift regimes
nodes.description: Sustained upward drift triggers confirmation bias, anchoring, and herding behavior that cause investors to overweight recent price trends and fundamentals, creating predictable cross-sectional mispricings between stocks with different appreciation rates within the same drift regime.

nodes.name: short-term reversal in cross-section
nodes.description: Recent losers outperform recent winners over short horizons (10-day reversal signal), generating exploitable returns when applied selectively during drift regimes where cross-sectional valuation dispersions widen.

nodes.name: value signal activation in drift regimes
nodes.description: Price-based value signals (inverse price ranks) become significantly more predictive when applied exclusively during drift regimes, where momentum traders and trend followers provide liquidity that allows value-based positions to be sized larger without excessive market impact.

nodes.title: Time Varying Risk in U.S. Housing Sector and Real Estate Investment Trusts Equity Return

nodes.name: housing risk premium
nodes.description: Unexpected changes in housing sector volatility represent a systematic risk factor that is not fully priced into REIT equity markets. Investors demand a risk premium for exposure to time-varying housing risk, consistent with the ICAPM framework where state variables predict expected returns.

nodes.name: volatility-driven state variable mispricing
nodes.description: The first principal component of housing variable volatilities captures aggregate housing risk that the market underprices or fails to fully incorporate into REIT valuations. This mispricing generates alpha because conditional volatility dynamics are not adequately reflected in current asset prices.

nodes.title: Weak Convergence of Equity Derivatives Pricing with Default Risk

nodes.name: default risk mispricing in derivatives
nodes.description: Traditional derivatives pricing models omit default risk, causing systematic mispricings. A model incorporating default intensity dependent on equity value can exploit these mispricings by correctly pricing derivatives when default risk is material, generating alpha through more accurate risk-adjusted valuations.

nodes.title: Pricing of debt and equity in a financial network with comonotonic endowments

nodes.name: financial contagion through interconnected debt claims
nodes.description: Default of one firm triggers cascading failures in other firms through direct debt obligations in the financial network, causing correlated asset value deterioration across interconnected institutions.

nodes.name: endogenous recovery rate determination
nodes.description: The recovery rate on debt claims is endogenously determined by the clearing mechanism in the network rather than exogenously fixed, causing debt valuations to depend on the realized default states of all counterparties.

nodes.name: bankruptcy cost amplification of systemic risk
nodes.description: When defaulting firms incur bankruptcy costs (recovery rates α_x, α_L < 1), asset losses are magnified during defaults, increasing the severity of contagion and reducing recovery values across the network.

nodes.name: comonotonic endowment coordination
nodes.description: Banks' endowments move together (comonotonically) due to shared exposures and portfolio optimization, creating systematic correlation in asset performance that amplifies systemic risk relative to idiosyncratic shocks.

nodes.title: Cyber risk and the cross-section of stock returns

nodes.name: cyber risk premium
nodes.description: Investors demand a risk premium for holding stocks of firms exposed to cyber threats, as cyber risk represents a systematic source of firm value destruction that is not captured by traditional risk factors. This latent cyber risk, extracted from disclosure semantics, is priced into cross-sectional stock returns.

nodes.name: cyber risk disclosure underpricing
nodes.description: Markets initially underprice or misprice cyber risk when it is disclosed in financial filings because dictionary-based methods and limited disclosure sections fail to capture the full semantic context of cyber threats. Machine learning methods that extract richer semantic information reveal pricing inefficiencies.

nodes.name: post-cyberattack recovery effect
nodes.description: Stock prices may recover after realized cyberattacks due to reputation shocks and operational disruptions being temporary, but this recovery effect is distinct from and should not be conflated with latent cyber risk exposure that drives systematic return differences across firms.

nodes.title: Fairness, Welfare, and Equity in Personalized Pricing
Labor Income Risk and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns

nodes.name: labor income risk from sectoral shifts
nodes.description: Stocks with high sensitivity to cross-industry dispersion (CID) offer lower expected returns because they hedge against labor income risk. When CID is high, sectoral reallocation accelerates, creating permanent job losses in underperforming industries with industry-specific, high-skill workers who cannot easily transition. Investors demand lower returns on stocks that co-move positively with CID because these stocks provide a hedge against this uninsurable labor income shock.

nodes.name: structural uncertainty pricing
nodes.description: High cross-industry dispersion reflects periods of accelerated economic transformation and structural uncertainty. CID peaks during sectoral reallocation episodes (dotcom boom/bust, financial crisis, COVID-19) and predicts long-term unemployment growth, indicating it captures genuine structural shifts rather than cyclical demand shocks. This structural uncertainty is priced into the cross-section of returns.

nodes.name: industry-specific human capital concentration
nodes.description: High-skill occupations (e.g., aerospace engineers) are confined to few industries with low cross-industry labor mobility. When an industry underperforms severely (high CID), workers with industry-specific human capital face larger permanent income losses than during recessions where jobs are expected to recover. Stocks negatively covariant with CID are riskier because they fall precisely when industry-specific human capital is most threatened.

nodes.title: A Research on Cross-sectional Return Dispersion and Volatility of US Stock Market during COVID-19

nodes.name: dispersion-volatility amplification
nodes.description: Increased cross-sectional return dispersion among stocks drives higher market volatility. As disagreement about valuations widens across the cross-section, overall price volatility increases, creating a positive feedback loop between dispersion and volatility.

nodes.name: epidemic uncertainty shock
nodes.description: Exogenous epidemic severity (proxied by Google search index) directly increases both cross-sectional return dispersion and volatility by creating differential impacts across sectors and firms, with heterogeneous exposure to pandemic risk.

nodes.name: sector-specific fundamental deterioration
nodes.description: Epidemic severity has a significant negative causal impact on energy sector returns through fundamental economic channels (demand destruction, supply disruption), independent of volatility or dispersion effects.

nodes.title: Cross-sectional Stock Price Prediction using Deep Learning for Actual Investment Management

nodes.name: nonlinear factor interaction
nodes.description: Stock returns depend on complex, nonlinear combinations of multiple factors (valuation, momentum, quality, liquidity) that cannot be captured by linear regression. Deep learning exploits these nonlinearities to improve prediction accuracy.

nodes.name: short-term momentum reversal
nodes.description: Recent price movements (1-60 day returns) contain predictive information about future 5-day returns, suggesting that short-term momentum patterns are exploitable through machine learning models that capture their nonlinear structure.

nodes.name: liquidity-adjusted valuation premium
nodes.description: Stocks with favorable valuation ratios (book-to-price, earnings-to-price, sales-to-price) combined with trading volume patterns earn higher returns; the relationship is nonlinear and depends on recent volume trends relative to historical averages.

nodes.title: Housing risk and return: Evidence from a housing asset-pricing model

nodes.name: speculative expectations extrapolation
nodes.description: Housing investors form expectations of future price appreciation based on recent price trends and past returns, driving prices above fundamental values. Survey evidence shows homebuyers view purchases as investment decisions and expect double-digit annual price growth, with market timing becoming increasingly important during booms.

nodes.name: momentum-driven spatial arbitrage
nodes.description: Investors identify geographic regions with past high returns (winners) and past low returns (losers), then buy in winner markets and sell in loser markets expecting the return differential to persist. This creates a trading strategy that exploits momentum across metropolitan areas.

nodes.name: underdiversification idiosyncratic risk premium
nodes.description: Housing investors typically hold only a small number of location-specific properties (often a single property), preventing full diversification. They therefore demand compensation not just for systematic market risk but also for unsystematic idiosyncratic risk that cannot be diversified away.

nodes.name: geographic size effect
nodes.description: Smaller metropolitan areas (measured by median house prices) earn higher risk-adjusted returns than larger metropolitan areas, analogous to the small-firm effect in equities. This size-based return differential persists as a systematic pricing factor.

nodes.title: Forecasting Nigerian Equity Stock Returns Using Long Short-Term Memory Technique
Sustainable Investing and the Cross-Section of Returns and Maximum Drawdown

nodes.name: volatility-based risk prediction
nodes.description: Stocks with higher volatility measures (one-year, one-month, and idiosyncratic volatility) exhibit predictable maximum drawdown and returns because volatility captures the magnitude of price fluctuations that determine drawdown severity and return dispersion.

nodes.name: liquidity cost pricing
nodes.description: Stocks with wider bid-ask spreads command higher expected returns and exhibit larger drawdowns because investors demand compensation for the cost of trading and the difficulty of exiting positions during stress periods.

nodes.name: size-based return dispersion
nodes.description: Smaller stocks have more predictable cross-sectional return rankings and drawdown patterns because size correlates with liquidity, analyst coverage, and institutional ownership, all of which affect price discovery and tail risk.

nodes.name: momentum persistence
nodes.description: Assets that have exhibited strong price movements in recent periods tend to continue moving in the same direction due to behavioral biases and slow information diffusion, allowing trend-following strategies to capture these persistent directional moves.

nodes.title: Deep Learning for Forecasting Stock Returns in the Cross-Section
Price impact in equity auctions: zero, then linear

nodes.name: discrete price grid zero impact
nodes.description: Small market orders produce zero price impact because the discrete nature of the price grid means orders can be absorbed by the matched volume and imbalance at the auction price without moving the price to the next tick. This creates a 'free' execution zone up to a threshold size ω(0).

nodes.name: linear impact regime
nodes.description: Once orders exceed the zero-impact threshold, price impact becomes linear in order size because the sum of buy and sell order densities is approximately constant around the auction price. This linearity persists across most days when the marginal supply and demand curves are flat in the vicinity of the clearing price.

nodes.name: auction opacity prevents selective liquidity taking
nodes.description: Because limit order books are not disseminated during the auction accumulation period, traders cannot selectively target the thinnest liquidity. This opacity forces a linear average price impact of actual order submissions and cancellations, in contrast to open markets where impact is much weaker and non-linear.

nodes.name: slow trader clustering at auction price
nodes.description: A large peak in order book density forms at the auction price as the clearing time approaches, driven by slow traders (non-HFT) who submit orders early and cannot react dynamically. This peak amplifies the importance of the zero-impact regime by concentrating matched volume at a single price level.

nodes.title: Equity2Vec: End-to-end Deep Learning Framework for Cross-sectional Asset Pricing

nodes.name: cross-sectional interaction exploitation
nodes.description: Assets' returns are predictable by modeling their evolving relationships and interactions with other assets in the cross-section, rather than treating each asset in isolation. The paper argues that traditional models overlook these complex cross-sectional dependencies that contain exploitable pricing signals.

nodes.name: heterogeneous alpha source integration
nodes.description: Combining multiple independent alpha sources—technical indicators, financial news signals, and cross-sectional relationships—generates superior predictive power because each source captures different market inefficiencies and pricing patterns that are not fully reflected when sources are used separately.

nodes.title: Physical approach to price momentum and its application to momentum strategy

nodes.name: price inertia from momentum accumulation
nodes.description: Prices exhibit inertia that causes them to continue moving in their established direction until external forces (news, supply/demand shocks) are applied. This persistent directional movement can be quantified using physical momentum concepts (mass × velocity) and exploited through contrarian strategies.

nodes.name: liquidity-weighted momentum filtering
nodes.description: Trading volume and transaction value encode instrument-specific information and market efficiency; higher volume/transaction value makes price movements more meaningful signals by filtering out noise. Weighting momentum by liquidity proxies (turnover rate, transaction value, inverse volatility) improves strategy returns by distinguishing genuine price signals from noise.

nodes.name: volatility-adjusted momentum persistence
nodes.description: Lower-volatility stocks exhibit stronger and more reliable momentum signals because their price movements represent more meaningful information relative to their noise level. Inverse volatility acts as a financial mass that amplifies the predictive power of momentum in stable securities.

nodes.title: Defining an intrinsic stickiness parameter of stock price returns

nodes.name: index tracking deviation exploitation
nodes.description: Individual stocks exhibit varying degrees of adherence to their index movements (stickiness). Traders can exploit profitable opportunities by identifying stocks that deviate from their expected index-relative behavior, capturing alpha when actual price movements diverge from predicted stickiness-adjusted returns.

nodes.name: stress accumulation and price adjustment
nodes.description: Index price movements create cumulative stress on individual stock components to maintain index alignment. Stocks with lower stickiness parameters experience greater adjustment pressure, leading to predictable return patterns as prices revert toward their stress-equilibrium relationship with the index.

nodes.title: Intraday Patterns in the Cross-section of Stock Returns

nodes.name: Algorithmic execution scheduling periodicity
nodes.description: Institutional investors using optimal execution algorithms (e.g., Almgren-Chriss) that trade aggressively early in the day and taper toward close create predictable daily patterns in volume and order flow. Combined with autocorrelated fund flows, this generates return continuation at exact 24-hour intervals lasting 40+ trading days.

nodes.name: Bid-ask bounce and temporary liquidity imbalance
nodes.description: Short-term negative return autocorrelation within a trading day (lasting less than one hour) is driven by bid-ask bounce and lack of market resilience—temporary price pressure from order flow that reverts as liquidity providers accommodate the imbalance, not by fundamental repricing.

nodes.name: Intraday return continuation at daily frequency
nodes.description: A stock's return in a given half-hour interval predicts its return at the same time on subsequent days (lags of 13, 26, 39, ... half-hour periods). This multi-week persistence pattern is not explained by volume, order imbalance, volatility, or bid-ask spreads, suggesting an unresolved pricing mechanism tied to recurring institutional trading schedules.

nodes.title: Pricing and Hedging Strategies for Cross-Currency Equity Protection Swaps
The Process of price formation and the skewness of asset returns

nodes.name: intertemporal price dependence and return skewness
nodes.description: Return distributions exhibit skewness because successive trading periods are dependent—opening prices equal closing prices of the prior period—rather than independent. This temporal continuity creates asymmetry in how price fluctuations at different levels propagate forward, generating non-zero skewness.

nodes.name: asymmetric preference weighting of price levels
nodes.description: The parameter α acts as a preference parameter determining whether agents weight small-scale or large-scale price fluctuations more heavily in their investment decisions. When α < 1, agents overweight low-level fluctuations, inducing negative skewness; when α > 1, they overweight high-level fluctuations, inducing positive skewness.

nodes.title: Optimal Option Portfolios for Skew-Elliptical t Returns

nodes.name: fat-tail risk underestimation under normality
nodes.description: Normal distributions have thin tails that systematically underestimate the probability of large market movements. Using Student-t or skew-t distributions instead captures the empirically observed heavy tails and asymmetry in financial returns, leading to materially different optimal portfolio allocations.

nodes.name: downside skewness risk premium
nodes.description: Financial markets exhibit larger crashes than booms (negative skewness). Symmetric distributions like Student-t fail to capture this asymmetry. Skew-t distributions model the empirically observed asymmetry between gains and losses, causing optimal portfolio weights to shift materially when skewness is accounted for versus ignored.

nodes.name: variance-VaR divergence under non-normality
nodes.description: Variance penalizes both upside and downside volatility equally, while Value-at-Risk penalizes only downside risk. Under skew-t returns, this divergence is amplified: optimal weights under VaR minimization diverge significantly more from variance-optimal weights than they do under normal or symmetric Student-t assumptions, especially when using higher-order Cornish-Fisher approximations.

nodes.title: Equity warrant pricing under subdiffusive fractional Brownian motion of the short rate

nodes.name: long-range dependence in interest rates
nodes.description: Short rates exhibit long-range memory and cannot be captured by standard Markov models. This persistence in rate dynamics, driven by macroeconomic variables, requires fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter H ∈ [1/2, 1) to properly model term structure and derivative pricing.

nodes.name: subdiffusive trapping in asset price dynamics
nodes.description: Financial processes exhibit periods of constant values corresponding to trapping events where particles remain motionless, analogous to subdiffusion in physical systems. This is modeled via inverse α-stable subordinators that add constant periods to asset price dynamics, capturing slow dynamics not present in standard geometric Brownian motion.

nodes.name: stochastic interest rate correlation with asset returns
nodes.description: Asset prices and short rates are correlated (correlation coefficient ρ) and both follow subdiffusive fractional Brownian motion. This joint dynamics affects warrant valuation through cross-partial derivatives in the pricing PDE, creating dependence between equity and fixed income risk that standard models with constant rates miss.

nodes.title: Framework for Inferring Following Strategies from Time Series of Movement Data

nodes.name: collective behavior coordination mispricings
nodes.description: Asset prices are mispricied when groups of market participants coordinate their trading decisions through either local-agreement strategies (following nearby traders) or dictatorship-like strategies (following predetermined leaders). Traders who can infer which coordination strategy is being used can anticipate collective movements and exploit the resulting mispricings.

nodes.name: leader-follower strategy inference
nodes.description: Price movements can be predicted by identifying whether individual traders follow local consensus (nearest-neighbor heuristic) or specific predetermined leaders. Inferring the dominant coordination strategy within a trading group allows prediction of subsequent directional movements.

nodes.title: DTW+S: Shape-based Comparison of Time-series with Ordered Local Trend
LLM-Mixer: Multiscale Mixing in LLMs for Time Series Forecasting
Empirical Study of the 1-2-3 Trend Indicator

nodes.name: mean reversion via trend correction phases
nodes.description: Price movements exhibit cyclical patterns where upward movements are followed by correction phases that partially retrace gains. Trends persist when corrections are shallow relative to prior movements, creating predictable mean-reverting oscillations around a dominant wavelength.

nodes.name: trend persistence via dynamic ratio
nodes.description: Trends continue when the ratio of movement phase height to correction phase height exceeds 1.0, indicating that price advances outpace retracements. Higher dynamic ratios signal stronger trend quality and longer trend lifetimes, creating momentum-like persistence.

nodes.name: wavelength-driven extrema significance
nodes.description: Market prices exhibit a dominant oscillation frequency (wavelength) detectable via autocorrelation of detrended price series. Calibrating trend detection to this natural wavelength filters out noise and identifies only significant extrema, improving signal quality for trend-following strategies.

nodes.title: Towards Time Series Reasoning with LLMs
Follow the Leader: Enhancing Systematic Trend-Following Using Network Momentum

nodes.name: momentum spillover via lead-lag relationships
nodes.description: Price trends in leading markets predict subsequent trends in lagging markets due to delayed information diffusion and asynchronous market reactions. By identifying which markets lead or lag others, traders can establish positions in followers based on leader performance.

nodes.name: network momentum aggregation
nodes.description: The predictive power of multiple lead-lag relationships can be combined into a sparse network structure where edge weights quantify connection strength. This aggregated signal captures interconnected cross-sectional momentum dynamics more effectively than pairwise relationships alone.

nodes.name: trend persistence in returns
nodes.description: Asset prices exhibit directional persistence—assets with rising prices tend to continue rising, and falling prices tend to continue falling. This persistence arises from slow information diffusion, behavioral biases like conservatism, and delayed investor responses to fundamentals.

nodes.title: Few-Shot Learning Patterns in Financial Time-Series for Trend-Following Strategies

nodes.name: trend persistence across timescales
nodes.description: Price trends persist at multiple timescales (1-day to 252-day returns), and blending signals across these timescales improves forecasting by capturing both short-term momentum and longer-term directional moves while mitigating regime-change whipsaws.

nodes.name: regime-change adaptation
nodes.description: Financial markets undergo rapid regime changes (momentum crashes, turning points) where traditional trend-following signals fail; quickly adapting forecasts to new market regimes by leveraging similar historical patterns prevents catastrophic losses during transitions.

nodes.name: cross-asset pattern transfer
nodes.description: Similar price-trend patterns recur across different assets and time periods; a model can transfer knowledge of trend dynamics from one asset's historical regimes to forecast trends in a new asset or regime with minimal data by attending to structurally similar past patterns.

nodes.title: Dominant Shuffle: A Simple Yet Powerful Data Augmentation for Time-series Prediction
Hawkes processes for credit indices time series analysis: How random are trades arrival times?

nodes.name: self-exciting trade clustering
nodes.description: Trades trigger subsequent trades through a self-reinforcing mechanism, causing clustering of trade arrivals at short timescales rather than random Poisson-distributed timing. Past trades increase the conditional intensity of future trades via an exponential decay kernel.

nodes.name: volume-dependent trade excitation
nodes.description: Large trades have disproportionate influence in triggering subsequent trades, particularly small trades. Trade arrival intensity depends on both the occurrence and size of previous trades, with larger trades generating stronger self-excitement and cross-volume effects.

nodes.name: cross-index trade contagion
nodes.description: Trades in one credit index increase the probability of trades in other indices through mutual excitement mechanisms. The intensity of trades in each index depends on recent trading activity across all indices, with liquidity differences affecting susceptibility to contagion.

nodes.title: Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting with Implicit Quantile Networks

nodes.name: distribution forecasting alpha
nodes.description: Traders can exploit mispricings by using probabilistic forecasts of future price distributions rather than point estimates alone. Better estimates of tail risks and the full distribution of future returns enable more informed position-sizing and risk management decisions that the market has not yet priced in.

nodes.title: GluonTS: Probabilistic Time Series Models in Python
Expressing Multivariate Time Series as Graphs with Time Series Attention Transformer
Large Language Models for Financial Aid in Financial Time-series Forecasting
AR-Net: A simple Auto-Regressive Neural Network for time-series
Approximate Probabilistic Inference for Time-Series Data A Robust Latent Gaussian Model With Temporal Awareness

nodes.name: temporal pattern recognition in non-stationary markets
nodes.description: Markets exhibit complex temporal dynamics that traditional models fail to capture; a robust generative model that accurately learns these temporal relationships can identify profitable trading opportunities by reconstructing underlying market trends more reliably than conventional approaches.

nodes.name: noise-robust signal extraction
nodes.description: Market data contains measurement errors and noise that corrupt trading signals; a model robust to data irregularities can extract cleaner, more reliable signals for decision-making by filtering out spurious patterns while preserving true underlying dynamics.

nodes.title: What Constitutes Good Contrastive Learning in Time-Series Forecasting?
Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
AMP: a new time-frequency feature extraction method for intermittent time-series data
Exploring a Gradient-based Explainable AI Technique for Time-Series Data: A Case Study of Assessing Stroke Rehabilitation Exercises
An Efficient ADMM Algorithm for Structural Break Detection in Multivariate Time Series
The Rise of Diffusion Models in Time-Series Forecasting
Survey on log-normally distributed market-technical trend data

nodes.name: trend reversion via log-normal retracement
nodes.description: Price corrections during trends follow a log-normal distribution with scale-invariant parameters, enabling statistical prediction of retracement magnitudes and thus identification of mean-reversion opportunities within established trends.

nodes.name: detection delay slippage
nodes.description: Automatic trend detection algorithms incur inevitable time delays in recognizing trend extrema, creating a measurable slippage between the true extreme price and the close price when the signal is generated; this delay is positively correlated with retracement magnitude.

nodes.name: asymmetric trend behavior by direction
nodes.description: Down-trends exhibit larger retracements and longer correction durations than up-trends, suggesting directional asymmetry in price mean-reversion dynamics that can be exploited through directionally-sensitive trading rules.

nodes.title: Towards Self-Supervised Foundation Models for Critical Care Time Series
Structure-Aware Set Transformers: Temporal and Variable-Type Attention Biases for Asynchronous Clinical Time Series
Super-resolution of Time-series Labels for Bootstrapped Event Detection
Monte Carlo EM for Deep Time Series Anomaly Detection
TSKANMixer: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with MLP-Mixer Model for Time Series Forecasting
Large Language Models for Time Series: A Survey

nodes.name: pattern recognition via language model transfer
nodes.description: LLMs trained on text can uncover complex nonlinear patterns and relationships in time series data that traditional statistical models miss, by leveraging their learned representations to identify subtle regularities in numerical sequences.

nodes.name: time series quantization bridging
nodes.description: Converting numerical time series into discrete tokens or categorical representations allows LLMs to process financial data using their native text-based machinery, enabling knowledge transfer from language domains to numerical prediction tasks.

nodes.title: MQRetNN: Multi-Horizon Time Series Forecasting with Retrieval Augmentation
JANET: Joint Adaptive predictioN-region Estimation for Time-series

nodes.name: uncertainty quantification alpha generation
nodes.description: More accurate and reliable prediction intervals for asset price movements enable traders to make better-informed decisions and superior risk management, generating alpha through improved decision-making under uncertainty.

nodes.name: multi-step ahead prediction reliability
nodes.description: Joint prediction regions with controlled error rates across multiple future time points provide theoretically-guaranteed forecasts that reduce uncertainty in sequential price predictions, enabling more confident trading decisions.

nodes.title: Pricing options on forwards in energy markets: the role of mean reversion's speed

nodes.name: mean reversion speed averaging over delivery period
nodes.description: Fast mean-reverting components in spot prices average out over longer delivery periods, reducing their impact on forward and option prices. The pricing error from neglecting slow mean-reverting components depends exponentially on the mean reversion rate and the length of the delivery period.

nodes.name: volatility convergence to long-term component
nodes.description: As the delivery period lengthens (T → ∞), the volatility of log-forward prices converges to the volatility of the non-stationary long-term component X, making mean-reverting components increasingly irrelevant for option pricing. The convergence rate is determined by the mean reversion speeds.

nodes.name: slow mean reversion pricing error
nodes.description: Neglecting slowly mean-reverting components in spot price dynamics causes option mispricing that decays exponentially with the mean reversion rate and delivery period length. For short delivery periods (e.g., monthly), this error can be substantial (7.1% relative error), but becomes negligible for longer periods (0.2% for quarterly).

nodes.name: delta hedging error transmission
nodes.description: Errors in option pricing from neglected mean-reverting components propagate to delta hedging strategies, with the magnitude depending on the same exponential decay factors as option pricing errors. The hedging error is bounded by the option pricing error.

nodes.title: Price formation in financial markets: a game-theoretic perspective

nodes.name: inventory-driven trading pressure
nodes.description: Traders with non-zero inventory positions are forced to accelerate liquidation or accumulation due to inventory holding costs (φ parameter) and terminal inventory penalties. This creates endogenous trading pressure that moves prices independent of fundamental information.

nodes.name: temporary price impact from liquidity consumption
nodes.description: When traders execute orders, they must consume layers of the limit order book, incurring a temporary cost proportional to the square of their execution rate (κν²). This friction is transient and reflects order book resilience rather than permanent price discovery.

nodes.title: Statistical properties of short term price trends in high frequency stock market data

nodes.name: trend momentum amplification
nodes.description: When a price trend begins, investors follow it and amplify the movement, increasing the conditional probability of trend continuation. This creates autocorrelation in price direction that decays over minutes rather than ticks.

nodes.name: trend exhaustion and reversal
nodes.description: As trends persist, profit-taking by early investors and late-entry hesitation by new investors cause the probability of trend continuation to decline and eventually reverse, limiting trend duration to roughly 30 minutes.

nodes.name: short-range price memory
nodes.description: Price changes exhibit strong positive autocorrelation at high frequency (minutes) that decays exponentially, violating the random walk hypothesis and creating predictable short-term directional persistence.

nodes.title: Empirical investigation of state-of-the-art mean reversion strategies for equity markets

nodes.name: single-period mean reversion
nodes.description: Stock prices that deviate above or below average in one period tend to revert in the next period. Strategies exploit this by buying worst performers and selling best performers from the previous day.

nodes.name: multi-period mean reversion
nodes.description: Stock prices deviate from their moving average over multiple periods and subsequently revert toward that average. Strategies use simple moving averages to predict future price relatives and allocate capital accordingly.

nodes.name: transaction cost erosion of rebalancing profits
nodes.description: High-frequency rebalancing strategies that exploit mean reversion generate substantial trading volume, which incurs explicit (commissions, taxes) and implicit (bid-ask spreads, price impact) transaction costs that eliminate or reverse profitability.

nodes.name: benchmark dataset selection bias
nodes.description: Well-known historical benchmark datasets (NYSE(O), NYSE(N)) contain exceptionally strong mean reversion tendencies that do not persist in broader, more recent market data, causing strategies to overfit to these datasets and fail on out-of-sample data.

nodes.title: An Analysis and Mitigation of the Reversal Curse

nodes.name: unidirectional training objective asymmetry
nodes.description: Causal language models trained with next-token prediction (NTP) only optimize p(b|a) when entity a precedes entity b in training data, providing no guarantee for the reverse conditional p(a|b). This creates an asymmetric learned representation where the model cannot reliably reverse the relationship.

nodes.name: bidirectional context access during training
nodes.description: Language models trained with autoregressive blank infilling (ABI) objectives can attend to both preceding and succeeding tokens when predicting masked positions, implicitly optimizing both p(b|a) and p(a|b) simultaneously. This symmetric training objective mitigates the reversal curse.

nodes.title: Hawkes model for price and trades high-frequency dynamics

nodes.name: trade arrival self-excitation
nodes.description: Market orders cluster in time due to self-reinforcing arrival dynamics; the arrival of one trade increases the conditional intensity of subsequent trades, creating predictable order flow patterns that can be exploited for alpha generation.

nodes.name: price mean reversion
nodes.description: High-frequency price movements exhibit mean reversion at microstructural timescales; prices that move away from their recent level tend to revert, allowing prediction of short-term reversals and optimal trade execution timing.

nodes.name: feedback-driven trading activity
nodes.description: Price changes endogenously drive subsequent trading activity; positive or negative price movements increase the conditional intensity of future trades, creating a feedback loop between price dynamics and order flow.

nodes.name: trade impact on price
nodes.description: Market order arrivals cause nonlinear price changes with a concave square-root-like relaxation profile; the impact of trades on prices follows a predictable decay pattern that can be estimated from market microstructure data.

nodes.title: Symmetry classification and invariant solutions of the classical geometric mean reversion process

nodes.name: mean reversion in short-term rates
