nodes.description: Interest rates exhibit mean-reverting dynamics rather than following geometric Brownian motion, allowing traders to predict price movements by identifying deviations from long-run equilibrium and positioning for reversion.

nodes.name: supply-responsive price dynamics
nodes.description: Supply responds endogenously to price changes, creating more realistic price dynamics than models assuming fixed supply; this supply elasticity affects the speed and magnitude of mean reversion in interest rates.

nodes.title: On-Line Portfolio Selection with Moving Average Reversion

nodes.name: multiple-period mean reversion
nodes.description: Stock prices exhibit temporary deviations from their moving average over multiple periods, and prices tend to revert toward this moving average. This multi-period reversion pattern can be exploited for alpha generation, particularly in volatile or non-stationary markets where single-period mean reversion fails.

nodes.title: Short-term market reaction after extreme price changes of liquid stocks

nodes.name: intraday overreaction and mean reversion
nodes.description: Extreme intraday price moves (both increases and decreases) trigger a reversal within 10-60 minutes as the market corrects the initial overreaction. The price overshoots in response to the shock, then reverts toward fundamental value.

nodes.name: bid-ask spread widening effect
nodes.description: After extreme price changes, bid-ask spreads widen sharply on the NYSE, which eliminates most of the economic profit from contrarian trading strategies despite the statistical significance of price reversals. On NASDAQ, spreads remain relatively constant, allowing abnormal profits to persist.

nodes.name: volatility and volume persistence after shocks
nodes.description: Volatility and trading volume spike sharply during extreme price events and then decay according to a power-law, remaining significantly elevated for days afterward. This elevated microstructure activity reflects ongoing market uncertainty and adjustment following the shock.

nodes.title: Trading multiple mean reversion

nodes.name: mean reversion harvesting
nodes.description: Traders profit by taking positions proportional to deviations from long-term mean, buying when assets are below mean and selling when above. Position sizing increases with mean reversion speed and decreases as terminal time approaches for risk-averse agents.

nodes.name: hedging via correlated assets
nodes.description: When multiple mean-reverting assets are available, traders use positions in slower-reverting or non-reverting correlated assets to hedge exposure in faster-reverting assets. Higher absolute correlations improve hedge efficiency, allowing larger positions in the primary mean-reverting asset.

nodes.name: reversion rate misspecification asymmetry
nodes.description: Optimal strategy is highly sensitive to assumed mean reversion rates, with asymmetric costs: underestimating reversion rates reduces utility uncertainty and is safer, while overestimating leads to excessively aggressive positions and larger losses.

nodes.title: Comparison of Classical and Nonlinear Models for Short-Term Electricity Price Prediction

nodes.name: nonlinear price pattern capture
nodes.description: Regression decision trees and recurrent neural networks capture nonlinear patterns and fluctuations in electricity prices that traditional linear models (ARIMA) miss, enabling more accurate short-term forecasts that generate alpha through superior prediction.

nodes.name: volatile market forecasting advantage
nodes.description: In highly volatile electricity markets like ERCOT, nonlinear forecasting models provide disproportionate predictive advantage by better capturing extreme price movements and regime changes, allowing market participants to improve bidding and operational decisions.

nodes.title: Short-term Volatility Estimation for High Frequency Trades using Gaussian processes (GPs)

nodes.name: price censoring constraint effect
nodes.description: Stock prices at JSE are subject to upper and lower limits due to market control strategies. When actual prices approach these thresholds, the censoring constraint influences volatility forecasts and return predictions, requiring explicit probabilistic modeling rather than simple thresholding.

nodes.name: volume-price interaction in volatility
nodes.description: Trading volume and historical stock prices are the dominant drivers of short-term volatility forecasts, with volume having particular influence on volatility estimation. The relationship between corrected prices and volumes must be modeled jointly to capture volatility dynamics.

nodes.name: intraday jump capture in volatility
nodes.description: Short-term volatility forecasting must account for intraday price jumps that occur over 1-3 hour horizons, as daily squared returns alone fail to capture these movements. High-frequency volatility is driven by rapid intraday price movements that are invisible to daily models.

nodes.title: Entropy of the Nordic electricity market: anomalous scaling, spikes, and mean-reversion

nodes.name: demand-driven capacity constraint spike generation
nodes.description: During high-consumption periods (winter), the electricity system operates near capacity limits. Small incremental demand increases force the marginal cost of production to jump dramatically because only expensive generation sources remain available, creating price spikes.

nodes.name: seasonal volatility clustering
nodes.description: Price spike events cluster non-uniformly across seasons due to consumption patterns: winter months experience frequent extreme price movements while summer months show quiescence. This temporal inhomogeneity violates Poisson assumptions and generates anomalous scaling in inter-spike waiting times.

nodes.name: mean reversion from fundamental anchoring
nodes.description: Electricity prices exhibit anti-persistent (negatively correlated) increments because prices are driven by a strong restoring force toward a fundamental equilibrium level determined by production capacity and consumption demand, causing prices to revert after deviations.

nodes.title: Fast mean-reversion asymptotics for large portfolios of stochastic volatility models

nodes.name: fast mean-reversion volatility averaging
nodes.description: When asset volatilities mean-revert rapidly to their long-run levels, time-averaged volatility over finite horizons converges to the stationary mean, allowing constant-volatility approximations to accurately capture portfolio loss distributions without simulating stochastic volatility paths.

nodes.name: systemic correlation dampening under fast mean-reversion
nodes.description: In fast mean-reverting volatility environments, the effective correlation between asset prices and systemic factors is reduced because volatility fluctuations that would amplify systemic shocks are quickly mean-reverted, weakening the transmission of market-wide noise to individual asset dynamics.

nodes.name: default barrier proximity under stochastic volatility
nodes.description: Asset default risk in structural models depends on distance-to-default processes that are jointly driven by asset returns and stochastic volatility; when volatility is correlated with returns through systemic factors, it affects the probability of hitting the default barrier and thus portfolio loss distribution.

nodes.title: Speckle Memory Effect in the Frequency Domain and Stability in Time-Reversal Experiments
The Price Reversal Phenomenon: When Cheaper Reasoning Models Cost More

nodes.name: thinking token consumption heterogeneity
nodes.description: Models with lower listed API prices may consume vastly more thinking tokens on the same query (up to 900% more), causing their actual total cost to exceed higher-priced competitors despite cheaper per-token rates. This heterogeneity dominates cost differences on single-turn reasoning tasks.

nodes.name: interaction turn overaction
nodes.description: Cheaper reasoning models require substantially more environment interaction turns to solve agentic tasks (up to 10x more turns), causing cumulative costs to exceed higher-priced models. This effect dominates on multi-turn tasks and is amplified by task difficulty.

nodes.name: listed price-actual cost decoupling
nodes.description: Listed API pricing (per-token rates) is an unreliable proxy for actual total cost because it ignores model-specific efficiency differences in token consumption and interaction patterns. In 32% of model pairs, the cheaper-listed model incurs higher actual cost, with reversals reaching 28x magnitude.

nodes.name: cost stochasticity and irreducible prediction noise
nodes.description: Identical model-query pairs produce highly variable costs across repeated runs (up to 9.7x variation), establishing an irreducible noise floor that makes per-query cost prediction fundamentally difficult and necessitates cost distribution estimation rather than point prediction.

nodes.title: Efficiency of the Price Formation Process in Presence of High Frequency Participants: a Mean Field Game analysis

nodes.name: liquidity imbalance price pressure
nodes.description: When one side of the orderbook accumulates excess queue size relative to the other side, the transaction price moves away from fair value. This occurs because traders anticipate future execution and adjust their willingness to transact based on queue depth imbalances.

nodes.name: waiting cost order selection
nodes.description: Traders strategically choose between limit orders (patient, incur waiting costs) and market orders (impatient, immediate execution) based on anticipated queue dynamics and the cost of remaining in the queue. Higher waiting costs incentivize market orders; lower costs incentivize limit orders.

nodes.name: HFT liquidity provision efficiency gain
nodes.description: High-frequency traders with lower latency and faster order cancellation ability can exploit orderbook imbalances more efficiently than institutional investors, reducing the macro-level price distortions caused by liquidity calls for liquidity. However, this efficiency gain accrues primarily to HFT, not to other market participants.

nodes.title: A threshold model for local volatility: evidence of leverage and mean reversion effects on historical data

nodes.name: leverage effect
nodes.description: Negative returns increase subsequent volatility more than positive returns of equal magnitude. The volatility scaling parameter ωᵢ depends on lagged return signs, creating an asymmetric return-volatility correlation where bad news raises risk more than good news.

nodes.name: mean-reversion effect
nodes.description: Asset prices exhibit mean-reverting behavior, particularly during crisis periods, where the drift parameters satisfy b− > 0 and b+ < 0, causing prices to revert toward a fundamental threshold level. The speed of reversion increases during periods of high economic uncertainty.

nodes.name: threshold-driven regime switching
nodes.description: A fixed price threshold endogenously separates two regimes—a bull market above the threshold with low volatility and positive drift, and a bear market below with high volatility and negative drift. This creates a spatial (price-level) segmentation rather than temporal segmentation, producing cyclical market behavior.

nodes.title: Time reversal invariance in finance

nodes.name: time reversal asymmetry in price dynamics
nodes.description: High-frequency foreign exchange prices exhibit non-time-reversal-invariant structures—asymmetries that differ when price sequences are run forward versus backward in time. These directional asymmetries in the underlying price process can be exploited as a systematic trading signal.

nodes.name: multi-timescale volatility clustering
nodes.description: ARCH processes with multi-timescale structure (but not simple GARCH(1,1)) reproduce the empirical time-reversal asymmetries observed in FX prices. This suggests volatility clustering across different frequencies creates exploitable directional patterns that pure stochastic volatility models fail to capture.

nodes.title: Optimum Output Long Short-Term Memory Cell for High-Frequency Trading Forecasting

nodes.name: order flow information lag exploitation
nodes.description: High-frequency traders can profit by rapidly processing limit order book information without processing delays to forecast the next mid-price movement before other market participants react to the same information.

nodes.name: inventory-driven price dynamics
nodes.description: Rapid changes in stock inventory held by market participants directly affect stock prices in the limit order book, creating predictable short-term price movements that can be exploited through fast detection of inventory shifts.

nodes.title: Mean-Reversion and Optimization

nodes.name: temporary correlation breakdown mean-reversion
nodes.description: Historically correlated securities experience temporary deviations from their typical co-movement due to unusual market conditions; profits are captured when correlations are restored as prices revert to historical relationships.

nodes.name: risk-adjusted position sizing
nodes.description: Dollar position sizes should be inversely weighted by stock-level variance (or volatility squared) to achieve both dollar neutrality and risk management, preventing high-volatility stocks from creating unintended risk concentrations in mean-reversion strategies.

nodes.name: cross-sectional return demeaning
nodes.description: Within clusters (industries or factor groups), stocks with positive demeaned returns are overpriced relative to their cluster peers, while those with negative demeaned returns are underpriced; shorting the rich and buying the cheap exploits this mispricing.

nodes.name: volatility-adjusted alpha suppression
nodes.description: Regressed returns (alphas) should be suppressed by the square of volatility rather than volatility itself when constructing positions, because this weighting maximizes the Sharpe ratio and prevents volatile stocks from dominating portfolio holdings.

nodes.title: Dense for the Price of Sparse: Improved Performance of Sparsely Initialized Networks via a Subspace Offset
Short Text Classification via Term Graph
Forecasting Intraday Volume in Equity Markets with Machine Learning

nodes.name: intraday seasonality pattern
nodes.description: Trading volume exhibits predictable U-shaped or J-shaped intraday patterns driven by information-based trading at market open, portfolio rebalancing at market close, and mutual fund execution benchmarked to closing prices. This time-of-day seasonality can be systematically forecasted.

nodes.name: volume autocorrelation persistence
nodes.description: Intraday trading volume exhibits significant autocorrelation at specific lag periods (30 minutes and 2 hours), allowing past volume observations to predict future volume within the same trading day.

nodes.name: cross-sectional volume commonality
nodes.description: Trading volumes are correlated across stocks within clusters and across the broader market, enabling improved forecasts by incorporating predictors from related assets rather than relying solely on individual stock information.

nodes.name: order flow composition effect
nodes.description: Different dimensions of order flow—notional trading value, share quantity, and trade count—contain complementary information for volume prediction, with trade count and lit order activity providing incremental predictive power beyond aggregate volume.

nodes.title: Equilibrium price in intraday electricity markets

nodes.name: Demand forecast convergence volatility
nodes.description: Price volatility increases as delivery approaches because demand forecast errors decrease deterministically over time. As uncertainty about customer consumption shrinks, the relative importance of heterogeneous agent marginal costs in determining equilibrium price grows, amplifying price movements.

nodes.name: Agent heterogeneity amplification of price volatility
nodes.description: When agents have different marginal costs, liquidity access costs, and weather correlations, the equilibrium price becomes a time-varying convex combination of their forecasted marginal costs. This heterogeneity is necessary for price volatility to increase despite decreasing demand forecast errors, as identical agents would eliminate the effect.

nodes.name: Production outage precautionary position adjustment
nodes.description: When a low-cost producer faces potential capacity outages (modeled as Markov chain jumps), she reduces her selling position and shifts toward buying, as a precaution against being forced to purchase at high prices if her capacity fails. This reflects agents' strategic response to production uncertainty.

nodes.title: Probabilistic intraday electricity price forecasting using generative machine learning
Bayesian Hierarchical Probabilistic Forecasting of Intraday Electricity Prices
Ensemble Forecasting for Intraday Electricity Prices: Simulating Trajectories

nodes.name: no-trade frequency effect on volatility
nodes.description: Price volatility in intraday electricity markets is driven by the frequency of trading activity. Periods with sparse transactions (night/morning hours) show higher no-trade event frequency, while closer to delivery with more trading activity, volatility spikes due to increased transaction density and information revelation.

nodes.name: time-to-delivery volatility clustering
nodes.description: Price volatility exhibits a strong non-random-walk pattern with a pronounced spike in the final 30 minutes before gate closure, indicating that uncertainty and trading intensity concentrate near delivery as market participants finalize positions and resolve remaining imbalances.

nodes.name: heavy-tailed price innovation distribution
nodes.description: Price changes follow a heavy-tailed distribution (Student's t with low degrees of freedom, possibly <4) rather than normal, indicating that extreme price movements occur with non-negligible probability, requiring explicit modeling of tail risk in forecasting.

nodes.name: fundamental supply-demand pressure on prices
nodes.description: Intraday prices are driven by fundamental factors including wind and solar generation forecasts, load forecasts, and time-to-maturity effects, which capture the resolution of uncertainty about renewable generation and demand between day-ahead and delivery, explaining deviations from day-ahead prices.

nodes.title: The Impact of Renewable Energy Forecasts on Intraday Electricity Prices

nodes.name: forecast error supply curve shift
nodes.description: Errors in wind and solar power forecasts cause the actual supply curve to differ from the day-ahead forecast, shifting equilibrium prices in the intraday market as the true supply becomes known. The magnitude of price impact depends non-linearly on which sector of the merit-order curve the equilibrium occurs in.

nodes.name: demand-dependent non-linear price sensitivity
nodes.description: The same forecast error magnitude produces different intraday price deviations depending on the realized demand level, because forecast errors shift supply curves horizontally while demand curves are non-linear. Low demand scenarios show larger price impacts than high demand scenarios for identical forecast errors.

nodes.name: asymmetric forecast error response
nodes.description: Positive and negative forecast errors in renewable generation are modeled separately, suggesting that market participants respond asymmetrically to overestimation versus underestimation of wind and solar supply, potentially due to different balancing costs or risk preferences.

nodes.title: Price formation and optimal trading in intraday electricity markets

nodes.name: forecast-driven demand pressure
nodes.description: Agents with uncertain demand/supply forecasts trade to hedge their terminal imbalance risk, creating predictable price movements correlated with forecast revisions. As delivery approaches, forecast uncertainty decreases, reducing trading pressure and allowing prices to stabilize.

nodes.name: imbalance penalty amplification
nodes.description: Quadratic penalties on terminal imbalances force agents to trade more aggressively to match their forecasts, increasing both trading volume and price impact. Higher penalty parameters directly increase observed price volatility.

nodes.name: liquidity-driven volatility
nodes.description: Market liquidity (captured by the trading cost function α(t)) varies over time, with lower liquidity near delivery. Lower instantaneous trading costs allow agents to trade more actively, amplifying price movements. Competition among agents reduces individual profit opportunities and dampens volatility.

nodes.name: linear permanent market impact
nodes.description: Each agent's trades permanently move the market price proportionally to their cumulative position relative to the market average. This creates strategic interdependence where agents internalize the cost of their price impact when optimizing execution.

nodes.title: Simulation-based Forecasting for Intraday Power Markets: Modelling Fundamental Drivers for Location, Shape and Scale of the Price Distribution

nodes.name: merit-order regime volatility amplification
nodes.description: Steeper merit-order curves (flatter supply elasticity) amplify price volatility and tail risk because the same forecast error or outage change moves prices more sharply. The merit-order regime is derived from day-ahead auction curves and acts as a multiplier on intraday price sensitivity.

nodes.name: time-to-delivery volatility acceleration
nodes.description: Volatility and tail heaviness increase sharply as delivery approaches, particularly in the final 60 minutes before delivery. This reflects reduced time for forecast updates and position adjustment, concentrating trading pressure into a narrower window.

nodes.name: trading activity tail risk
nodes.description: The kurtosis (tail heaviness) of the price distribution is driven primarily by lagged absolute price changes and trading volume rather than fundamental variables, suggesting that past trading intensity predicts extreme price moves independent of supply-demand fundamentals.

nodes.name: renewable forecast update information efficiency
nodes.description: Intraday renewable generation forecast updates and outage information have no predictive power for expected returns, indicating the market efficiently prices in this information immediately. This supports weak-form market efficiency in continuous intraday trading.

nodes.title: Multivariate Probabilistic Forecasting of Intraday Electricity Prices using Normalizing Flows
IVE: Enhanced Probabilistic Forecasting of Intraday Volume Ratio with Transformers

nodes.name: intraday volume seasonality predictability
nodes.description: Trading volume follows a U-shaped intraday pattern with predictable seasonal structure (opening and closing spikes, midday lows). This pattern can be forecasted using historical volume curves and absolute time information, enabling better execution timing.

nodes.name: volume uncertainty as volatility signal
nodes.description: The predicted standard deviation of volume ratios correlates with actual volume spikes and market uncertainty. High prediction uncertainty signals periods of elevated volume volatility, which can be exploited to anticipate and time order execution around volume concentration events.

nodes.name: liquidity-dependent volume curve heterogeneity
nodes.description: Stocks with different liquidity levels exhibit distinct volume curve shapes and dynamics. Incorporating stock-specific characteristics and historical trading data allows the model to capture each stock's unique volume profile, improving execution precision across heterogeneous liquidity regimes.

nodes.title: Econometric modelling and forecasting of intraday electricity prices

nodes.name: volume-dependent price scatter
nodes.description: Low trading volume in intraday electricity markets causes prices to become scattered and jump temporally, making last-transaction prices misleading as a price measure. This motivates the use of volume-weighted averaging windows (ID3-Price) to smooth out noise.

nodes.name: information concentration near delivery
nodes.description: Market participants concentrate trading activity in the final hours before delivery (over 70% of hourly and 80% of quarter-hourly trades occur in the ID3 window), suggesting that price discovery accelerates as delivery approaches and uncertainty resolves.

nodes.name: day-ahead anchor effect
nodes.description: Intraday prices exhibit weekly patterns similar to day-ahead prices (lower on weekends, stable Tuesday-Friday), suggesting that day-ahead auction results serve as an informational anchor that influences subsequent intraday price formation.

nodes.title: An Intraday GARCH Model for Discrete Price Changes and Irregularly Spaced Observations

nodes.name: market microstructure noise bid-ask bounce
nodes.description: High-frequency price changes exhibit strong negative first-order autocorrelation due to bid-ask bounce and other microstructure effects, causing prices to mean-revert within short intervals. This is captured by an MA(1) process in the mean dynamics.

nodes.name: trade duration volatility clustering
nodes.description: Longer intervals between trades are associated with higher price volatility, reflecting that market activity and information arrival are concentrated in time. Shorter durations near market open/close correspond to higher volatility; longer durations at midday correspond to lower volatility.

nodes.name: intraday volatility seasonality
nodes.description: Return volatility exhibits systematic intraday patterns driven by time-of-day variations in order flow intensity and market microstructure conditions, with these patterns persisting even during extraordinary market conditions.

nodes.title: Price formation and optimal trading in intraday electricity markets with a major player

nodes.name: strategic order splitting to minimize market impact
nodes.description: A major player with significant market share reduces trading costs by splitting large orders into smaller chunks over time, rather than executing immediately. This allows the major player to trade at lower effective costs than minor agents who post orders immediately.

nodes.name: information asymmetry advantage of minor agents
nodes.description: Minor agents observe both the major player's forecast and their own private demand forecasts, while the major player only observes the common forecast. This information advantage allows minor agents to anticipate and react to the major player's actions, offsetting the major player's first-mover advantage.

nodes.name: linear market impact from aggregate position
nodes.description: The equilibrium price responds linearly to the aggregate position of all minor agents and the position of the major agent. Individual minor agents have negligible impact, but their collective position and the major player's position both move prices proportionally, creating feedback effects on trading strategies.

nodes.title: Multivariate Simulation-based Forecasting for Intraday Power Markets: Modelling Cross-Product Price Effects

nodes.name: forecast revision price pressure
nodes.description: Intraday prices respond to revisions in renewable energy forecasts (wind, solar) rather than absolute fundamental levels. As forecasts update between day-ahead and intraday trading, price changes reflect the marginal impact of forecast errors on supply-demand balance.

nodes.name: cross-product correlation spillover
nodes.description: Prices for adjacent delivery hours exhibit strong positive correlation because they share common underlying drivers (renewable forecasts, load forecasts, transmission constraints). Modelling this dependence structure improves forecasting relative to treating each delivery hour independently.

nodes.name: SIDC order book coupling impact
nodes.description: Opening and closing of cross-border shared order books (SIDC waves at d-1 18:00 and d-1 22:00) creates structural breaks in trading activity and price distribution. The coupling allows arbitrage across European markets, affecting the correlation and volatility structure of German intraday prices.

nodes.title: Intraday Seasonalities and Nonstationarity of Trading Volume in Financial Markets: Individual and Cross-Sectional Features

nodes.name: overnight information shock relaxation
nodes.description: News and events that accumulate overnight are transferred to stock prices at market open, creating a shock that the market relaxes from via power-law dynamics. The relaxation speed (exponent α) increased post-2008 financial crisis, indicating faster information absorption.

nodes.name: intraday volume seasonality shift
nodes.description: The U-shaped (∩-shaped) intraday volume profile transformed post-2008: morning relaxation became faster (steeper convexity decrease) while afternoon volume became steeper, shifting the pattern from ∩ toward a t-shape. This structural change relates to regulatory changes (2007 short-selling rules) and crisis-driven market behavior.

nodes.name: heterogeneous agent participation by session
nodes.description: Morning high volume is driven by idiosyncratic stock-specific trading (wayward stocks), while afternoon high volume reflects cohesive, coordinated increases across the market. These two parts of the session operate under different statistical and dynamical rules, with divergence stressed during high market volatility periods.

nodes.title: OrderFusion: Encoding Orderbook for End-to-End Probabilistic Intraday Electricity Price Forecasting

nodes.name: buy-sell interaction dynamics
nodes.description: Buyers and sellers iteratively adjust their bids and offers based on observed quotes from the opposite side, creating strategic interactions that drive price formation. This buy-sell interaction structure is the primary driver of intraday price movements and must be explicitly modeled rather than aggregated away.

nodes.name: imbalance pressure effect
nodes.description: As delivery time approaches, market participants face increasing settlement risk and imbalance exposure, leading to last-minute trading under pressure. This manifests as price spikes and volatility in the final trading window (ID1) as participants urgently adjust positions closer to delivery.

nodes.name: recency bias in order informativeness
nodes.description: Recent trades carry more predictive information than older trades under the market efficiency hypothesis, as recent orders reflect the most current market conditions and information. The model prioritizes recent trades through temporal masking to improve forecast accuracy.

nodes.title: Forecasting Electricity Spot Prices using Lasso: On Capturing the Autoregressive Intraday Structure

nodes.name: intraday autoregressive cross-hour dependency
nodes.description: Electricity prices at a given hour depend not only on the same hour from previous days, but also on prices from different hours of the previous day, with time-varying correlation patterns. This cross-hour dependency structure is strongest between consecutive hours and between evening and morning hours.

nodes.name: time-varying weekday effects
nodes.description: The impact of day-of-week on electricity prices varies across hours of the day. Weekend prices differ systematically from weekday prices, and transition effects occur on Monday mornings and Friday afternoons, with the magnitude of these effects changing hour-by-hour.

nodes.title: Econometric Modeling of Intraday Electricity Market Price with Inadequate Historical Data
A structural Heath-Jarrow-Morton framework for consistent intraday, spot, and futures electricity prices

nodes.name: structural supply-demand equilibrium pricing
nodes.description: Forward electricity prices are fundamentally determined by the expected equilibrium of supply and demand at the delivery time, captured through a structural component that maps market state variables (demand, load, weather) to prices. This equilibrium expectation is independent of trading time and forms the martingale expectation of prices.

nodes.name: market noise disturbance of equilibrium
nodes.description: Incomplete market information and illiquidity cause deviations from the structural equilibrium price. Market participants with incomplete information about future conditions (e.g., weather uncertainty) introduce multiplicative noise that depends on both trading time and delivery time, creating a wedge between observed prices and fundamental supply-demand equilibrium.

nodes.name: spike smoothing across delivery horizons
nodes.description: Day-ahead spot prices exhibit spikes due to short delivery periods and high noise sensitivity, but these spikes are smoothed out in longer-dated futures contracts through averaging over extended delivery periods. The same forward kernel model generates both spike-prone short-term and smooth long-term prices without requiring separate probability measures.

nodes.title: Electricity intraday price modeling with marked Hawkes processes

nodes.name: increasing baseline intensity near maturity
nodes.description: Market activity and trading intensity increase exponentially as delivery time approaches because forecast accuracy for renewable production and consumption improves only hours before delivery, motivating traders to rebalance imbalances closer to maturity.

nodes.name: self-exciting jump clustering
nodes.description: Positive and negative price jumps exhibit self-exciting behavior where the occurrence of one type of jump increases the intensity of both jump types, creating clustering of price movements rather than random arrivals.

nodes.name: microstructure mean reversion
nodes.description: At high frequencies, prices exhibit mean-reverting behavior where positive jumps are often followed by negative jumps (and vice versa), creating round-trip reversals that cause realized volatility to decrease at higher sampling frequencies, visible in the signature plot.

nodes.name: Samuelson effect (volatility increase near maturity)
nodes.description: Price volatility increases as time to delivery decreases because uncertainty about final supply-demand equilibrium is resolved only near maturity, causing prices to become more volatile at macroscopic scales closer to delivery.

nodes.title: Equilibrium Effects of Intraday Order-Splitting Benchmarks

nodes.name: TWAP trajectory price pressure
nodes.description: TWAP benchmarks create deterministic intraday order-splitting schedules that generate predictable price pressure patterns. Traders can anticipate these systematic liquidity demands at specific times and exploit the resulting price movements.

nodes.name: VWAP randomness-induced volatility
nodes.description: VWAP benchmarks introduce randomness into intraday target trajectories because volume is stochastic, which creates unpredictable variations in price-pressure patterns and increases overall intraday volatility relative to deterministic benchmarks.

nodes.name: benchmark-driven liquidity reduction
nodes.description: Both TWAP and VWAP order-splitting strategies systematically reduce available market liquidity at certain intraday intervals, which increases price impact and volatility relative to a scenario with only terminal trading targets.

nodes.title: A Common Shock Model for multidimensional electricity intraday price modelling with application to battery valuation

nodes.name: Samuelson effect (intensity acceleration)
nodes.description: Price change intensity and volatility increase exponentially as time to maturity decreases. Traders must react more urgently to balance positions as delivery approaches, causing more frequent price movements.

nodes.name: Samuelson correlation effect
nodes.description: Price correlation between different delivery maturities decays exponentially with the distance between maturities. Traders' simultaneous reactions to common supply-demand shocks are stronger for nearby maturities and weaker for distant ones.

nodes.name: Common shock propagation
nodes.description: Unexpected events (e.g., asset failures, forecast revisions) trigger price movements across multiple consecutive delivery hours simultaneously. The probability of a shock affecting m successive maturities decreases with m, creating dependence structure.

nodes.title: Forecasting directional movements of stock prices for intraday trading using LSTM and random forests

nodes.name: intraday mean reversion
nodes.description: Short-term price movements during the trading day reverse overnight as intraday trading patterns unwind and market participants rebalance positions, creating predictable overnight return patterns.

nodes.name: multi-horizon return autocorrelation
nodes.description: Past returns at multiple time horizons (1-20 days and 40-240 days) contain predictive information about future intraday directional movements. Recent short-term and longer-term momentum patterns jointly predict whether a stock will outperform or underperform the median intraday return.

nodes.title: No Arbitrage Conditions For Simple Trading Strategies

nodes.name: strict local martingale arbitrage under simple strategies
nodes.description: Non-negative strict local martingales admit arbitrage opportunities when traders are restricted to simple trading strategies (no doubling strategies), because the constraint prevents unbounded loss hedging that would normally eliminate such opportunities. The strong Markov property ensures no arbitrage exists under these constraints for certain process classes.

nodes.name: short-sale constraint binding inefficiency
nodes.description: When short-sale restrictions are imposed on simple trading strategies, additional no-arbitrage conditions become binding, creating exploitable inefficiencies that would not exist under unrestricted trading. The constraint prevents traders from fully arbitraging away mispricings.

nodes.title: Building Trust Takes Time: Limits to Arbitrage for Blockchain-Based Assets

nodes.name: settlement latency arbitrage friction
nodes.description: Cross-exchange arbitrageurs face price risk while waiting for blockchain validation of asset transfers between exchanges. Risk-averse arbitrageurs require larger price differences to compensate for this settlement latency exposure, limiting arbitrage activity and allowing price deviations to persist.

nodes.name: exchange default risk premium
nodes.description: Off-chain settlement exposes arbitrageurs to exchange custody risk (hacks, theft, exit scams). Arbitrageurs demand a risk premium to hold inventory at less-trusted exchanges, making inventory arbitrage more costly and reducing its use as a friction-mitigation strategy relative to cross-exchange arbitrage.

nodes.name: settlement latency uncertainty premium
nodes.description: Variance in settlement latency (due to proof-of-work computational randomness) creates additional price risk for arbitrageurs beyond mean latency. High uncertainty in settlement timing increases the required price difference threshold, contributing substantially (>40%) to marginal arbitrage costs independent of mean latency.

nodes.name: trust-driven arbitrage capital allocation
nodes.description: Arbitrageurs preferentially deploy inventory capital to exchanges perceived as more trustworthy (proxied by Bitcoin custody holdings). Higher trust reduces default risk and enables inventory arbitrage, narrowing price differences between trusted exchanges even when settlement latency remains constant.

nodes.title: Bertram's Pairs Trading Strategy with Bounded Risk

nodes.name: mean reversion in cointegrated price spreads
nodes.description: Price differences between cointegrated asset pairs follow an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process that mean-reverts; deviations from equilibrium create profitable trading opportunities as prices revert to their long-run relationship.

nodes.name: parameter estimation risk in mean-reversion strategies
nodes.description: Optimal trading strategies derived from estimated process parameters suffer performance degradation when true parameters differ from estimates; this estimation uncertainty creates a wedge between theoretical and realized alpha.

nodes.title: Quantum Quantitative Trading: High-Frequency Statistical Arbitrage Algorithm

nodes.name: mean reversion of cointegrated spreads
nodes.description: Commodity pairs that share a long-run equilibrium relationship (cointegrated) experience temporary deviations from their equilibrium spread that predictably revert. Trading profits arise from buying the underperforming commodity and shorting the outperforming one when spreads deviate, capturing the reversion.

nodes.name: multicollinearity detection via condition number
nodes.description: Securities with high multicollinearity (large condition numbers and small eigenvalues) are more likely to be cointegrated. By preselecting portfolios with condition numbers above a threshold, one can efficiently identify candidate pairs for statistical arbitrage before formal cointegration testing.

nodes.title: Harnessing Deep Q-Learning for Enhanced Statistical Arbitrage in High-Frequency Trading: A Comprehensive Exploration

nodes.name: real-time market state adaptation
nodes.description: The agent continuously updates its understanding of market conditions by observing price movements, technical indicators, and microstructure variables, allowing it to adapt trading decisions dynamically as market states change rapidly in HFT environments.

nodes.name: reward-based strategy refinement
nodes.description: The agent learns to maximize risk-adjusted returns by iteratively updating its action-value estimates based on realized profits, losses, and volatility feedback, causing the trading strategy to converge toward higher Sharpe ratio trades over time.

nodes.name: experience decorrelation stabilization
nodes.description: By randomly sampling past trading experiences from a replay buffer rather than learning sequentially, the algorithm breaks temporal correlations in market data, reducing oscillations in strategy updates and enabling more stable learning in non-stationary financial environments.

nodes.title: 151 Estrategias de Trading (151 Trading Strategies)
Ensemble properties of high frequency data and intraday trading rules

nodes.name: intraday volatility mean reversion
nodes.description: Morning volatility decays according to a power law with scaling exponent D < 0.5, creating predictable volatility patterns that mean-revert within the trading day. This time-inhomogeneous decay in volatility can be exploited by trend-following strategies that adapt to the changing volatility regime.

nodes.name: afternoon volatility acceleration
nodes.description: After midday (around 13:20 NY time), volatility reverses from decaying to accelerating with scaling exponent D > 0.5, creating a distinct afternoon regime. This regime shift reflects changing market microstructure and participant behavior in the latter part of the trading day.

nodes.name: non-Markovian return dependence
nodes.description: Returns exhibit strong non-linear dependence (volatility clustering and heteroskedasticity) despite weak linear correlation, indicating memory effects in the return-generating process. This persistent dependence structure allows conditioned forecasting to outperform standard martingale models.

nodes.name: model-based price bound violations
nodes.description: Deviations of realized prices from model-predicted density forecast bounds reveal small but exploitable arbitrage opportunities. These violations reflect linear correlations present in empirical data but absent in the martingale model, enabling trend-following trading signals.

nodes.title: AI for trading strategies
Advanced Statistical Arbitrage with Reinforcement Learning

nodes.name: mean reversion of paired spreads
nodes.description: Paired stocks that historically move together form spreads that deviate from their long-term mean and subsequently revert to equilibrium. Traders profit by taking positions when spreads are dislocated and closing when they converge back to the mean.

nodes.name: empirical reversion speed optimization
nodes.description: The speed at which a spread reverts to its mean (measured by time from local extremes to mean crossings) varies with portfolio coefficients. Minimizing empirical mean reversion time identifies optimal asset weightings that exhibit faster mean reversion, enabling quicker profit capture.

nodes.name: adaptive momentum-reversal regime switching
nodes.description: Recent price momentum (captured as discretized directional sequences) signals whether the spread is in a continuation or reversal regime. The RL agent learns to exploit momentum continuation when weak and reversal when strong, dynamically adapting entry and exit decisions without fixed deviation thresholds.

nodes.title: Criteria for the absence of arbitrage in general diffusion markets

nodes.name: arbitrage opportunity detection via scale-speed characterization
nodes.description: Market inefficiencies arise when the scale function and speed measure of the asset price process violate deterministic no-arbitrage conditions, creating exploitable arbitrage opportunities that allow traders to achieve unbounded profits with bounded risk.

nodes.name: martingale measure absence
nodes.description: When no equivalent martingale measure exists for the asset price process, the market fails to satisfy fundamental no-arbitrage conditions (NA, NUPBR, NFLVR), indicating structural pricing inefficiencies.

nodes.title: Asymptotic arbitrage in the Heston model

nodes.name: variance process mean reversion mispricing
nodes.description: Market prices deviate from theoretical values implied by the Heston model's ergodic variance process. Traders can exploit these mispricings by trading on the discrepancy between observed market prices and equivalent martingale measure valuations as the variance process reverts to its long-run mean.

nodes.name: asymptotic arbitrage from volatility dynamics
nodes.description: The ergodicity of the variance process in the Heston framework creates asymptotic arbitrage opportunities—trading strategies with zero initial cost that generate positive expected profits over long horizons as volatility mean-reverts and market mispricings are corrected.

nodes.title: Statistical arbitrage in multi-pair trading strategy based on graph clustering algorithms in US equities market

nodes.name: mean reversion within correlation clusters
nodes.description: Stocks within graph-clustered groups (identified by correlation structure) exhibit short-term mean reversion, where stocks with returns below cluster mean tend to revert upward and vice versa. This exploits temporary deviations from established intra-cluster relationships.

nodes.name: signal quality filtering
nodes.description: Machine learning classifiers can distinguish between high-quality and low-quality mean-reversion signals generated by the graph clustering strategy, improving profitability by filtering out false positives before execution.

nodes.name: optimal position sizing via Kelly criterion
nodes.description: Scaling position sizes according to signal strength and win probability (via Kelly criterion) improves risk-adjusted returns by allocating more capital to higher-confidence trades and less to lower-confidence ones.

nodes.title: Reinforcement Learning Pair Trading: A Dynamic Scaling approach

nodes.name: mean reversion of correlated asset spreads
nodes.description: Two statistically correlated assets experience temporary price divergences; when the spread between them deviates beyond a threshold, it tends to revert to the mean, creating arbitrage profit opportunities by longing the underpriced asset and shorting the overpriced one.

nodes.name: adaptive threshold selection based on market volatility
nodes.description: Fixed entry/exit thresholds are suboptimal across varying market conditions; a moving-window mechanism that adjusts thresholds dynamically to market volatility allows the strategy to capture opportunities in both stable and volatile regimes without over-trading or missing signals.

nodes.name: opportunity quality discrimination via dynamic position sizing
nodes.description: Not all mean-reversion opportunities are equally likely to succeed; an RL agent can learn to allocate larger position sizes to higher-quality trading signals (based on spread magnitude and market zone) and smaller sizes to marginal opportunities, improving risk-adjusted returns compared to fixed-quantity trading.

nodes.title: Detecting data-driven robust statistical arbitrage strategies with deep neural networks

nodes.name: mean reversion breakdown in pairs trading
nodes.description: Pairs trading strategies rely on mean-reversion of spreads between cointegrated assets, but this relationship breaks down over time, causing strategies to fail when spreads no longer converge to equilibrium. The paper shows statistical arbitrage can be profitable even when this mechanism fails.

nodes.name: model ambiguity in probability measures
nodes.description: Markets exhibit uncertainty about the true underlying probability distribution governing returns. By constructing an ambiguity set of admissible measures (using Wasserstein distance around historical returns), strategies can remain profitable across multiple plausible probability models rather than assuming a single fixed measure.

nodes.name: conditional expectation violations across measures
nodes.description: A trading strategy can generate non-negative conditional expected payoffs (given terminal values) under all measures in an ambiguity set, while being profitable under at least one measure. This exploits the gap between what different probability models predict about future price movements.

nodes.name: trading cost friction exploitation
nodes.description: Statistical arbitrage opportunities persist because transaction costs, bid-ask spreads, and borrowing costs create friction that prevents immediate elimination of mispricings. Strategies that account for these costs can still be profitable when the underlying price deviations are sufficiently large.

nodes.title: Deep Learning Statistical Arbitrage

nodes.name: law of one price violation
nodes.description: Similar assets trade at different prices due to temporary market frictions or slow information diffusion, creating exploitable temporal price discrepancies between economically equivalent securities.

nodes.name: conditional latent factor mispricing
nodes.description: Assets with similar exposures to latent pricing factors deviate from their conditional fair values, generating residual portfolio signals that can be extracted and traded when they revert.

nodes.name: temporal pattern exploitation via deep learning
nodes.description: LSTM networks capture complex temporal dependencies and nonlinear patterns in time series that traditional models miss, enabling more accurate trend forecasting and alpha generation through superior predictive accuracy.

nodes.title: Detecting and repairing arbitrage in traded option prices

nodes.name: illiquidity-induced arbitrage in option prices
nodes.description: Arbitrage violations in option price data arise from infrequent price updates and wide bid-ask spreads on illiquid options (especially deep OTM and ITM), rather than from true market inefficiency. The 'fair' price lies within the bid-ask bounds, and sparse perturbations within these bounds can eliminate apparent arbitrage.

nodes.name: static arbitrage constraint violation
nodes.description: Option prices violate model-independent no-arbitrage relations (vertical spreads, calendar spreads, butterfly spreads, and convexity constraints) that must hold for any arbitrage-free pricing model. These violations prevent exact calibration of arbitrage-free models and distort risk-neutral density estimation.

nodes.title: Generalized statistical arbitrage concepts and related gain strategies

nodes.name: path-dependent pricing kernel effect
nodes.description: When the pricing kernel depends on the entire price path history rather than only the final state, statistical arbitrage opportunities emerge because the deflated payoff process is no longer a martingale and exhibits systematic trends exploitable by trading strategies.

nodes.name: state-contingent probability mismatch
nodes.description: When the real-world probability distribution over final states differs from the risk-neutral probability distribution in a way that violates path-independence (e.g., P(ω2)/P(ω3) ≠ Q(ω2)/Q(ω3)), traders can construct strategies that earn positive expected gains conditional on specific state partitions while maintaining non-negative payoffs in each state.

nodes.name: information-conditional mean reversion
nodes.description: Trading strategies can achieve positive average gains when conditioned on partial information systems (σ-algebras) that partition the state space, such as price ranges or maximum price levels, even when unconditional arbitrage is absent. This exploits mean-reverting patterns within information-defined scenarios.

nodes.title: Dynamic Grid Trading Strategy: From Zero Expectation to Market Outperformance

nodes.name: mean reversion via geometric grid spacing
nodes.description: Price oscillations around a central level create repeated buy-low/sell-high arbitrage opportunities. The geometric grid structure ensures proportional spacing that captures profits across different volatility regimes, exploiting the tendency of prices to revert toward the grid center.

nodes.name: transaction cost drag on arbitrage profits
nodes.description: Grid trading generates zero expected value before fees because arbitrage gains are offset by the cost of frequent buy-sell cycles. Smaller grid sizes amplify this drag as transaction fees consume a larger fraction of per-trade profits, while larger grids reduce trading frequency and profitability.

nodes.name: capital reinvestment through grid reset
nodes.description: Continuously resetting the grid at new price extremes and reinvesting arbitrage profits as principal for subsequent grids compounds returns over time. This converts a zero-expected-value strategy into positive returns by allowing the strategy to adapt to trending markets and accumulate gains across multiple grid cycles.

nodes.title: A Stochastic Thermodynamics Approach to Price Impact and Round-Trip Arbitrage: Theory and Empirical Implications

nodes.name: temporary impact dissipation
nodes.description: Trading activity incurs deterministic losses through temporary price impact (bid-ask spread and execution slippage). These losses accumulate as dissipated work proportional to the square of trading intensity, making round-trip strategies unprofitable in expectation regardless of price direction.

nodes.name: inventory risk from market noise
nodes.description: Positions held during execution are exposed to random price fluctuations (market noise). The probability of profitable round-trip cycles is exponentially suppressed by the ratio of dissipated work to accumulated inventory variance and volatility, making larger or longer-held positions less likely to profit.

nodes.name: execution strategy entropy trade-off
nodes.description: Traders face a fundamental trade-off between minimizing impact costs (via slow execution) and minimizing inventory risk (via fast execution). The market temperature parameter governs this trade-off: at high competitive pressure (low temperature), all traders converge to optimal execution; at low pressure (high temperature), strategies diversify and become speculative.

nodes.title: Backtest of Trading Systems on Candle Charts
Statistical arbitrage portfolio construction based on preference relations

nodes.name: mean reversion of relative mispricing
nodes.description: When two securities with similar characteristics deviate from their historical price relationship, the mispricing corrects as the market prices them back into alignment. This assumes that significant deviations from the mean price spread between paired securities represent temporary mispricings that will revert.

nodes.name: limited attention hypothesis
nodes.description: In markets with many tradeable securities, investors have limited attention and cannot efficiently process information about all securities simultaneously. This causes common market shocks to diffuse slowly into subsets of securities, creating exploitable relative pricing inefficiencies across multiple security pairs rather than individual pairs.

nodes.title: Attention Factors for Statistical Arbitrage

nodes.name: residual mean reversion
nodes.description: After controlling for systematic factor exposures, residual returns exhibit predictable mean-reverting patterns that can be exploited through long-short trading. The arbitrage strategy profits when temporary deviations from factor-implied fair prices revert back to equilibrium.

nodes.name: factor-based mispricing identification
nodes.description: Assets with similar exposures to latent factors should move together; when their prices diverge, the residual component represents temporary mispricing that can be exploited. The factors identify 'similar' assets whose relative price deviations signal arbitrage opportunities.

nodes.name: characteristic-driven factor structure
nodes.description: Firm characteristics (momentum, value, profitability, size, etc.) contain information about which assets should co-move together. Attention mechanisms over embedded characteristics allow flexible, nonlinear discovery of factor loadings that better capture true similarity for arbitrage purposes than linear methods.

nodes.name: trading cost optimization in factor selection
nodes.description: Factors estimated purely to explain return variation (PCA) have high turnover and large short positions, degrading net returns. Jointly optimizing factor construction with trading objectives and transaction cost penalties produces lower-turnover, more tradable factors that preserve profitability after costs.

nodes.title: A Multi-factor Adaptive Statistical Arbitrage Model

nodes.name: cointegration mean reversion
nodes.description: Cointegrated cryptocurrency pairs exhibit temporary deviations from their long-run equilibrium relationship; trading signals exploit the predictable reversion of mispriced pairs back to their equilibrium, generating returns as the spread normalizes.

nodes.name: multi-factor portfolio similarity
nodes.description: Portfolios identified through multiple dimensions (fundamental ratios, momentum, volatility) beyond price alone exhibit stronger and more persistent cointegration relationships than price-only selection, because characteristically similar firms move together more reliably.

nodes.name: cross-sectional clustering stability
nodes.description: Stocks grouped by K-means clustering on fundamental and statistical factors form more profitable trading pairs than those identified by inverse correlation structure alone, because clustering captures stable cross-sectional behavior while graphical lasso captures only historical price comovement.

nodes.title: Optimal Investment, Demand and Arbitrage under Price Impact

nodes.name: inventory-based price impact
nodes.description: Market makers adjust their pricing rules in response to changes in inventory from investor orders. As an investor submits larger orders, the market maker's inventory and hence pricing rule changes, causing non-linear price impact that increases with order size.

nodes.name: non-linear hedging costs
nodes.description: The cost to hedge a derivative position is not linear in position size due to price impact. As hedging demand increases, the investor must trade with market makers at progressively worse prices, making large hedges prohibitively expensive and limiting the scalability of arbitrage opportunities.

nodes.name: constrained trading effect
nodes.description: Price impact creates an effective constraint on the investor's feasible trading strategies. The set of achievable portfolio allocations is neither closed nor convex, and depends on the market maker's risk aversion and endowment, limiting which positions the investor can actually take.

nodes.title: Quantifying immediate price impact of trades based on the $k$-shell decomposition of stock trading networks

nodes.name: network position price impact amplification
nodes.description: Trades initiated by traders in the core (kernel) of the trading network have larger immediate price impacts than those in peripheral positions, because core traders execute larger orders that are matched against multiple counterparties, creating greater mid-price movement.

nodes.name: order size sensitivity to network position
institutional order execution strategy dampening
nodes.description: Institutional traders professionally employ trading strategies (e.g., order splitting, timing) that reduce the sensitivity of their price impact to trade size, whereas individual traders use less sophisticated strategies and experience price impact that scales more aggressively with order size.

nodes.name: order fill status price impact divergence
nodes.description: Partially filled limit orders produce price impacts approximately 10 times larger than fully filled orders at the same volume, because partial fills indicate unexecuted demand that moves the mid-price, while filled orders represent completed transactions with less residual information.

nodes.title: The price dynamics of common trading strategies

nodes.name: trend-following noise amplification
nodes.description: Trend followers amplify price noise by taking positions correlated with recent price movements, creating positive feedback that magnifies incoming random shocks into larger price swings and temporal correlations in volatility.

nodes.name: value-fundamental mean reversion
nodes.description: Value investors trade against deviations from fundamental value, creating a stabilizing force that pulls prices back toward equilibrium; however, under certain conditions (high trend follower fraction, risk-neutral market makers), this stabilization can fail and produce limit cycles or instability.

nodes.name: order flow market impact
nodes.description: Market makers set prices as a log-linear function of net order imbalance, causing buy orders to push prices up and sell orders to push them down; this creates path-dependent price dynamics where accumulated order flow determines price levels.

nodes.title: SpotV2Net: Multivariate Intraday Spot Volatility Forecasting via Vol-of-Vol-Informed Graph Attention Networks

nodes.name: volatility spillover via co-volatility of volatility
nodes.description: Asset volatilities are interconnected through time-varying co-movements in their volatility dynamics. When the co-volatility of volatility between two assets spikes, it signals stronger instantaneous spillover effects, allowing the model to weight neighboring assets' information differently when forecasting volatility.

nodes.name: sector-driven volatility clustering
nodes.description: Assets in the same sector experience correlated volatility bursts during market stress events. The strength of this clustering is captured by elevated spot co-volatility of volatility between same-sector pairs, which exceeds that of cross-sector pairs, enabling selective attention to relevant peer information.

nodes.name: intraday volatility persistence with long memory
nodes.description: Spot volatility exhibits strong temporal dependence at intraday frequencies, with lagged volatility values containing predictive power for future volatility. This long-memory property is better captured by deep learning models than traditional linear autoregressive approaches.

nodes.title: Volatility forecasting with machine learning and intraday commonality

nodes.name: intraday volatility commonality
nodes.description: Stock volatilities co-move strongly within intraday horizons due to shared market-wide factors, with this commonality being more stable and pronounced at intraday frequencies (10-min to 65-min) than at daily frequencies. This co-movement can be exploited for improved volatility forecasting by pooling cross-sectional data.

nodes.name: time-of-day volatility clustering
nodes.description: Intraday volatility exhibits a reverse-J-shaped diurnal pattern with elevated volatility near market open and close, and commonality in volatility peaks near market close in contrast to the overall diurnal pattern. This time-varying structure provides predictive information for intraday volatility forecasts.

nodes.name: nonlinear volatility interactions
nodes.description: Complex latent interactions exist among volatility predictors across assets and time horizons that are not captured by linear models. Neural networks can uncover these nonlinear relationships, yielding superior forecasting performance compared to parametric GARCH models and linear regressions.

nodes.name: high-frequency information content in intraday volatility
nodes.description: Past intraday realized volatilities at multiple horizons (10-min, 30-min, 65-min) contain additional predictive information for future daily volatility beyond what traditional daily-frequency models capture, allowing better utilization of available high-frequency data.

nodes.title: Realized Volatility Forecasting for New Issues and Spin-Offs using Multi-Source Transfer Learning

nodes.name: structural break in volatility regimes
nodes.description: Volatility series exhibit structural breaks over time, causing similarity measurements computed over long historical periods to become biased. By using short non-overlapping subsequences rather than entire asset histories, the method avoids contamination from regime shifts and captures only relevant volatility dynamics.

nodes.name: temporal similarity matching via dynamic time warping
nodes.description: Assets with similar recent volatility patterns (measured by DTW distance on lagged volatility features) are more informative for forecasting a new asset's future volatility than assets with dissimilar patterns. Selecting source subsequences with lowest DTW distance to the target's recent volatility trajectory transfers relevant knowledge while avoiding negative transfer.

nodes.name: data scarcity constraint on volatility forecasting
nodes.description: New issues and spin-offs have insufficient historical data to train accurate volatility models using standard methods. Augmenting the sparse target data with carefully selected similar subsequences from mature assets enables model training and forecasting even immediately after the first trading day.

nodes.title: TimeCatcher: A Variational Framework for Volatility-Aware Forecasting of Non-Stationary Time Series

nodes.name: latent dynamic undermodeling in non-stationary regimes
nodes.description: Standard MLP-based forecasting models rely on implicit local stationarity assumptions and fail to capture complex stochastic temporal dependencies encoded in latent space, causing systematic over-smoothing of predictions during regime changes and structural breaks.

nodes.name: volatility amplification of abrupt fluctuations
nodes.description: Sudden price movements and structural breaks in non-stationary financial time series are smoothed away by standard models; explicitly detecting and amplifying significant local variations via learnable weighting mechanisms restores sensitivity to critical market events.

nodes.title: Forecasting intermittent time series with Gaussian Processes and Tweedie likelihood
Quantile Regression for Qualifying Match of GEFCom2017 Probabilistic Load Forecasting
Lasso estimation for GEFCom2014 probabilistic electric load forecasting
Bayesian Dynamic Modeling of Realized Volatility in Financial Asset Price Forecasting

nodes.name: volatility leverage effect
nodes.description: Price changes and volatility are asymmetrically related through both contemporaneous and lagged channels. Negative price shocks increase subsequent volatility more than positive shocks of equal magnitude, and this relationship operates through both immediate feedback and delayed effects that can be captured by including current and lagged realized volatility as predictors of returns.

nodes.name: volatility feedback effect
nodes.description: An unexpected increase in squared return volatility raises the stochastic discount rate (cost of capital), causing an immediate decline in the present value of future dividends and thus in stock price. This price decline generates additional return volatility as markets adjust to the higher cost of capital.

nodes.name: realized volatility measurement precision
nodes.description: High-frequency intraday data provides lower-noise estimates of true conditional variance compared to daily returns alone. Incorporating realized volatility measures (constructed from OHLC or high-frequency returns) improves volatility state inference and reduces uncertainty in price forecasts by providing an additional, more precise signal of the latent volatility process.

nodes.title: Probabilistic Hierarchical Forecasting with Deep Poisson Mixtures
Unexpected volatility and intraday serial correlation

nodes.name: unexpected volatility amplifies intraday mean reversion
nodes.description: Volatility that cannot be forecasted from recent history (unexpected volatility) drives positive intraday serial correlation, meaning price movements tend to reverse within 4-20 minute windows. This suggests that unpredictable shocks trigger temporary overshooting followed by correction.

nodes.name: predictable volatility suppresses intraday mean reversion
nodes.description: Volatility that is forecastable from recent history (predictable volatility) is negatively related to intraday serial correlation, consistent with the LeBaron effect. When volatility is expected, market participants adjust behavior to reduce mean reversion, improving price efficiency.

nodes.name: opinion reinforcement in illiquid markets
nodes.description: In less liquid markets, investors observing correlated movements in substitute securities reinforce their trading decisions, creating positive correlation between volatility and intraday serial correlation. This mechanism is weaker in highly liquid markets like US index futures.

nodes.title: DeepVol: Volatility Forecasting from High-Frequency Data with Dilated Causal Convolutions

nodes.name: microstructure noise filtering in high-frequency data
nodes.description: Higher sampling frequencies in intraday data contain more microstructure noise, but also more information about true volatility. Models must learn to optimally balance extracting signal from dense observations while filtering noise, a trade-off that varies by asset liquidity and sampling frequency.

nodes.name: volatility clustering from intraday price dynamics
nodes.description: Large price shocks tend to cluster together within and across days. Raw high-frequency intraday returns contain information about this clustering that is lost when data is aggregated into daily realized measures, allowing models to better predict next-day volatility by observing the full intraday sequence.

nodes.name: information loss from realized measure aggregation
nodes.description: Pre-computing realized measures (e.g., realized variance from 5-minute returns) summarizes intraday data into a single scalar, discarding the temporal structure and relative weighting of intraday shocks. Direct modeling of raw high-frequency sequences preserves this information and allows dynamic, data-driven aggregation rather than static formulas.

nodes.title: LASSO Principal Component Averaging -- a fully automated approach for point forecast pooling
Modeling and forecasting exchange rate volatility in time-frequency domain

nodes.name: heterogeneous investment horizon volatility dynamics
nodes.description: Traders operate at different investment horizons (minutes to months), and volatility dynamics vary across these timescales. Decomposing volatility into frequency components reveals that short-horizon (high-frequency) information dominates volatility forecasting, particularly the 10-minute scale.

nodes.name: jump variation separation from integrated variance
nodes.description: Jump discontinuities and continuous price variation have different impacts on future volatility. Disentangling jump variation from integrated variance improves volatility forecasting because these two components follow distinct dynamics and contain different information for prediction.

nodes.name: microstructure noise contamination of volatility estimates
nodes.description: High-frequency price observations are contaminated with microstructure noise that biases realized volatility estimators. Two-scale and wavelet-based estimators reduce this bias by using multi-grid subsampling and denoising, improving volatility measurement and forecasting accuracy.

nodes.title: Hurricane Forecasting: A Novel Multimodal Machine Learning Framework
Forecasting Realized Volatility Matrix With Copula-Based Models
The impacts of asymmetry on modeling and forecasting realized volatility in Japanese stock markets

nodes.name: leverage effect on volatility
nodes.description: Past negative returns increase future volatility more strongly than positive returns of the same magnitude. This asymmetric response reflects how losses amplify risk perception and volatility forecasts.

nodes.name: realized semivariance decomposition
nodes.description: Volatility driven by negative intraday returns ('bad volatility') has stronger predictive power for future volatility than volatility from positive returns ('good volatility'). This asymmetry improves model fit and forecast accuracy.

nodes.name: asymmetric jump impact
nodes.description: Positive and negative price jumps have differential effects on realized volatility, with negative jumps potentially having stronger influence on future volatility dynamics than positive jumps.

nodes.title: Dynamic functional time-series forecasts of foreign exchange implied volatility surfaces

nodes.name: agent learning and expectation formation
nodes.description: Options market participants learn about future economic scenarios and update their expectations based on forward-looking information embedded in option prices. This learning behavior drives predictable patterns in implied volatility surface shapes across different time-to-expiry horizons, which can be exploited for forecasting.

nodes.name: temporal autocorrelation in volatility surfaces
nodes.description: Daily implied volatility surfaces exhibit moderate to strong temporal dependence, where the shape and level of IV smiles on one day are correlated with previous days. This autocorrelation structure can be captured through long-run covariance estimation to improve forecasting accuracy beyond static variance-based approaches.

nodes.name: cross-maturity information spillovers
nodes.description: Implied volatility smiles across different maturities (1-month, 6-month, 2-year) are correlated with each other due to underlying economic fundamentals and risk factors. Jointly modeling these correlated functional time-series rather than treating them independently improves forecast accuracy by capturing shared latent drivers.

nodes.title: Nonparametric Pricing and Hedging of Volatility Swaps in Stochastic Volatility Models

nodes.name: zero vanna smile extraction
nodes.description: The fair strike of a volatility swap can be read directly from the implied volatility surface at the strike where vanna (cross-gamma of spot and volatility) equals zero. This strike location encodes the market's pricing of realized volatility risk in stochastic volatility models.

nodes.name: historical volatility adjustment for seasoned swaps
nodes.description: As a volatility swap ages and accumulates realized volatility, its fair value must be adjusted by incorporating the historical realized volatility path into the zero vanna calculation. The adjustment uses a synthetic 'historical adjusted' spot process that blends past realized volatility with forward-looking implied volatility.

nodes.name: skew-adjusted delta hedging
nodes.description: Volatility swaps cannot be hedged with a simple delta-neutral option position because the zero vanna strike drifts over time as the smile evolves. The hedge requires a skew-adjusted delta that accounts for how the zero vanna strike moves with spot price changes, plus a vega-weighted notional adjustment.

nodes.name: convexity correction via variance swap replication
nodes.description: When hedging volatility swaps with variance swaps instead of options, a second-order convexity correction arises from the nonlinear relationship between variance and volatility. This correction equals half the second derivative of implied variance at the zero vanna strike, providing an intuitive measure of smile curvature risk.

nodes.title: A probabilistic forecast methodology for volatile electricity prices in the Australian National Electricity Market

nodes.name: extreme price spike filtering
nodes.description: Extreme price spikes in electricity markets are rare outliers driven by supply-demand imbalances and grid constraints, but their high magnitude distorts training of models targeting central quantiles (0.025-0.975). Removing spikes via robust quantile-based classification improves forecast accuracy for non-extreme quantiles by allowing models to focus on the regular price distribution.

nodes.name: autoregressive residual adjustment
nodes.description: Recent price deviations from model expectations contain information about current market conditions beyond the 24-hour lagged price used in base models. Applying autoregression to post-process forecasts by shifting the entire predicted density up or down based on whether current prices exceed expectations captures this temporal dependency and improves accuracy.

nodes.name: ensemble training window diversification
nodes.description: Electricity price dynamics change over time due to evolving market structure, renewable penetration, and weather patterns. Combining forecasts trained on varying lengths of historical data (different 'memory' windows) creates an adaptive ensemble that captures both short-term regime shifts and longer-term structural patterns better than any single training window.

nodes.title: Forecast Evaluation in Large Cross-Sections of Realized Volatility

nodes.name: volatility forecast improvement via shrinkage
nodes.description: An augmented HAR model with LASSO shrinkage produces more accurate out-of-sample forecasts of realized volatility by reducing estimation error in cross-sectional settings, allowing traders to better anticipate volatility regimes and adjust positions before mispricings correct.

nodes.name: measurement error correction in volatility estimation
nodes.description: Adjusting realized volatility forecasts for microstructure noise and measurement errors improves prediction accuracy, reducing false signals that would otherwise lead to suboptimal position sizing and timing.

nodes.name: cross-sectional jump component adjustment
nodes.description: Explicitly modeling and adjusting for jump components in cross-sectional volatility measures prevents large discrete price movements from distorting volatility forecasts, improving prediction accuracy for continuous volatility regimes.
