nodes.title: Forecasting security's volatility using low-frequency historical data, high-frequency historical data and option-implied volatility

nodes.name: option-implied volatility feedback on realized volatility
nodes.description: Investors adjust their volatility expectations and investment decisions based on observed option-implied volatility, which directly influences the future realized volatility of the underlying security through market behavior.

nodes.name: option-implied volatility as noisy measure of latent conditional variance
nodes.description: Option-implied volatility contains useful information about the underlying security's future volatility but does not directly cause volatility changes; instead, it is a measurement with noise of the latent conditional variance implied by the security's own dynamics.

nodes.name: intraday volatility persistence across frequencies
nodes.description: High-frequency intraday price movements (modeled as continuous-time Itô processes) interact with low-frequency daily volatility dynamics, allowing volatility information from different sampling frequencies to jointly predict future volatility.

nodes.title: Multivariate Realized Volatility Forecasting with Graph Neural Network

nodes.name: cross-sectional volatility spillover
nodes.description: Realized volatility of one stock is predictable from limit order book conditions and volatility patterns of related stocks (via sector, supply chain, or feature correlation), because shocks and liquidity conditions propagate across economically connected firms.

nodes.name: temporal volatility clustering
nodes.description: Realized volatility at time t is predictable from LOB features and volatility patterns at historically similar past timestamps, because market microstructure regimes and volatility states persist and recur.

nodes.title: Modeling and Forecasting Realized Volatility with Multivariate Fractional Brownian Motion

nodes.name: long-memory persistence in volatility
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits autocorrelation structure governed by the Hurst exponent H, where H > 0.5 implies positive autocorrelations and non-summable autocovariances, causing volatility shocks to persist over long horizons and making past volatility informative for future forecasts.

nodes.name: cross-asset volatility co-movement with heterogeneous persistence
nodes.description: Realized volatilities across different assets move together contemporaneously (high correlation) while exhibiting different autocorrelation structures (different Hurst exponents), allowing multivariate modeling to extract forecasting value by exploiting these heterogeneous persistence patterns even when univariate models fail.

nodes.title: Data-Efficient Realized Volatility Forecasting with Vision Transformers

nodes.name: nonlinear IV surface feature extraction
nodes.description: The implied volatility surface encodes nonlinear relationships about market dynamics, sentiment, and future realized volatility that can be learned by deep transformer architectures but not by simpler linear models, enabling superior volatility forecasting.

nodes.name: seasonal pattern recognition in volatility
nodes.description: Temporal information (month, day of week) augmented into the IV surface allows models to capture recurring seasonal trends in realized volatility, with ablation showing modest but consistent predictive value.

nodes.title: HARNet: A Convolutional Neural Network for Realized Volatility Forecasting
Forecasting crude oil market volatility: can the Regime Switching GARCH model beat the single-regime GARCH models?

nodes.name: regime switching volatility clustering
nodes.description: Crude oil volatility exhibits distinct regimes (high and low volatility states) that persist and switch according to a Markov process. Structural breaks in variance are better captured by allowing GARCH parameters to vary across regimes rather than assuming a single constant regime, improving volatility forecasts especially at high frequencies.

nodes.name: asymmetric leverage effect
nodes.description: Negative returns correlate with volatility increases more strongly and over shorter timescales than positive returns do, reflecting that price declines trigger faster volatility spikes than price gains, with mean reversion occurring on a different (shorter) timescale than volatility clustering.

nodes.name: frequency-dependent forecast degradation
nodes.description: The superiority of regime-switching models over single-regime models diminishes as data frequency decreases from daily to weekly to monthly. High-frequency data better captures nonlinearities and regime transitions, while low-frequency aggregation smooths volatility patterns and reduces the benefit of regime switching.

nodes.title: Sector Volatility Prediction Performance Using GARCH Models and Artificial Neural Networks

nodes.name: volatility clustering persistence
nodes.description: High or low volatility periods tend to follow each other sequentially, creating predictable patterns in volatility evolution that can be exploited through time-series models that capture conditional heteroskedasticity.

nodes.name: leverage effect asymmetry
nodes.description: Negative market returns generate disproportionately higher subsequent volatility compared to positive returns of equal magnitude, reflecting an asymmetric relationship between price movements and volatility.

nodes.name: volatility shock sensitivity
nodes.description: Market shocks create immediate spikes in conditional volatility that decay over time at different rates depending on asset characteristics. Assets with high shock sensitivity require models that can capture rapid volatility responses to recent price movements.

nodes.title: From GARCH to Neural Network for Volatility Forecast

nodes.name: asymmetric volatility response
nodes.description: Negative news shocks have a larger impact on future volatility than positive news shocks of equal magnitude, causing volatility to rise more sharply following downward price movements.

nodes.name: long-memory volatility effect
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits long-lasting impact on its subsequent evolution through hyperbolic decay of historical shocks rather than exponential decay. This allows volatility to retain information from distant past observations, captured by FI-GARCH models using fractionally integrated lag structures.

nodes.title: Long-term Memory and Volatility Clustering in Daily and High-frequency Price Changes

nodes.name: higher-frequency autocorrelation
nodes.description: High-frequency data (1-minute, 5-minute) exhibits stronger autocorrelation in returns than low-frequency (daily) data. This elevated autocorrelation in high-frequency series contributes to residual long-term memory in volatility even after GARCH filtering, suggesting microstructure effects sustain memory at intraday timescales.

nodes.title: Estimating the volatility of Bitcoin using GARCH models

nodes.name: volatility clustering
nodes.description: Large price movements tend to be followed by large price movements of either sign, and small movements by small movements. This persistence in volatility arises from time-varying risk premia or information arrival clustering.

nodes.name: asymmetric news response
nodes.description: Bad news (negative returns) increases volatility more than good news (positive returns) of the same magnitude. This leverage effect is captured by the threshold term in tGARCH, where negative shocks have an amplified impact on conditional variance.

nodes.title: Combining Deep Learning and GARCH Models for Financial Volatility and Risk Forecasting
Volatility Modeling of Stocks from Selected Sectors of the Indian Economy Using GARCH
Unified GARCH-Recurrent Neural Network in Financial Volatility Forecasting

nodes.name: volatility clustering with nonlinear mean reversion
nodes.description: Financial volatility exhibits both linear autoregressive dynamics (captured by GARCH) and nonlinear temporal dependencies that standard linear models miss. By embedding GARCH structure within recurrent neural networks, the model captures how volatility shocks persist and mean-revert through complex nonlinear pathways, improving forecasts especially during regime changes.

nodes.name: stress-period volatility forecast accuracy
nodes.description: During market turbulence and extreme stress periods (e.g., COVID-19), hybrid GARCH-RNN models maintain superior forecasting accuracy and well-calibrated tail risk estimates compared to classical approaches. This suggests the model adapts to changing market regimes where nonlinear dynamics become more pronounced, enabling better risk management when it matters most.

nodes.title: Measuring Volatility Clustering in Stock Markets
A Heterogeneous Spatiotemporal GARCH Model: A Predictive Framework for Volatility in Financial Networks

nodes.name: spatial volatility spillover via correlated innovations
nodes.description: Volatility shocks propagate across firms through contemporaneous spatial correlation in the innovation process, which then feeds forward into future volatility via the recursive GARCH mechanism. Firms with similar balance sheet characteristics experience correlated return shocks that amplify each other's conditional variance over time.

nodes.name: volatility clustering with spatial heterogeneity
nodes.description: Large return innovations tend to be followed by periods of high volatility, but the persistence and magnitude of this clustering varies smoothly across firms based on their structural economic characteristics (balance sheet positions). Firms in different regions of the latent economic space exhibit distinct baseline volatility, shock responsiveness, and mean reversion rates.

nodes.name: network contagion through squared return dependence
nodes.description: Spatial dependence in squared returns (which drive the GARCH recursion) decays more slowly than dependence in raw innovations, creating a mechanism by which volatility shocks at one firm influence the conditional variance of economically similar firms with a longer effective range than the underlying shock correlation.

nodes.title: The relationship between trading volumes, number of transactions, and stock volatility in GARCH models

nodes.name: information arrival rate proxy
nodes.description: Trading volume and transaction count serve as observable proxies for the latent rate of information arrivals to the market. Higher information arrival rates drive both increased trading activity and volatility clustering.

nodes.name: volatility persistence
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits strong autocorrelation (GARCH effects, α+β close to 1), meaning past volatility and past squared returns predict current volatility. This persistence may reflect incomplete information incorporation or latent information arrival dynamics not fully captured by observable trading metrics.

nodes.title: GARCH-Informed Neural Networks for Volatility Prediction in Financial Markets

nodes.name: volatility prediction alpha
nodes.description: Improved forecasting of market volatility through hybrid GARCH-LSTM models enables traders to better assess risk and optimize entry/exit timing, generating alpha by outperforming traditional volatility prediction methods.

nodes.title: Introducing the $σ$-Cell: Unifying GARCH, Stochastic Fluctuations and Evolving Mechanisms in RNN-based Volatility Forecasting
The Hybrid Forecast of S&P 500 Volatility ensembled from VIX, GARCH and LSTM models

nodes.name: market sentiment fear gauge signal
nodes.description: The VIX index captures real-time investor sentiment and market expectations about future volatility, providing forward-looking information that improves volatility forecasts beyond backward-looking historical measures.

nodes.title: Autoencoder Enhanced Realised GARCH on Volatility Forecasting

nodes.name: intraday volatility information content
nodes.description: High-frequency intraday price movements contain more accurate and timely information about true volatility than daily squared returns, because they capture price variability at fine time scales (minute-by-minute) rather than relying on end-of-day closing prices, reducing noise from idiosyncratic daily shocks.

nodes.name: microstructure noise contamination
nodes.description: High-frequency realised volatility measures are contaminated by market microstructure effects (bid-ask bounce, discreteness of prices, irregular trading) that introduce noise unrelated to true price discovery, requiring smoothing or robust estimation techniques to isolate genuine volatility signals.

nodes.name: nonlinear measure synthesis
nodes.description: Multiple realised volatility estimators (Realised Variance, Realised Kernel, Bipower Variation, etc.) each capture different aspects of volatility; combining them through nonlinear dimension reduction (autoencoder) rather than linear methods (PCA, ICA) better preserves complex interdependencies and improves forecast accuracy by enabling more flexible parameter adaptation.

nodes.title: Impact of COVID-19 on Exchange rate volatility of Bangladesh: Evidence through GARCH model

nodes.name: pandemic uncertainty shock to exchange rate volatility
nodes.description: Increases in confirmed COVID-19 cases create economic uncertainty that directly elevates exchange rate volatility through reduced export demand, FDI flows, and current account disruptions. The effect is strongest during the sustained pandemic period (after peak cases) when structural economic damage becomes apparent.

nodes.name: volatility clustering in crisis periods
nodes.description: Large exchange rate movements tend to be followed by further large movements during pandemic stress, creating persistent volatility clustering that is captured by GARCH effects. This clustering is more pronounced during the sustained pandemic phase than the initial outbreak phase.

nodes.title: Institutional Differences, Crisis Shocks, and Volatility Structure: A By-Window EGARCH/TGARCH Analysis of ASEAN Stock Markets

nodes.name: crisis amplification of volatility persistence
nodes.description: External shocks (Taper Tantrum, COVID-19, rate hikes) increase the persistence of volatility (α + β approaching unity), causing uncertainty to linger longer in markets and shocks to take extended time to dissipate.

nodes.name: bad-news amplification during crises
nodes.description: During crisis periods, negative shocks exert disproportionately stronger effects on volatility (γ increases significantly) compared to positive shocks, reflecting intensified investor fear and liquidity constraints that magnify downside risk.

nodes.name: institutional buffering of volatility recovery
nodes.description: Markets with stronger institutional frameworks (regulatory transparency, macroprudential governance, market depth) recover faster from crises—volatility persistence and asymmetry normalize more quickly—whereas weaker institutions prolong instability and bad-news sensitivity.

nodes.name: fat-tail amplification under stress
nodes.description: During crises, the degrees of freedom (ν) in return distributions decline, indicating heavier tails and increased probability of extreme price movements, reflecting heightened tail risk when markets face external shocks.

nodes.title: Adjust factor with volatility model using MAXFLAT low-pass filter and construct portfolio in China A share market

nodes.name: noise filtering via volatility-adjusted factors
nodes.description: Traditional factor models contain noise that degrades risk-adjusted returns. Filtering factor signals through a MAXFLAT low-pass volatility model removes high-frequency noise while preserving persistent trend components, improving factor quality and portfolio alpha.

nodes.name: volatility regime adaptation
nodes.description: Factor exposures and their predictive power vary across volatility regimes. Adjusting factor loadings dynamically based on a MAXFLAT volatility model captures time-varying risk premia and reduces systematic underperformance during high-volatility periods.

nodes.title: GARCH-FIS: A Hybrid Forecasting Model with Dynamic Volatility-Driven Parameter Adaptation

nodes.name: volatility-regime-adaptive forecasting
nodes.description: Market predictability varies with volatility regime; a model that dynamically adjusts its inference granularity (widening during high volatility, narrowing during stability) can capture nonlinear dynamics more accurately across different market conditions, generating alpha through regime-aware parameter adaptation.

nodes.name: error-accumulation mitigation in multi-step forecasting
nodes.description: Recursive multi-step forecasts suffer from compounding prediction errors; dynamically adjusting model parameters at each forecast step—incorporating the most recent predicted price and updated volatility estimates—reduces error propagation and maintains forecast stability over extended horizons.

nodes.title: The VIX as Stochastic Volatility for Corporate Bonds

nodes.name: volatility-driven credit spread widening
nodes.description: Corporate bond spreads widen during periods of high market volatility (VIX) because investors demand higher compensation for increased default risk. The VIX term enters the spread regression with positive coefficient c, reflecting that turbulent times coincide with elevated default probabilities.

nodes.name: mean-reverting spread dynamics
nodes.description: Corporate bond spreads exhibit mean reversion (b < 1) because the additional default risk premium cannot increase indefinitely. Spreads widen in crises but eventually revert as economic conditions normalize and default risk subsides.

nodes.name: duration-driven bond return sensitivity
nodes.description: Bond returns depend on two components: yield income (proportional to initial rate) and interest rate risk (proportional to duration and rate changes). Price declines when yields rise, creating negative sensitivity to rate increases that scales with bond duration.

nodes.title: Minimizing the Probability of Lifetime Ruin under Stochastic Volatility
Multiple time scales and the exponential Ornstein-Uhlenbeck stochastic volatility model

nodes.name: leverage effect (negative return-volatility correlation)
nodes.description: Negative correlation between past returns and future volatility: negative price movements predict higher subsequent volatility with exponential decay. This asymmetric volatility response operates on a short timescale (10-20 days) distinct from the long-memory volatility autocorrelation.

nodes.name: multiscale volatility mean reversion
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits long memory with at least two distinct timescales: a short timescale (weeks, ~35 days for DJIA) governing rapid mean reversion, and a long timescale (hundreds of days, ~550 days for DJIA) governing slow decay. The model captures this via exponential Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics with log-normal volatility distribution.

nodes.name: log-normal volatility distribution
nodes.description: Volatility is log-normally distributed in stationary state rather than Gaussian, matching empirical observations better. This non-Gaussian distribution generates skewness and excess kurtosis in returns that simple constant-volatility models cannot capture.

nodes.title: Analysis of Spin Financial Market by GARCH Model

nodes.name: herding-driven volatility clustering
nodes.description: Agents imitate neighboring agents (ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor interaction), causing coordinated buy/sell behavior that alternates with contrarian minority effects. This creates persistent high- and low-volatility regimes as the system switches between ordered and disordered phases.

nodes.name: bubble-driven phase transitions
nodes.description: When magnetization (aggregate order imbalance) grows large, agents switch to minority positions to avoid losses when the bubble bursts. This anti-ferromagnetic global interaction causes the system to oscillate between ferromagnetic (low volatility) and disordered (high volatility) phases, generating intermittent return spikes.

nodes.name: time-varying volatility with stable return distribution
nodes.description: Returns follow a mixture-of-distribution hypothesis where r(t) = σ_t × ε_t, with time-varying volatility σ_t and independent Gaussian shocks ε_t. Standardizing returns by estimated volatility removes fat tails and autocorrelation in absolute returns, leaving approximately normal standardized returns.

nodes.title: Option Pricing with Stochastic Volatility, Equity Premium, and Interest Rates
Parallel Gaussian Process Regression for Big Data: Low-Rank Representation Meets Markov Approximation
American Option Pricing Under Time-Varying Rough Volatility: A Signature-Based Hybrid Framework

nodes.name: time-varying roughness regime switching
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits time-varying Hurst parameter H(t) that drifts below 0.5 during stress and toward 0.5+ during calm periods. Pricing engines should switch between rough Bergomi (H<0.5) and Heston (H≥0.5) models to match the current market regime, improving valuation accuracy over fixed-roughness assumptions.

nodes.name: rough volatility path dependence
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits non-Markovian, fractionally-integrated dynamics (H < 1/2) that create path-dependent pricing effects. Standard approximation schemes diverge without renormalization because the quadratic covariation between rough volatility and returns does not exist in classical sense, requiring explicit correction terms.

nodes.name: leverage effect correlation
nodes.description: Asset returns and volatility changes exhibit negative correlation (leverage effect), which must be estimated and incorporated into stochastic volatility models via the correlation parameter ρ. This correlation structure affects the joint dynamics of price and variance and influences early-exercise decisions.

nodes.title: Parallel Gaussian Process Regression with Low-Rank Covariance Matrix Approximations
Capital Asset Pricing Model with Size Factor and Normalizing by Volatility Index

nodes.name: size-driven beta variation
nodes.description: Smaller stocks exhibit higher systematic risk (beta) relative to large-cap benchmarks due to their smaller market capitalization. This manifests as a linear relationship where beta increases as relative size decreases, with empirical estimates showing small-cap beta around 1.27 versus mid-cap at 1.15.

nodes.name: mean-reversion of relative size
nodes.description: Portfolio relative size (log ratio of target to benchmark market cap) exhibits mean-reversion over time. Small stocks tend to grow faster than large stocks on average, causing formerly small portfolios to become larger and vice versa, maintaining long-term stability of the market structure.

nodes.name: volatility normalization of returns
nodes.description: Raw returns and equity premia exhibit time-varying volatility and non-Gaussian distributions with autocorrelated absolute values. Dividing returns by the VIX (volatility index) normalizes them to approximate IID Gaussian distributions, improving model fit and statistical properties.

nodes.title: Stock Price Dynamics and Option Valuations under Volatility Feedback Effect

nodes.name: time-varying dividend yield risk premium
nodes.description: The market price of diffusion return risk (equity risk premium) determines the sensitivity of dividend yield to return volatility. Higher risk aversion increases the stochastic risk premium, which lowers the price-dividend ratio and raises dividend yield, affecting option valuations through the cost of capital channel.

nodes.title: An application of the method of moments to volatility estimation using daily high, low, opening and closing prices

nodes.name: after-hours information jump
nodes.description: Price jumps at market open due to information arrival during after-hours periods, which can be modeled as an unobserved virtual trading day. This jump creates a discontinuity between closing and opening prices that must be accounted for in volatility estimation.

nodes.name: intraday range volatility
nodes.description: The daily high-low range of prices contains information about intraday volatility that is independent of drift and can be extracted via the expected range of an arithmetic Brownian motion, providing a more efficient volatility estimator than close-to-close returns alone.

nodes.name: option mispricing exploitation
nodes.description: By accurately modeling pathwise price dynamics through rough path signatures, traders can identify systematically mispriced options in the market and exploit these inefficiencies for alpha generation.

nodes.title: The Low-volatility Anomaly and the Adaptive Multi-Factor Model

nodes.name: differential factor exposure across volatility regimes
nodes.description: Low-volatility and high-volatility portfolios load on fundamentally different risk factors. The outperformance of low-volatility stocks is not due to volatility being an independent risk, but rather due to the equilibrium performance of the specific factors that low-volatility stocks happen to expose to.

nodes.name: leverage constraints on high-volatility demand
nodes.description: Retail, pension, and mutual fund investors face leverage constraints that prevent them from using leverage to amplify returns on low-volatility stocks. This constraint-induced demand for high-volatility stocks (as a substitute for leveraged low-volatility positions) drives up their valuations and depresses their risk-adjusted returns.

nodes.name: lottery demand and behavioral bias toward high-beta stocks
nodes.description: Behavioral biases including lottery-like demand for high-volatility stocks, combined with limits to arbitrage, cause investors to overpay for high-beta securities. Sell-side analyst over-emphasis on high-volatility stocks further inflates their valuations relative to fundamentals.

nodes.title: Dark Matter in (Volatility and) Equity Option Risk Premiums

nodes.name: unspanned jump risk premium
nodes.description: Jump risks that cross option strike prices are not fully priced into the market because they cannot be hedged using the underlying asset alone. This mispricing creates negative risk premiums for out-of-the-money options, allowing traders to exploit the underpricing of jump tail risk.

nodes.name: unspanned volatility risk premium
nodes.description: Equity return volatility contains unspanned risks—volatility fluctuations that cannot be replicated by trading the underlying stock. These unspanned volatility components command negative risk premiums, creating systematic mispricing in options sensitive to volatility dynamics.

nodes.name: local time mispricing
nodes.description: The local time component of option payoffs (related to realized quadratic variation near the strike) carries unspanned risk that the market prices with a negative premium, creating exploitable mispricings in straddles and other volatility-sensitive strategies.

nodes.title: Valuation equations for stochastic volatility models
Marked Hawkes process modeling of price dynamics and volatility estimation

nodes.name: trade clustering self-excitation
nodes.description: Past trades exhibit self-exciting clustering behavior that predicts future price movements. The timing and intensity of recent trades increase the probability of imminent trades, allowing prediction of emerging trends before they fully materialize.

nodes.name: mean reversion from directional reversal
nodes.description: The frequency of up movements increases following down movements and vice versa, creating mean-reverting price dynamics at ultra-high frequency. This mutual excitation between opposite directions causes short-term reversals lasting less than a few seconds.

nodes.name: jump size amplification of future intensity
nodes.description: Larger price jumps (marks) magnify future event intensities more than smaller jumps through a linear impact function. The empirical estimates show significant positive slope parameters, meaning larger moves beget more volatile future activity.

nodes.name: microstructure noise mean-reversion
nodes.description: High-frequency price returns are strongly anticorrelated due to the discrete structure of the limit order book. When a price jump occurs in one direction, the next jump is likely to reverse, creating mechanical mean-reversion that inflates realized volatility at fine observation frequencies.

nodes.title: Indifference prices and implied volatilities

nodes.name: risk aversion premium in incomplete markets
nodes.description: In incomplete markets, an investor with exponential utility demands a bid-ask spread between buyer and seller indifference prices because they face unhedgeable volatility risk. The spread arises from the investor's optimal portfolio choice under incomplete information about non-traded volatility drivers.

nodes.name: volatility risk compensation
nodes.description: The indiference price incorporates compensation for exposure to stochastic volatility (Y) that cannot be perfectly hedged by trading only the underlying asset (S). The nonlinear terms in the pricing PDE reflect the investor's marginal utility cost of bearing this unhedgeable volatility risk.

nodes.name: hedging demand under local-stochastic volatility
nodes.description: An investor holding an option on a traded asset must dynamically hedge by trading the underlying stock, but the optimal hedge ratio depends on both the asset price (X) and the unobservable volatility state (Y). This creates a nonlinear feedback between the option payoff and the volatility process, generating path-dependent hedging costs that appear in the indiference price.

nodes.title: A lattice framework for pricing display advertisement options with the stochastic volatility underlying model
Price sensitivities for a general stochastic volatility model

nodes.name: volatility risk mispricings from model misspecification
nodes.description: Stochastic volatility models that fail to accurately capture true volatility dynamics leave hedging gaps, allowing traders to exploit mispricings between model-implied and realized volatility by using more precise price sensitivities.

nodes.name: hedging efficiency gains from improved price sensitivities
nodes.description: More accurate calculation of price sensitivities (Greeks) using Malliavin calculus enables superior hedging strategies that better isolate and manage financial risks, reducing unhedged exposure and improving risk-adjusted returns.

nodes.title: Calibrated rank volatility stabilized models for large equity markets

nodes.name: rank volatility mean reversion
nodes.description: Stocks with extreme rank-based volatilities tend to revert toward the cross-sectional mean volatility, creating predictable relative price movements. This mean reversion in the volatility ranking of stocks generates growth-optimal trading signals.

nodes.name: market weight collision exploitation
nodes.description: When stocks experience market weight collisions (rapid changes in relative market capitalization rankings), the model exploits the temporary mispricing and rebalancing pressure to generate relative arbitrage opportunities against the market portfolio.

nodes.name: relative arbitrage via portfolio rebalancing
nodes.description: The growth-optimal portfolio derived from rank volatility stabilized models can outperform the market portfolio by systematically rebalancing across stocks with different rank-volatility characteristics, exploiting the ergodic properties of ranked market weights over long horizons.

nodes.title: Variance and Volatility Swaps and Futures Pricing for Stochastic Volatility Models

nodes.name: convexity correction in volatility pricing
nodes.description: The nonlinearity of the square root function in realized volatility creates a convexity bias: the expected value of volatility (square root of variance) is less than the square root of expected variance. This bias must be corrected when pricing volatility swaps, and the magnitude depends on the variance of realized variance.

nodes.name: mean reversion of stochastic volatility
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits mean reversion toward a long-run average level (theta parameter), with speed determined by the mean reversion coefficient (kappa). This mean-reverting dynamics affects both the expected path of future volatility and its variance, which in turn determines the fair strike prices for volatility derivatives.

nodes.name: jump risk premium in volatility derivatives
nodes.description: Asset price jumps (modeled via Poisson processes in Merton and Bates models) contribute an additional source of variance beyond continuous diffusion. The jump intensity, jump size distribution, and their moments directly affect the fair variance and volatility strike prices, creating a jump risk component separate from diffusive volatility.

nodes.title: Behavioral Finance -- Asset Prices Predictability, Equity Premium Puzzle, Volatility Puzzle: The Rational Finance Approach

nodes.name: predictability from Stratonovich integral structure
nodes.description: Asset prices follow Stratonovich α-integrals rather than Itô integrals, which 'look into the future' and generate predictable price dynamics. The degree of predictability depends on the excess predictability parameter ρ = γ - α, where traders may have superior or inferior information about the true price process.

nodes.name: heavy-tailed consumption growth distribution
nodes.description: Consumption growth follows a Normal-Inverse Gaussian (NIG) distribution with heavy tails and excess kurtosis rather than log-normal, which generates a larger equity premium through tail risk compensation. This explains why observed equity premiums are higher than log-normal models predict without requiring implausibly high risk aversion coefficients.

nodes.name: excess volatility from investor belief disagreement
nodes.description: Stock prices exhibit excess volatility because investors disagree about or overestimate the variability of mean dividend growth rates, causing prices to fluctuate more than fundamentals alone would justify. This rational disagreement about growth rate distributions drives volatility beyond what discounted cash flow models predict.

nodes.title: Volatility conditional on price trends

nodes.name: trend-induced volatility clustering
nodes.description: Past price trends (measured as products of non-overlapping returns) causally induce future realized volatility. Trending prices lead to increased volatility while drifting prices lead to decreased volatility, creating a predictable volatility pattern conditional on recent price behavior.

nodes.title: Volatility-based strategy on Chinese equity index ETF options

nodes.name: implied volatility overpricing
nodes.description: Option premiums are inflated above fair value due to hedging demand from large institutions and retail preference for lottery-like payoffs, creating a persistent gap between implied and realized volatility that short-volatility strategies can exploit.

nodes.name: volatility mean reversion
nodes.description: Realized volatility exhibits mean-reverting behavior where high volatility periods tend to be followed by lower volatility, and vice versa. This predictability allows dynamic position adjustment based on volatility forecasts to improve strategy returns.

nodes.name: market regime shift in volatility pricing
nodes.description: Post-2018, Chinese equity markets experienced structural changes (increased quant fund activity, higher baseline volatility) that eliminated the historical overpricing of volatility, causing previously profitable short-volatility strategies to deteriorate as market participants better price volatility risk.

nodes.title: Entropy Rate for Hidden Markov Chains with rare transitions
Context-specific kernel-based hidden Markov model for time series analysis
Optimal control of risk process in a regime-switching environment
Hidden Markov processes in the context of symbolic dynamics
Sequential Tracking of a Hidden Markov Chain Using Point Process Observations
Regime Switching Optimal Growth Model with Risk Sensitive Preferences

nodes.name: regime-dependent production shock response
nodes.description: Investment returns depend on both current capital allocation and the underlying economic regime (expansion/recession), with regime transitions affecting optimal consumption-investment decisions. Agents must account for regime-switching productivity shocks when allocating resources.

nodes.name: risk-sensitive preference adjustment
nodes.description: Under non-expected utility with risk aversion parameter γ > 0, the agent assigns higher probability weight to worse-case scenarios (lower value states) when making consumption decisions. This creates a worst-case probability measure that differs from the standard equilibrium measure, causing more conservative investment behavior in uncertain regimes.

nodes.title: Human in the Loop: Interactive Passive Automata Learning via Evidence-Driven State-Merging Algorithms

nodes.name: implicit domain knowledge exploitation
nodes.description: Market inefficiencies arise because traders and models fail to capture implicit domain expertise about market microstructure. By incorporating human insights directly into algorithmic learning, the model can uncover hidden patterns in market dynamics that purely data-driven approaches miss, generating alpha through superior understanding of regime changes.

nodes.name: adaptive market regime detection
nodes.description: Market conditions change over time in ways that static models cannot capture. An interactive learning algorithm that incorporates human feedback can adapt more effectively to regime shifts, improving predictive power by dynamically updating the underlying state automaton as market structure evolves.

nodes.title: Continuous-time reinforcement learning for optimal switching over multiple regimes
Statistical identification with hidden Markov models of large order splitting strategies in an equity market

nodes.name: order splitting to minimize price impact
nodes.description: Large institutional orders are split into smaller pieces and executed incrementally over time to reduce the price impact of the full order size and lower overall execution costs. By revealing only partial demand, traders can execute portions at prices less affected by their own trading activity.

nodes.name: directional state persistence in order execution
nodes.description: Market members exhibit prolonged periods of consistent buy or sell activity (high diagonal transition probabilities in the Markov chain), indicating that once a large order execution begins in one direction, the trader tends to continue in that direction rather than switching randomly. This persistence reflects the strategic commitment to completing a hidden order.

nodes.name: buy-sell asymmetry in execution strategy
nodes.description: Buy and sell patches exhibit different statistical properties (number, length, fraction of market orders, participation rate) that depend on local market trend. This asymmetry suggests traders use different execution tactics for buys versus sells, potentially due to different inventory risk or information asymmetries in each direction.

nodes.title: Risk Sensitive Portfolio Optimization with Default Contagion and Regime-Switching

nodes.name: default contagion intensity modulation
nodes.description: Default intensities of surviving securities are affected simultaneously by default events of other stocks in the portfolio, creating feedback effects that alter risk dynamics and optimal allocation decisions.

nodes.name: regime-dependent default risk
nodes.description: Default intensities, drift, and volatility coefficients of stocks all depend on macroeconomic regime states, causing portfolio risk and optimal strategies to shift with regime transitions.

nodes.name: risk-sensitive growth rate optimization
nodes.description: Investors maximize long-run portfolio growth rate adjusted by a volatility penalty (controlled by risk-sensitivity parameter θ), which creates a dynamic trade-off between expected returns and variance of realized growth rates.

nodes.title: Hidden Markov Models and their Application for Predicting Failure Events
Detection of Structural Regimes and Analyzing the Impact of Crude Oil Market on Canadian Stock Market: Markov Regime-Switching Approach

nodes.name: regime-dependent oil price transmission
nodes.description: Oil price shocks have asymmetric effects on stock returns depending on market regime: negative impact during positive-return regimes (when growth is strong) but positive impact during negative-return regimes (when growth is weak). This reflects differential sensitivity of equity valuations to commodity price movements across economic states.

nodes.name: regime-dependent volatility asymmetry
nodes.description: Stock market volatility differs systematically across regimes, with positive-return regimes exhibiting higher volatility than negative-return regimes. This creates state-dependent risk premia that affect how external shocks (like oil prices) propagate into equity returns.

nodes.name: lagged oil price effect reversal
nodes.description: The sign of oil price impact on stock returns reverses at a two-period lag depending on regime: lagged oil price decreases returns in positive-return regimes but increases returns in negative-return regimes. This suggests delayed adjustment mechanisms or regime-specific expectations about commodity-equity linkages.

nodes.title: A Hybrid Learning Approach to Detecting Regime Switches in Financial Markets

nodes.name: crisis regime identification via macroeconomic aggregation
nodes.description: Financial markets transition between distinct regimes (crisis vs. non-crisis) that can be identified by clustering patterns in aggregated macroeconomic indicators. Crisis periods exhibit systematically different combinations of productivity, income, and expenditure metrics that precede or coincide with market stress.

nodes.name: regime-dependent asset return reversal
nodes.description: Assets exhibit fundamentally different expected return patterns across regimes: positive returns during normal economic periods (regime 1) and negative returns during crisis periods (regime 2). This regime-dependent mean reversion allows tactical switching strategies to capture alpha by rotating exposure based on predicted regime.

nodes.name: drawdown concentration in crisis regimes
nodes.description: Maximum drawdowns are concentrated in identifiable crisis regimes rather than distributed randomly across time. By detecting regime switches, investors can reduce exposure during high-drawdown periods, thereby lowering portfolio maximum drawdown without sacrificing long-term returns.

nodes.title: Learning Markov State Abstractions for Deep Reinforcement Learning
Detecting bearish and bullish markets in financial time series using hierarchical hidden Markov models

nodes.name: regime-dependent return distribution
nodes.description: Markets operate in distinct hidden regimes (bullish, bearish, volatile) where each regime generates returns from a different distribution with different mean and variance. Short-term price fluctuations within a regime should not be misinterpreted as regime switches.

nodes.name: multi-scale trend separation
nodes.description: Long-term market trends (lasting months) operate on a different timescale than short-term daily fluctuations. A hierarchical model structure is needed to simultaneously capture both scales; single-scale models confound short-term noise with long-term regime changes.

nodes.title: Stock Market Trend Analysis Using Hidden Markov Model and Long Short Term Memory
Empirical comparison of three models for determining market clearing prices in Turkish day-ahead electricity market

nodes.name: non-convexity-induced bid paradox
nodes.description: Indivisibility constraints on block bids create non-convex market clearing problems where the welfare-maximizing solution may reject bids with positive surplus (paradoxically rejected bids) or accept bids with negative surplus (paradoxically accepted bids), preventing Walrasian equilibrium.

nodes.name: block bid all-or-nothing constraint premium
nodes.description: All-or-nothing requirements on block bids force discrete acceptance/rejection decisions that cannot be partially filled, creating surplus losses relative to a convex market where all bids could be continuously matched. The cost of enforcing either 'no loss' or 'no missed profit' rules is approximately 2,000 Turkish liras per day in foregone total surplus.

nodes.name: supply-demand imbalance price pressure
nodes.description: When supply block bid volume substantially exceeds demand block bid volume (83% supply in 2015), the market clearing mechanism that prevents paradoxically accepted bids (M3) produces lower clearing prices (~2 Turkish liras lower) than mechanisms that prevent paradoxically rejected bids (M2), due to the asymmetric composition of binding constraints.

nodes.title: Testing the Number of Regimes in Markov Regime Switching Models
Nonlinear Filters for Hidden Markov Models of Regime Change with Fast Mean-Reverting States

nodes.name: fast mean reversion to regime-dependent equilibrium
nodes.description: Hidden state variables (velocity, volatility) rapidly revert to a regime-dependent mean controlled by a continuous-time Markov chain. As mean reversion speed increases (ϵ → 0), the posterior distribution of fast-reverting states converges to an invariant measure, allowing dimension reduction in filtering.

nodes.name: regime-switching state dynamics
nodes.description: A hidden Markov chain controls the shifting mean of mean-reverting processes. Regime transitions occur at finite rates, and the transition intensities can depend on the current state value, creating path-dependent filtering dynamics that simplify under fast mean reversion.

nodes.name: discrete observation sampling enables state averaging
nodes.description: When observations arrive discretely (e.g., daily prices), the fast mean-reverting state has time to relax to its invariant distribution between observations. This allows the nonlinear filter to average over the fast state and reduce to a lower-dimensional filter tracking only the regime Markov chain.

nodes.title: An Adaptive Tabu Search Algorithm for Market Clearing Problem in Turkish Day-Ahead Market
Stock Market Trend Analysis Using Hidden Markov Models

nodes.name: mean-reverting regime switching
nodes.description: Stock prices transition between hidden regimes (very low to very high states) based on price momentum. The HMM captures that price movements follow predictable state sequences where regimes tend to alternate, allowing trend forecasting.

nodes.title: Analyticity of Entropy Rate of Hidden Markov Chains
On the design of sell-side limit and market order tactics

nodes.name: adverse price selection on passive orders
nodes.description: Limit orders filled passively suffer adverse selection because they are more likely to execute before unfavorable price moves than favorable ones. The probability asymmetry between upticks and downticks (qa = qdn - qup) quantifies informed order flow that exploits passive traders.

nodes.name: queue position information leakage
nodes.description: High-frequency traders exploit latency advantages to detect and front-run passive limit orders posted at inferior queue positions. Orders at the bottom of the queue face higher adverse selection than orders at the top, creating hidden transaction costs from information leakage.

nodes.name: market impact decay with order splitting
nodes.description: Splitting large orders into smaller trades over time reduces instantaneous market impact but creates long-memory effects through a power-law decay kernel. Frequent order splitting amplifies cumulative price impact due to information leakage about the parent order.

nodes.name: liquidity availability constraint on execution schedule
nodes.description: Available liquidity fluctuates stochastically and is not consistently available at all times, making conventional optimal execution schedules (block trading at open/close) infeasible. Traders must adapt schedules dynamically based on realized liquidity constraints rather than following deterministic plans.

nodes.title: A polyhedral Markov field - pushing the Arak-Surgailis construction into three dimensions
Optimal execution with nonlinear transient market impact

nodes.name: transient market impact decay
nodes.description: Trading activity causes immediate price impact that decays over time according to a power-law kernel. The price relaxation after an order allows subsequent trades to be executed at better prices, creating an intertemporal tradeoff in execution strategy.

nodes.name: nonlinear instantaneous impact
nodes.description: The immediate price impact of a trade is a concave function of volume (empirically approximated by power laws with exponent 0.2-0.5), meaning larger trades have diminishing per-share impact. This nonlinearity creates incentives for front-loaded execution strategies.

nodes.name: transaction-triggered price manipulation
nodes.description: Under nonlinear transient impact, round-trip strategies (buy then sell, or vice versa) can generate negative expected costs by exploiting the concavity of impact and time-decay of price effects. Intermediate trades in the opposite direction can reduce overall execution costs below zero.

nodes.title: Market Microstructure of Non Fungible Tokens

nodes.name: hype-driven price discovery
nodes.description: NFT prices are formed primarily through market sentiment and hype rather than fundamental information, leading to prices that reflect collective psychology and FOMO rather than intrinsic value. This makes price discovery vulnerable to speculation and sentiment-driven volatility.

nodes.name: wash-trading artificial inflation
nodes.description: Market participants execute self-dealing trades to artificially inflate trading volume and asset prices, creating false signals of market activity and value. This manipulation is motivated by market-making (price inflation), rate-making (artist reputation), platform incentives, and project promotion.

nodes.name: information asymmetry in decentralized markets
nodes.description: The lack of pre-trade and post-trade transparency in decentralized NFT marketplaces creates information asymmetries between informed and uninformed traders. Market makers exploit this asymmetry through bid-ask spreads, while the absence of regulatory oversight enables manipulation.

nodes.name: secondary market liquidity hoarding
nodes.description: Owners strategically withhold NFTs from secondary markets (HODL behavior) waiting for opportune moments to sell, reducing secondary market liquidity and price discovery efficiency. The absence of secondary market activity can signal either speculative waiting or abandoned communities.

nodes.title: Stock market microstructure inference via multi-agent reinforcement learning

nodes.name: mean-reverting microstructure pressure
nodes.description: Short-lag negative autocorrelation in returns arises from order book clearing mechanics where prices are set at the marginal clearing level, causing temporary deviations from fundamental value to reverse as the order book re-equilibrates.

nodes.name: volatility clustering via order flow persistence
nodes.description: Large price movements tend to be followed by similarly large movements because agents' learned trading policies respond to recent market microstructure conditions and volatility states, creating persistence in order flow intensity and thus in realized volatility.

nodes.name: chartist-fundamental strategy divergence
nodes.description: Agents learn mixed pricing strategies that blend chartist (price-based) and fundamental (intrinsic value-based) signals; when these diverge significantly, agents' heterogeneous learned policies create non-Gaussian return distributions with fat tails and skewness as different agent cohorts trade against each other.

nodes.title: Foreign Exchange Market Microstructure and the WM/Reuters 4pm Fix

nodes.name: order flow compression volatility
nodes.description: Concentration of large trading volume into a narrow 60-second fixing window creates temporary order imbalances that deplete liquidity on one side of the order book, causing elevated volatility and extreme price movements in anticipation of the fix.

nodes.name: unequal liquidity supply pressure
nodes.description: When order flow is compressed into the fixing window, surplus orders on one side of the order book deplete liquidity on the opposite side, forcing prices to move to extreme levels to clear the accumulated imbalance.

nodes.name: benchmark-driven execution clustering
nodes.description: Institutional investors executing trades at the WM/R 4pm fix create synchronized order flow that clusters execution into the 60-second fixing interval, generating predictable market microstructure distortions distinct from information-driven price movements.

nodes.title: The Inelastic Market Hypothesis: A Microstructural Interpretation

nodes.name: latent liquidity adjustment
nodes.description: Market participants hold latent (non-posted) trading intentions at reservation prices that remain sticky over a memory timescale. When order flow forces price moves, these reservation prices gradually realign toward the new market price, creating transient square-root impact that decays to permanent linear impact over longer horizons.

nodes.name: reservation price stickiness
nodes.description: Investors' reservation prices (their willingness-to-trade thresholds) do not adjust instantaneously to new market prices but remain sticky over a characteristic memory timescale. This creates temporary barriers to price adjustment and explains why impact is non-linear in the short run.

nodes.name: self-generated volatility from feedback trading
nodes.description: A large fraction of market volatility (≳80%) is self-generated through self-exciting feedback loops in trading activity rather than driven by exogenous news. Trades trigger further trades, creating bursts of volatility independent of fundamental information.

nodes.title: Semi Markov model for market microstructure

nodes.name: volatility clustering via activity intensity
nodes.description: Market activity alternates between high and low intensity phases independently of intraday seasonality. Jump times follow a Markov renewal process where the hazard rate of the next price jump depends on time elapsed and the direction of recent jumps, creating bursts of trading activity.

nodes.name: trend-reversal asymmetry in jump timing
nodes.description: The distribution of inter-arrival times between price jumps differs significantly depending on whether consecutive jumps are in the same direction (trend) or opposite directions (mean-reverting). Trend jumps are rare and have longer, more variable inter-arrival times, while mean-reverting jumps cluster more tightly, reflecting different underlying market dynamics.

nodes.title: Market Microstructure During Financial Crisis: Dynamics of Informed and Heuristic-Driven Trading

nodes.name: loss-aversion contrarian demand
nodes.description: Investors exhibiting loss-aversion and mental accounting increase demand for risky assets following market losses (and decrease following gains), creating contrarian order flow that is captured by the probability of heuristic-driven trading (PH). This behavior is driven by investors raising their required returns after losses, which they satisfy by increasing leverage or shifting to riskier assets.

nodes.name: information asymmetry liquidity provision
nodes.description: The probability of informed trading (PIN) varies significantly with market conditions and structural shocks (e.g., Lehman collapse), reflecting changes in the proportion of informed traders relative to uninformed liquidity traders. During high-volatility crises, rational informed traders withdraw, leaving uninformed liquidity traders to dominate order flow.

nodes.name: size-dependent information asymmetry
nodes.description: Larger firms have lower probability of informed trading (PIN) due to greater public information availability and analyst coverage, whereas smaller firms exhibit higher PIN. This size effect on information asymmetry does not apply to heuristic-driven trading, which is uniformly present across all market capitalizations.

nodes.title: Can Agent-Based Models Probe Market Microstructure?

nodes.name: order book state feedback on liquidity provision
nodes.description: Liquidity providers adjust their limit order placement depth in response to the current imbalance in buy/sell market order flow (qtaker), causing orders to be placed deeper or shallower in the book depending on whether takers are biased toward buying or selling. This creates a dynamic feedback loop where order book state directly influences subsequent order placement.

nodes.name: order flow imbalance on price dynamics
nodes.description: The time-varying buy probability of liquidity takers (qtaker) evolves as a mean-reverting random walk and directly drives the execution of market orders against the limit order book, which in turn determines the mid-price through the best bid-ask spread. Persistent order flow imbalance creates directional price pressure.

nodes.name: order cancellation-driven liquidity depletion
nodes.description: Liquidity providers randomly cancel their limit orders with probability δ each period, reducing available depth in the order book. This stochastic cancellation mechanism affects the resilience of the limit order book and the ability of the market to absorb order flow without large price moves.

nodes.title: Consistency of MLE for partially observed diffusions, with application in market microstructure modeling
Neural Extended Kalman Filters for Learning and Predicting Dynamics of Structural Systems
Comparing Prediction Market Structures, With an Application to Market Making

nodes.name: inventory-driven price pressure
nodes.description: Market maker adjusts prices mechanically based on accumulated inventory position rather than information about true value, causing prices to drift away from equilibrium and fail to converge when trader beliefs remain dispersed.

nodes.name: information asymmetry learning
nodes.description: Market maker updates beliefs about true value by inferring trader information from observed trade direction and size, allowing rapid convergence to equilibrium when initial beliefs are correct but causing slow adaptation after market shocks due to overconfidence.

nodes.name: uncertainty-adaptive spread widening
nodes.description: Market maker widens bid-ask spreads when uncertainty about true value increases (detected via likelihood ratio tests on recent trade history), allowing quick adaptation to market shocks while accepting occasional false-positive spread widening during equilibrium.

nodes.title: International Trade Finance from the Origins to the Present: Market Structures, Regulation and Governance

nodes.name: standardization liquidity premium
nodes.description: Trade finance instruments that become standardized and centralized (like the sterling bill of exchange) command lower financing costs and higher liquidity than idiosyncratic local instruments, because standardization reduces information asymmetry and increases the pool of potential buyers.

nodes.name: market centralization efficiency
nodes.description: Consolidation of trade finance around dominant trading centers (Antwerp → Amsterdam → London) improves price discovery and reduces transaction costs by concentrating counterparty relationships and enabling network effects in instrument adoption.

nodes.name: de-globalization credit contraction
nodes.description: Periods of geopolitical fragmentation and capital controls (interwar period, Bretton Woods) cause trade finance markets to disintegrate into localized, illiquid segments, raising financing costs and reducing cross-border trade credit availability.

nodes.title: Risk-dependent centrality in economic and financial networks

nodes.name: risk-dependent network centrality shift
nodes.description: A node's importance and systemic risk exposure in a financial network changes as external risk levels vary, without any change to the network topology itself. Entities central under low-risk conditions may become peripheral under high-risk conditions and vice versa, causing ranking interlacement.

nodes.name: contagion propagation through network paths
nodes.description: Financial distress spreads from infected nodes to susceptible neighbors through network connections at a rate proportional to the number of infected neighbors and the infection rate per link. Early-stage contagion (before recovery mechanisms activate) follows a Susceptible-Infected dynamic where infection is irreversible.

nodes.name: crisis-amplified sensitivity to network position
nodes.description: During periods of market crisis, nodes with high risk-dependent centrality exhibit greater sensitivity to external market variations. Companies ranking high in risk-centrality during crises show less resilient reactions to market turmoil, indicating that network position becomes a stronger determinant of vulnerability during stress periods.

nodes.title: Financial Time Series Forecasting using CNN and Transformer
FinTSBridge: A New Evaluation Suite for Real-world Financial Prediction with Advanced Time Series Models
StockEmotions: Discover Investor Emotions for Financial Sentiment Analysis and Multivariate Time Series

nodes.name: investor emotion sentiment signal
nodes.description: Fine-grained investor emotions expressed on social media (optimism, excitement, anxiety, disgust, etc.) contain predictive information about future price movements. Emotions beyond simple bullish/bearish sentiment capture psychological states that drive trading decisions and market dynamics.

nodes.name: social media text sentiment predictability
nodes.description: Text-based sentiment extracted from investor comments on StockTwits contains information that improves stock price forecasting when combined with historical price data. The semantic content of investor discourse provides a forward-looking signal beyond price history alone.

nodes.title: Benchmarking Deep Sequential Models on Volatility Predictions for Financial Time Series
DMS, AE, DAA: methods and applications of adaptive time series model selection, ensemble, and financial evaluation

nodes.name: yield curve inversion as recession signal
nodes.description: Inversions in the yield curve precede economic downturns and stock market collapses. The paper uses yield curve slope as a predictive feature for future index returns, exploiting the well-documented relationship between curve inversion and macroeconomic contraction.

nodes.name: VIX curve inversion as volatility signal
nodes.description: Inversions in the VIX futures curve signal future declines in equity markets. The paper demonstrates that VIX curve shape contains predictive information about stock index returns, particularly during regime shifts and market stress periods.

nodes.name: regime-dependent model performance
nodes.description: The optimal forecasting model for returns changes over time as market regimes shift. Static model selection fails because the distribution of time series data changes abruptly; adaptive selection that reweights models based on recent forecasting errors captures these regime switches and improves predictions.

nodes.title: Generative modelling of financial time series with structured noise and MMD-based signature learning
Some notes on trees and paths
Path Imputation Strategies for Signature Models of Irregular Time Series
Domain Adaptation for Time series Transformers using One-step fine-tuning
Multiple Time Series Ising Model for Financial Market Simulations

nodes.name: cross-asset volatility synchronization
nodes.description: When agents imitate trading decisions across correlated stocks (via inter-stock coupling parameter γ), volatility clustering becomes synchronized between assets. Stronger cross-asset imitation increases the correlation of volatility spikes across stocks.

nodes.name: mean reversion via inventory pressure
nodes.description: Agents exhibit contrarian behavior proportional to accumulated imbalance (the −αs_i|M| term), creating a restoring force that prevents unbounded price movements and generates mean-reverting dynamics in magnetization and returns.

nodes.title: Modeling stylized facts for financial time series

nodes.name: heavy tails from extreme price movements
nodes.description: Return distributions exhibit fat tails (∼dξ/ξ⁴) rather than Gaussian tails, meaning extreme price movements occur more frequently than normal distribution predicts. This reflects the empirical reality that large price swings are more probable than classical random walk models suggest.

nodes.title: Why Do Transformers Fail to Forecast Time Series In-Context?

nodes.name: transformer architectural inefficiency in autoregressive forecasting
nodes.description: Transformer models with Linear Self-Attention cannot achieve lower expected MSE than classical linear models when forecasting autoregressive processes, despite their architectural complexity. This inefficiency persists because the self-attention mechanism fails to extract additional predictive information beyond what linear models capture from historical context.

nodes.name: mean reversion collapse under chain-of-thought inference
nodes.description: When Transformers employ Chain-of-Thought style reasoning for time series forecasting, predictions exponentially collapse toward the mean rather than maintaining the true autoregressive dynamics. This occurs because the intermediate reasoning steps degrade the model's ability to preserve temporal dependencies.

nodes.title: Modality-aware Transformer for Financial Time series Forecasting
Dataset-Driven Channel Masks in Transformers for Multivariate Time Series
Data Augmentation for Multivariate Time Series Classification: An Experimental Study
Scaling transformation and probability distributions for financial time series

nodes.name: multifractal scaling exploitation
nodes.description: Price increments exhibit multifractal behavior revealed through non-linear scaling transformations of their moment distributions. Traders can exploit these overlooked scaling properties and volatility patterns to improve predictive accuracy and capture price dynamics missed by traditional unifractal models.

nodes.title: Rough path stability of (semi-)linear SPDEs
Rough stochastic filtering
The inverse problem for rough controlled differential equations
When Frictions are Fractional: Rough Noise in High-Frequency Data

nodes.name: microstructure noise roughness exploitation
nodes.description: Market microstructure noise exhibits fractional Brownian motion characteristics that create predictable patterns in high-frequency price data. Traders can exploit mispricing of volatility dynamics by accurately estimating the roughness parameter of this noise, generating alpha during periods of elevated noise.

nodes.name: volatility dynamics mispricing
nodes.description: The market systematically misprice volatility by failing to account for the rough, serially dependent structure of microstructure noise. This creates exploitable inefficiencies when traders use more accurate estimations of integrated price and noise volatilities.

nodes.title: A partial rough path space for rough volatility
PPMC RL Training Algorithm: Rough Terrain Intelligent Robots through Reinforcement Learning
Rough differential equations driven by signals in Besov spaces
Is Volatility Rough ?

nodes.name: realized volatility proxy estimation error
nodes.description: The measurement error between observed realized volatility and true latent volatility induces spurious scaling properties in log-volatility time series, causing standard estimation methods to incorrectly infer roughness (low Hurst parameter) even when the true volatility process is smooth.

nodes.name: rough volatility path regularity
nodes.description: Volatility follows a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter H < 0.5, implying rougher (less smooth) sample paths than standard semimartingales, which affects the autocorrelation structure and predictability of realized volatility increments.

nodes.title: Rough differential equations for volatility
Option Pricing under Fast-varying and Rough Stochastic Volatility

nodes.name: rough volatility mean reversion pricing
nodes.description: Option prices are mispriced when volatility exhibits rough (non-smooth) paths with fast mean reversion. Traders can exploit this by recognizing that rough volatility dynamics produce characteristic implied volatility surfaces that differ from standard smooth volatility models, allowing systematic pricing corrections.

nodes.name: implied volatility surface term structure exploitation
nodes.description: The characteristic term structure exponent governing volatility behavior across different market regimes creates exploitable mispricings in the implied volatility surface. By identifying which regime the market is in (fast/slow volatility factors, strong/small fluctuations), traders can systematically profit from term structure mispricing.

nodes.title: The rough Hawkes Heston stochastic volatility model

nodes.name: jump clustering in volatility
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits self-exciting jump clustering behavior where the intensity of volatility jumps is proportional to the current variance level itself, creating endogenous clusters of spikes particularly during crisis periods. This Hawkes-type mechanism generates the observed clustering of large volatility movements.

nodes.name: rough volatility memory effect
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits non-Markovian long-memory behavior characterized by a power-law kernel with exponent α ∈ (1/2, 1], capturing the persistence of volatility shocks due to meta-orders and automatic order flow in market microstructure. This rough trajectory structure controls the explosion rate of ATM skews across maturities.

nodes.name: leverage effect with common jumps
nodes.description: Negative correlation between asset returns and volatility changes is amplified by common jump events where volatility and underlying asset jump in opposite directions simultaneously. This mechanism generates the observed skew in implied volatility surfaces for both equity and volatility index options.

nodes.title: A Rough Super-Brownian Motion
Smooth density for some nilpotent rough differential equations
Rough PDEs for local stochastic volatility models
On simulation of rough Volterra stochastic volatility models
The Averaging Principle for Non-autonomous Slow-fast Stochastic Differential Equations and an Application to a Local Stochastic Volatility Model
Local volatility under rough volatility

nodes.name: rough volatility skew mispricing
nodes.description: Options are mispriced when market participants use the traditional 1/2 skew rule to relate at-the-money implied and local volatility skews, but rough volatility models generate a different constant ratio of 1/(H + 3/2). Traders exploiting the correct skew relationship can identify and profit from these mispricings.

nodes.title: Volatility models in practice: Rough, Path-dependent or Markovian?

nodes.name: rough volatility model mispricing
nodes.description: Rough volatility models with Hurst parameter H ∈ (0,1/2) generate incorrect power-law skew dynamics that increase too steeply at short maturities and decay too slowly at longer maturities, causing systematic mispricing of options relative to observed SPX smile dynamics.

nodes.name: path-dependent volatility structure
nodes.description: Non-rough path-dependent models better capture the actual evolution of volatility smiles across maturities by incorporating history-dependent dynamics that rough models fail to represent, enabling more accurate option pricing.

nodes.name: markovian volatility structure
nodes.description: Two-factor Markovian models with memoryless volatility dynamics outperform rough volatility models in capturing SPX smile behavior across short to medium-term maturities by better matching the observed cross-sectional shape of implied volatility.

nodes.title: Rough volatility: fact or artefact?

nodes.name: realized volatility estimation error masking true roughness
nodes.description: Realized volatility computed from high-frequency price observations exhibits apparent roughness (Hurst exponent H < 0.5) even when the underlying spot volatility process has smooth dynamics (H ≥ 0.5). This spurious roughness arises from microstructure noise and discretization error inherent in estimating volatility from discrete samples, not from the true volatility process itself.

nodes.name: model misspecification in fractional volatility parameterization
nodes.description: Parametric models using a single Hurst exponent H to simultaneously capture both long-range dependence (autocorrelation decay over long timescales) and short-range roughness (path regularity over short timescales) conflate two distinct properties that should be modeled separately. This conflation causes the estimated H to reflect a mixture of these properties rather than true roughness.

nodes.title: A regularity structure for rough volatility

nodes.name: correlation-induced renormalization bias
nodes.description: When asset returns are correlated with rough volatility (ρ ≠ 0), naive discrete approximations to the volatility integral diverge at rate ε^(H-1/2). Convergence requires subtracting a diverging periodic renormalization function C_ε(t) that depends on the Hurst parameter and correlation structure, creating a systematic pricing adjustment absent in classical stochastic volatility.

nodes.name: microstructure-driven rough volatility
nodes.description: Market microstructure models based on Hawkes processes generate rough volatility dynamics through stochastic Volterra equations in the scaling limit. This provides a causal foundation for why realized volatility exhibits fractional Brownian motion structure (H ≈ 0.05) rather than classical semimartingale behavior, linking order flow clustering to volatility roughness.

nodes.title: Weak error approximation for rough and Gaussian mean-reverting stochastic volatility models

nodes.name: rough volatility persistence
nodes.description: Log-volatility exhibits fractional Brownian motion behavior with Hurst exponent H < 0.5, meaning volatility shocks have long-memory properties that decay slowly rather than mean-reverting quickly. This roughness is an intrinsic feature of volatility dynamics, not an artifact of measurement noise.

nodes.name: mean-reverting volatility clustering
nodes.description: Volatility follows a mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with stationary distribution (when κ₂ < 0), creating clustering where high volatility periods persist before reverting to long-run mean. This generates autocorrelated volatility that standard models fail to capture.

nodes.name: discretization error in volatility approximation
nodes.description: Numerical schemes that discretize the volatility process introduce approximation errors that accumulate over time. The weak error rate depends on the roughness parameter α and the discretization grid, with convergence rate O(v_n(α)) where v_n(α) varies with α ∈ (1/2, 1).

nodes.title: Time-inhomogeneous Gaussian stochastic volatility models: Large deviations and super roughness
Rough volatility, path-dependent PDEs and weak rates of convergence
Rough path theory and stochastic calculus
Randomisation of rough stochastic differential equations
Estimating the roughness exponent of stochastic volatility from discrete observations of the integrated variance

nodes.name: volatility roughness mispricing
nodes.description: Market participants misprice derivatives and volatility-linked instruments because they fail to accurately estimate the roughness exponent (Hurst parameter) of the volatility process. Traders who correctly estimate this pathwise property can identify mispricings in options and other derivatives whose values depend on volatility dynamics.

nodes.title: Log-modulated rough stochastic volatility models

nodes.name: volatility roughness and skew explosion
nodes.description: The instantaneous variance process exhibits rough (non-smooth) behavior characterized by a low Hurst index H, causing the at-the-money implied volatility skew to explode as time-to-maturity approaches zero according to a power law TH−1/2. This roughness in realized variance data drives the steep skew observed in option markets.

nodes.name: log-modulated kernel regularization of volatility roughness
nodes.description: A logarithmic modulation of the power-law kernel in the fractional Brownian motion allows the volatility process to remain well-defined and continuous even when the Hurst index approaches zero, preventing the singularities and non-semimartingale behavior that plague standard rough volatility models at H=0.

nodes.title: An Ephemerally Self-Exciting Point Process

nodes.name: transient sentiment momentum
nodes.description: Past market events (price movements, trading activity) trigger short-term directional pressure that decays over a random, finite duration. Traders can exploit these fleeting momentum signals before sentiment dissipates, generating alpha from temporary market overreaction.

nodes.title: A fractional Hawkes process II: Further characterization of the process
Performance of information criteria used for model selection of Hawkes process models of financial data
Functional Limit Theorems for Hawkes Processes
An estimation procedure for the Hawkes process

nodes.name: self-exciting order arrival clustering
nodes.description: Order arrivals exhibit self-exciting behavior through Hawkes processes: each new order increases the conditional intensity of future orders, which then decays back to baseline. This clustering of order arrivals directly drives price volatility in limit order books.

nodes.name: cross-exciting order flow interaction
nodes.description: Incoming market orders heavily excite the arrival intensity of limit orders (asymmetric cross-excitation), while limit order arrivals have minimal effect on market order flow. This asymmetry reflects how market orders deplete liquidity and trigger limit order replenishment.

nodes.name: order intensity mean reversion with inhibitory lags
nodes.description: Order arrival intensities exhibit inhibitory effects at very short lags (under 0.003 seconds) followed by excitatory effects at longer lags (0.01, 0.1, 0.5 seconds), reflecting both immediate order book depletion and subsequent replenishment cycles in limit order book dynamics.

nodes.title: Branching ratio approximation for the self-exciting Hawkes process

nodes.name: self-exciting clustering of price changes
nodes.description: Past mid-price changes trigger future price changes through endogenous feedback, causing events to cluster in time. This self-exciting dynamic is captured by the branching ratio of the Hawkes process, where each event has a probability of triggering additional events.

nodes.name: market reflexivity increase
