nodes.description: Over time, financial markets have become more reflexive (self-referential) due to rising high-frequency and algorithmic trading, causing the branching ratio of mid-price changes to increase from ~0.25 in 1998 to ~0.65 in 2010, making markets more prone to instability and flash crashes.

nodes.name: long-range dependence in event rate
nodes.description: Financial markets exhibit long-range temporal dependence in the rate of mid-price changes, detectable across extended observation windows. This persistence means the best-fitting stationary Hawkes model must be critical (branching ratio = 1) rather than subcritical, with an influence kernel that decays as a power law rather than exponentially.

nodes.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Hawkes Processes with self-excitation or inhibition
Hawkes and INAR($\infty$) processes
On the Hawkes Process with Different Exciting Functions

nodes.name: self-exciting clustering in order arrivals
nodes.description: Market events (trades, orders) cluster in time because past events increase the intensity of future events through self-excitation. This clustering arises from the immigration-birth structure where each event can spawn offspring events with generation-dependent intensities.

nodes.name: microstructure noise from event clustering
nodes.description: The self-exciting nature of order arrivals generates correlated microstructure noise in observed prices. When orders cluster, the noise structure deviates from standard assumptions, affecting price discovery and volatility estimation.

nodes.title: Renewal in Hawkes processes with self-excitation and inhibition
A Mutually Exciting Latent Space Hawkes Process Model for Continuous-time Networks
State-dependent Hawkes processes and their application to limit order book modelling

nodes.name: state-dependent order flow self-excitation
nodes.description: Order arrivals of a given type increase the intensity of subsequent orders of the same type, with the magnitude and duration of this self-exciting effect varying significantly based on the current state of the limit order book (e.g., bid-ask spread or queue imbalance). This captures how algorithmic traders react to recent order flow in a state-contingent manner.

nodes.name: state-dependent order flow cross-excitation
nodes.description: Order arrivals of one type increase the intensity of orders of different types, with this cross-exciting effect also depending on the LOB state. This captures how different order types interact and influence each other's arrival rates conditional on market microstructure conditions.

nodes.name: critical reflexivity endogeneity
nodes.description: The order flow exhibits high endogeneity (self-referential feedback) measured by the spectral norm of the Hawkes excitation kernel, and this endogeneity is itself state-dependent, being more pronounced in disequilibrium states of the LOB such as wide bid-ask spreads or imbalanced queues.

nodes.title: A buffer Hawkes process for limit order books

nodes.name: mutual excitation between market and limit orders
nodes.description: Market order executions trigger increases in limit order arrival intensity through a self-exciting Hawkes mechanism, while the size of the limit order book (buffer) drives the intensity of subsequent market order arrivals. This bidirectional feedback creates clustering in order flow.

nodes.name: buffer-regulated order intensity
nodes.description: The intensity of market order arrivals is proportional to the current size of the limit order book buffer. When the buffer is depleted (many executions, few new limit orders), market order intensity decreases; when the buffer is full, market order intensity increases. This self-regulating mechanism prevents explosive order accumulation.

nodes.title: A Fractional Hawkes process
General Compound Hawkes Processes in Limit Order Books

nodes.name: order flow dependent price changes
nodes.description: Mid-price changes are driven by the arrival of orders whose sizes depend on the state of the market (captured by a Markov chain). The volatility of price changes is directly expressed as a function of order arrival rates and the distribution of order sizes across market states.

nodes.name: order intensity volatility coupling
nodes.description: Price volatility is mechanically linked to the intensity of order arrivals through the Hawkes process parameters. Higher self-exciting intensity (larger excitation function) leads to greater clustering of orders and thus higher volatility in mid-price changes.

nodes.title: Queue-reactive Hawkes models for the order flow

nodes.name: queue-state-dependent intensity
nodes.description: The baseline arrival rate of limit, market, and cancel orders depends on current queue depth; traders respond to the visible state of the order book when deciding whether and what type of order to submit.

nodes.name: volume imbalance pressure on mid-price
nodes.description: Market order and mid-price change rates respond primarily to the imbalance between bid and ask queue sizes, while limit and cancel order arrival rates do not follow this pattern, indicating asymmetric information effects.

nodes.title: Nonlinear Hawkes Processes

nodes.name: regime-dependent market adaptation
nodes.description: Market microstructure transitions between different regimes (sublinear, sub-critical, critical, super-critical, explosive) with distinct time asymptotics. Trading signals must adapt to the current regime to maintain robustness and profitability across varying market conditions.

nodes.title: Hawkes Processes with Stochastic Excitations

nodes.name: contagion-driven intensity acceleration
nodes.description: Market events and their intensities mutually reinforce each other with time-varying contagion levels, allowing events to accelerate future event rates in a non-linear feedback loop that standard stationary models miss.

nodes.title: The Multivariate Community Hawkes Model for Dependent Relational Events in Continuous-time Networks
Transform Analysis for Hawkes Processes with Applications in Dark Pool Trading

nodes.name: liquidity clustering feedback
nodes.description: Trade arrivals in dark pools exhibit self-exciting behavior: the occurrence of a trade increases the probability of future trades, as institutional investors re-route orders back to pools where they obtained fills, and high-frequency traders are attracted by evidence of large orders. This positive feedback is captured by the Hawkes process intensity increasing with each trade event.

nodes.name: trade size intensity amplification
nodes.description: Larger arriving trades generate stronger increases in future trading intensity than smaller trades. The random jump sizes in the Hawkes intensity model capture the empirical feature that bigger trades signal more remaining liquidity in the pool, attracting more subsequent orders and creating larger intensity jumps proportional to trade size.

nodes.title: Scaling limits of coupled continuous time random walks and residual order statistics through marked point processes
Precise deviations for Hawkes processes
Fake News Mitigation via Point Process Based Intervention

nodes.name: self-exciting cascade amplification
nodes.description: Past events in a news campaign increase the conditional intensity of future events through self-excitation, creating cascading amplification of both fake and real news spread through the network.

nodes.name: mutual excitation between competing processes
nodes.description: Fake news and mitigation (real news) processes mutually excite one another in the network; strategically incentivizing real news activity can suppress fake news spread by competing for user attention and exposure.

nodes.name: exposure correlation effect
nodes.description: Users exposed to both fake and real news simultaneously are less likely to be convinced by fake news; mitigation effectiveness increases when real news exposure is correlated with fake news exposure across the user population.

nodes.title: Self-Exciting Multifractional Processes
Large deviations for Markovian nonlinear Hawkes processes
Compound Hawkes Processes in Limit Order Books

nodes.name: order flow imbalance regime switching
nodes.description: The background intensity of order arrivals switches between regimes (high, normal, low imbalance states) governed by a hidden Markov chain. Different imbalance regimes produce different order arrival rates and thus different price volatility, even conditional on the same order flow magnitude.

nodes.name: volatility scaling with order flow intensity
nodes.description: Price volatility is mechanically determined by the long-run intensity of order arrivals (scaled by the self-excitation parameter) and the magnitude of individual price changes. Higher order arrival rates directly increase realized volatility through more frequent price ticks.

nodes.title: Perfect Sampling of Multivariate Hawkes Process
Some asymptotic results for nonlinear Hawkes processes
Portfolio Liquidation Games with Self-Exciting Order Flow

nodes.name: self-exciting order flow feedback
nodes.description: Large investors' trading activity increases the base intensity of future market orders through a Hawkes process mechanism, creating an additional transient price impact. Traders anticipate this feedback and adjust liquidation strategies accordingly, potentially trading more aggressively early to benefit from the induced child order flow.

nodes.name: transient price impact from order book recovery
nodes.description: Past trades create a persistent shift in the mid-quote price (or effective spread) that decays over time at a rate determined by order book recovery. This impact is measured through a mean-reverting process that depends on the cumulative trading rate and recovery speed.

nodes.name: instantaneous execution cost
nodes.description: Trading at any moment incurs an immediate price concession proportional to the trading rate, independent of past or future trades. This represents the bid-ask spread and immediate market impact of the current order.

nodes.title: Byzantine-Resilient SGD in High Dimensions on Heterogeneous Data
Data Encoding for Byzantine-Resilient Distributed Optimization
Consentaneous agent-based and stochastic model of the financial markets

nodes.name: herding-driven volatility feedback
nodes.description: Agent herding interactions between fundamentalists and chartists (optimists/pessimists) endogenously drive volatility. When market price deviates from fundamental value, chartist herding intensifies, increasing transaction rates and volatility in a self-reinforcing cycle.

nodes.name: chartist-fundamentalist imbalance pressure
nodes.description: The excess demand imbalance between fundamentalists (who trade toward fundamental value) and chartists (who herd on momentum) directly drives log-price deviations. Fundamentalist demand pulls price toward fair value while chartist herding pushes it away, creating mean-reverting but volatile dynamics.

nodes.name: activity-dependent transaction rate modulation
nodes.description: Trading activity (transaction rate) scales with the absolute log-price deviation from fundamental value via a power-law relationship. Higher deviations trigger more frequent transactions, amplifying both endogenous noise from agent dynamics and exogenous information flow noise.

nodes.name: dual-noise composition of returns
nodes.description: Return fluctuations arise from two independent noise sources: exogenous noise from information flow and endogenous noise from complex agent population dynamics. The relative contribution of each shifts with market conditions, producing fat-tailed (q-Gaussian) return distributions and power-law autocorrelations.

nodes.title: The Power (Law) of Indian Markets: Analysing NSE and BSE trading statistics

nodes.name: universal power-law tail in price returns
nodes.description: Price return distributions across different stocks and markets exhibit fat tails following a power law with exponent α ≈ 3 (the 'inverse cubic law'), reflecting a universal statistical property of financial markets that holds across developed and emerging markets.

nodes.name: correlated stock movement driving index power-law behavior
nodes.description: Individual stocks in the Indian market exhibit high cross-correlations in their price movements, which causes the market index to inherit the power-law tail distribution of individual stock returns. The largest eigenvalue of the correlation matrix captures most market information.

nodes.name: market-specific log-normal volume distribution
nodes.description: Trading volume and number of trades follow a log-normal distribution in Indian markets, which differs from the power-law behavior observed in some developed markets (NYSE, Paris Bourse), indicating that volume/activity distributions are market-specific rather than universal.

nodes.title: Financial equilibria in the semimartingale setting: complete markets and markets with withdrawal constraints
Uncovering the Internal Structure of the Indian Financial Market: Cross-correlation behavior in the NSE

nodes.name: market-mode dominance in emerging markets
nodes.description: Emerging markets like India exhibit weak sector-specific clustering and strong market-wide co-movement, meaning individual stock returns are dominated by overall market trends rather than sector-specific factors. This reduces the dimensionality of return drivers compared to developed markets.

nodes.name: eigenvalue filtering for noise reduction
nodes.description: By filtering out the dominant market mode and random noise from the cross-correlation matrix, traders can isolate genuine sector-specific or stock-specific signals that deviate from bulk eigenvalue distributions, enabling more informed trading decisions with reduced exposure to random market fluctuations.

nodes.title: Contextual Sentence Analysis for the Sentiment Prediction on Financial Data
Emergence of Randomness in Temporally Aggregated Financial Tick Sequences

nodes.name: high-frequency correlation decay under temporal aggregation
nodes.description: Ultra-high frequency tick data exhibits strong serial correlation and predictability, but this structure decays and disappears as transaction time aggregation increases, transforming correlated microstructure patterns into apparently random returns. Traders can exploit the non-monotonic transition zones where predictability is partially but not fully eliminated.

nodes.name: microstructure noise masking under aggregation
nodes.description: At the tick level, high-frequency trading generates microstructure noise and order flow patterns that create detectable non-randomness. As temporal aggregation increases, this noise averages out, causing the return sequence to converge toward market efficiency and randomness, eliminating predictable patterns.

nodes.title: When Finance Meets Physics: The Impact of the Speed of Light on Financial Markets and their Regulation

nodes.name: information propagation latency arbitrage
nodes.description: Traders exploit the physical speed-of-light delay in information transmission between geographically separated exchanges. A trader with faster access to price updates from one exchange can execute trades on another exchange before that exchange receives the updated quote, capturing arbitrage profits.

nodes.name: trade-through rule violation from latency asymmetry
nodes.description: Due to the irreducible propagation delay of information at the speed of light, an exchange may execute a trade at an inferior price before receiving notification that a better price is available on a geographically distant exchange. This creates an enforcement problem for regulators trying to determine whether a trade-through violation actually occurred.

nodes.name: phantom liquidity uncertainty
nodes.description: Published quotes may be cancelled or filled before a trader's order reaches them due to latency, creating uncertainty about whether quoted liquidity is actually executable. Traders cannot know if a firm quote is real until they submit an order, analogous to quantum superposition—the quote exists in multiple states until observed.

nodes.name: catastrophic software glitch tail risk
nodes.description: Complex nonlinear market systems can experience extreme failure events from minor programming errors that penetrate quality control procedures, similar to quantum tunneling in physics. These freak events occur with nonzero probability regardless of safeguards and can cause massive losses.

nodes.title: The DEBS 2022 Grand Challenge: Detecting Trading Trends in Financial Tick Data
No Arbitrage in Continuous Financial Markets
Small scale behavior of financial data

nodes.name: nonlinear serial dependence in high-frequency returns
nodes.description: Consecutive price increments exhibit nonlinear functional relationships at sub-minute timescales (1-15 seconds), causing return distributions to deviate from Gaussian much faster than at longer timescales. This nonlinearity is evidenced by the breakdown of linear autocorrelation while permutation destroys the effect.

nodes.name: fat-tail acceleration at small timescales
nodes.description: The probability mass in the distribution tails (beyond 10 standard deviations) increases sharply as timescale decreases below ~100 seconds, indicating extreme price moves become disproportionately more likely at high frequencies. This acceleration is driven by the nonlinear dependencies between consecutive increments.

nodes.title: Integrating Tick-level Data and Periodical Signal for High-frequency Market Making

nodes.name: inventory risk accumulation
nodes.description: Market makers accumulate unintended inventory positions when their quoted bid/ask orders execute asymmetrically due to adverse price movements, forcing them to hold positions at unfavorable prices and realize losses.

nodes.name: adverse selection risk
nodes.description: Information asymmetry allows informed traders to exploit market makers' stale quotes by trading against them when the true fair price has moved, extracting profits from slower-reacting market makers.

nodes.name: tick-level microstructure information advantage
nodes.description: Processing event-driven tick-level limit order book data (order placements, cancellations, executions) provides more timely and granular information about instantaneous supply and demand than periodical snapshots, enabling faster and more precise inventory control.

nodes.name: periodical predictive signal integration
nodes.description: Extracting predictive features from fixed-interval aggregated market data (trades and quotes) captures longer-term price movement patterns that complement tick-level information, reducing adverse selection risk through forward-looking price predictions.

nodes.title: Tick size and price diffusion

nodes.name: price discretization stickiness
nodes.description: Larger tick sizes constrain prices to discrete levels, increasing the frequency of zero returns (no price change) because prices cannot move below the minimum increment. Smaller tick sizes reduce this constraint, allowing more frequent non-zero price movements.

nodes.name: tick size-driven volatility clustering amplification
nodes.description: Reducing tick size increases volatility autocorrelation and clustering by enabling more frequent order placement and cancellation at finer price levels, which creates persistent microstructural patterns that propagate into longer-term volatility persistence.

nodes.name: subordination hypothesis breakdown
nodes.description: The subordination hypothesis (that fat tails and volatility clustering arise from time-deformation by trading activity) explains price properties well under large tick sizes but loses explanatory power under small tick sizes, suggesting tick size fundamentally changes the mechanism generating return distributions.

nodes.title: The value of information in financial markets: An agent-based simulation

nodes.name: information asymmetry alpha generation
nodes.description: Traders with superior information integration across diverse sources can exploit market inefficiencies and generate excess returns, while average informed agents underperform. Only the most informed agents consistently beat the market due to their ability to leverage non-linear relationships between information levels and returns.

nodes.name: fundamentalist strategy persistence
nodes.description: Traders with the highest information levels are rewarded for maintaining a fundamentalist strategy (trading on fundamental value), while less informed traders benefit from switching to alternative information sources. Strategy optimality is non-monotonic in information level.

nodes.title: Frequency analysis of tick quotes on the foreign exchange market and agent-based modeling: A spectral distance approach

nodes.name: behavioral synchronization across currency pairs
nodes.description: Market participants in different geographic time zones develop similar decision-making thresholds and perception parameters when trading related currency pairs, causing their tick frequency patterns to converge. This synchronization increases over time due to information technology development, making trading behavior more homogeneous globally.

nodes.name: temporal clustering of market participant activity
nodes.description: Market participants in each geographic time zone exhibit periodic clustering in their trading activity, with tick frequency showing cyclical patterns tied to the opening and closing of regional markets. The spectral distance of tick frequencies is lowest during handoff periods between time zones when participants from adjacent zones are most active.

nodes.name: information interpretation uncertainty
nodes.description: Market participants face irreducible uncertainty when interpreting perceived information about market conditions and news, modeled as random noise in their decision process. This interpretation uncertainty, combined with heterogeneous decision thresholds, generates variation in trading activity and prevents perfect coordination of behavior across participants.

nodes.title: Synthetic Financial Data Generation for Enhanced Financial Modelling
Causality between investor sentiment and the shares return on the Moroccan and Tunisian financial markets

nodes.name: return-driven sentiment adjustment
nodes.description: Stock returns cause changes in investor sentiment rather than the reverse. Current returns predict future sentiment shifts, establishing a unidirectional causal flow from profitability to psychological state.

nodes.name: sentiment memory persistence
nodes.description: Changes in investor sentiment exhibit significant autocorrelation and memory over multiple days, allowing past sentiment changes to predict current sentiment dynamics. This contrasts with sentiment levels themselves, which show weak memory.

nodes.name: negative wealth-change sensitivity
nodes.description: Investors are sensitive to changes in wealth (returns) rather than absolute wealth levels. Variations in profitability negatively affect investor sentiment, consistent with prospect theory and loss aversion.

nodes.title: Deep Learning can Replicate Adaptive Traders in a Limit-Order-Book Financial Market

nodes.name: limit order book state adaptation
nodes.description: Traders adapt their quoting and execution decisions based on the current state of the limit order book (bid-ask spread, depth, price levels). By observing LOB snapshots and trader actions, a DLNN can learn to replicate this adaptive decision-making process.

nodes.name: client order execution optimization
nodes.description: Sales traders seek to execute client orders at prices better than the client's limit price, capturing the difference as profit. The trader adapts execution timing and pricing strategy based on market conditions to maximize this execution advantage.

nodes.name: spread-crossing market impact learning
nodes.description: Traders learn to predict and adapt to the consequences of crossing the bid-ask spread through market orders versus placing limit orders on the book. This adaptive behavior reflects learning about execution costs and market impact.

nodes.title: Deep Generative Models for Synthetic Financial Data: Applications to Portfolio and Risk Modeling
A Multimodal Embedding-Based Approach to Industry Classification in Financial Markets

nodes.name: co-movement clustering
nodes.description: Companies with similar returns at the same point in time tend to be related and belong to the same industry sector, because firms in the same business sector exhibit correlated stock price fluctuations in response to common economic shocks.

nodes.name: news co-mention clustering
nodes.description: Companies frequently mentioned together in financial news articles are likely to be related and belong to the same industry, reflecting genuine business relationships, competitive dynamics, or shared market conditions.

nodes.title: High-frequency lead-lag relationships in the Chinese stock index futures market: tick-by-tick dynamics of calendar spreads

nodes.name: liquidity-driven price discovery
nodes.description: More liquid futures contracts (near-month with highest trading volume) discover prices first and lead less liquid contracts (next-month, quarterly, semi-annual) by one tick. Information flows from the most liquid to less liquid maturities because traders execute orders faster where liquidity is highest.

nodes.name: lead-lag spread mean reversion
nodes.description: When the lead-lag spread widens (leading asset rises much faster than lagging asset), high-frequency traders execute contrarian trades—selling the lead asset and buying the lagging asset—creating a negative feedback effect that predicts reversals in the leading asset's returns. This mean-reversion signal is strongest during high volatility.

nodes.name: cross-maturity level shift synchronization
nodes.description: When the most liquid near-month contract moves by one tick, other contracts (next-month, quarterly, semi-annual) tend to follow with approximately one-tick moves in the same direction, indicating a synchronized level shift across maturities driven by a common principal component.

nodes.title: An agent-based model for designing a financial market that works well

nodes.name: tick size price resolution constraint
nodes.description: When tick size is larger than the natural volatility of price movements (σt), the discrete price grid prevents accurate representation of market price dynamics, forcing order flow to migrate to competing venues with finer price resolution.

nodes.name: market fragmentation via price improvement incentives
nodes.description: Agents route orders to the market offering the best price when execution is immediate (market order), creating a competitive dynamic where smaller tick sizes attract order flow by enabling price improvement, even when initial market share is small.

nodes.name: fundamental-technical strategy switching
nodes.description: Agents dynamically weight fundamental value expectations against recent price momentum based on random parameters, causing order flow to shift between contrarian and trend-following behavior depending on market conditions and individual agent heterogeneity.

nodes.title: Endogenous versus Exogenous Crashes in Financial Markets

nodes.name: speculative bubble crash
nodes.description: Endogenous crashes arise from unsustainable speculative bubbles that build up through accelerating price dynamics, eventually becoming untenable and correcting sharply. These crashes are identifiable by log-periodic power law signatures (LPPS) that precede the drawdown, allowing traders to time exits before the correction.

nodes.name: exogenous information shock
nodes.description: Crashes without log-periodic signatures are driven by large external information events (news, policy changes, etc.) that cause sudden repricing. These shocks are unpredictable from price dynamics alone and reflect efficient market adjustment to new information.

nodes.title: A characteristic time scale of tick quotes on foreign currency markets

nodes.name: stochastic resonance in dealer decision-making
nodes.description: Dealers have decision thresholds for trading actions, but uncertainty (noise) in their minds allows weak exogenous periodic information to trigger synchronized trading activity even when the signal alone is below the threshold. This synchronization manifests as periodic clustering of quote submissions.

nodes.name: exogenous periodic information coordination
nodes.description: External periodic signals (e.g., scheduled economic announcements, regular information releases) cause dealers to coordinate their trading decisions, producing characteristic time scales in quote submission frequency. The periodicity observed (~2.5 minutes) reflects dealers' common response timing to these external events.

nodes.title: Impact of the tick-size on financial returns and correlations

nodes.name: tick-size discretization of return microstructure
nodes.description: The discrete tick-size quantizes price changes into multiples, creating clustering in the return distribution centered around specific price change levels. This discretization persists in returns despite their apparent continuity, distorting the measured return distribution's microstructure and tail behavior.

nodes.name: price-range-dependent tail behavior distortion
nodes.description: When a stock's price covers a large range over a short period, the division of discretized price changes by varying prices causes the return distribution to develop heavier tails than the underlying price change distribution. The effect depends on the ratio of maximum to minimum price, not on tick-size magnitude itself.

nodes.name: tick-size-induced correlation decay
nodes.description: Discretization errors from the tick-size create spurious noise in price changes that decorrelates asset pairs at small time intervals. This statistical artifact—not economic behavior—drives the observed decay of correlation coefficients toward smaller return intervals, known as the Epps effect.

nodes.title: A persistent-homology-based turbulence index & some applications of TDA on financial markets

nodes.name: correlation breakdown before crashes
nodes.description: Stock correlations increase sharply in the days preceding market crashes, reducing diversification benefits and signaling regime change. This topological shift in the correlation structure can be detected via persistent homology of correlation graphs.

nodes.name: topological volatility surge
nodes.description: High market volatility manifests as increased 1-dimensional topological cycles (loops) in point clouds of asset returns, which can be quantified via persistence landscape norms. These norms spike before crashes, providing an early warning signal.

nodes.name: regime shift detection via persistence distance
nodes.description: Market regime changes produce large Wasserstein distances between consecutive persistence diagrams of rolling-window return point clouds. Smoothed sequences of these distances (PHTI index) capture turbulent periods characterized by low returns, high volatility, and elevated asset correlations.

nodes.title: Functional Laws of Large Numbers for Marked Hawkes Processes and Compound Marked Hawkes Processes

nodes.name: self-exciting clustering in arrival processes
nodes.description: Events trigger increased intensity of future events through a feedback mechanism, causing arrivals to cluster in time. This self-excitation is captured by the Hawkes kernel which makes the conditional intensity depend on the history of past arrivals.

nodes.name: mark-dependent intensity modulation
nodes.description: The intensity of future arrivals depends on the marks (attributes) of past events through the kernel κ(t,A), allowing different event types to have heterogeneous effects on the arrival rate. This creates state-dependent dynamics where event characteristics influence subsequent clustering.

nodes.name: compound claim severity amplification
nodes.description: In insurance applications, claim sizes are random and independent of arrival times, but the total claim burden compounds with the self-exciting arrival process. The combination of clustering arrivals and random claim magnitudes creates amplified tail risk in the surplus process.

nodes.name: event intensity clustering and self-excitation
nodes.description: Market events (trades, order book changes) exhibit self-exciting behavior where past arrivals increase the conditional intensity of future events. By estimating this dynamic intensity from historical event times and marks, traders can predict periods of elevated activity and exploit the clustering of price-moving events.

nodes.name: mark-dependent event impact heterogeneity
nodes.description: Different types of market events (distinguished by their marks, such as buy vs. sell orders or different order sizes) have heterogeneous impacts on future price movements. Capturing these variable jump sizes and their conditional intensities allows prediction of price dynamics more accurately than models assuming uniform event impacts.

nodes.name: self-inhibiting intensity suppression
nodes.description: When the kernel h is negative or the nonlinear jump-rate function ψ exhibits self-inhibition, past events can suppress future event intensity. This creates mean-reversion in the event arrival rate.

nodes.name: mark-modulated intensity feedback
nodes.description: The severity or size of past events (marks Y_k) modulates their impact on future intensity through the function b(Y). Large-magnitude events have disproportionate influence on subsequent event propensity compared to small events.

nodes.description: Past events increase the intensity of future events through a decaying excitation function, creating clustering in event timing. The influence of each event on future intensities is mediated by history-dependent dynamics that adapt based on the full event sequence.

nodes.name: history-dependent dynamics adaptation
nodes.description: The decay rates and transformation matrices of the Hawkes process vary over time as a function of the entire event history, rather than remaining static. This allows the model to capture non-stationary patterns where the influence of past events changes based on subsequent context.

nodes.name: latent space decoupling
nodes.description: Event dynamics evolve in a high-dimensional latent space that is decoupled from the dimensionality of event marks, allowing richer interactions between events before projection to mark-specific intensities. This enables both excitatory and inhibitory effects while avoiding O(K²) parameter scaling.

nodes.name: trade intensity impact on prices
nodes.description: The intensity of trading events (frequency and magnitude of trades) has a causal impact on subsequent price movements; higher-intensity clustering predicts directional price changes.

nodes.name: fractional noise volatility clustering
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits long-range dependence and clustering because it is driven by fractional noise (increments of fractional Brownian motion) rather than fBm itself. The Hurst exponent H > 0.5 of the integrated log-volatility process generates apparent roughness at high frequency while maintaining long-memory correlation at longer scales.

nodes.name: limit order book microstructure pricing
nodes.description: On business-as-usual days, price fluctuations depend primarily on the limit order book price mechanism rather than individual trader actions. This explains why the fractional volatility model parameters estimated from one market's daily data remain consistent with a different market's high-frequency data after adjusting the observation time scale.

nodes.name: volatility mean reversion with stochastic noise
nodes.description: Log-volatility exhibits mean reversion toward a long-term level, superimposed on stochastic fractional noise. The deterministic mean-reverting component improves volatility forecasting beyond the pure fractional noise model, suggesting markets incorporate both random shocks and systematic volatility stabilization.

nodes.name: serial dependence in fractional processes
nodes.description: Time series exhibit predictable serial dependence (Joseph effect) between non-overlapping increments, characterized by the Hurst exponent H. When H deviates from 1/α, increments are positively or negatively correlated, enabling forecasting of future values from past observations.

nodes.name: tail risk concentration in stable increments
nodes.description: Time series exhibit fat-tailed (leptokurtic) distributions with extreme events occurring at higher probability than Gaussian models predict (Noah effect). The stability parameter α < 2 captures this tail behavior, and large increments carry predictive information distinct from serial correlation.

nodes.name: selective memory in fractional stable processes
nodes.description: Beyond traditional persistence, independence, and antipersistence regimes, a fourth regime exists for very small α values where the time series exhibits selective memory controlled by a few large increments. This regime decomposes the contribution of kurtosis separately from serial dependence.

nodes.name: mean reversion via stationary distribution convergence
nodes.description: Assets exhibiting multidimensional stochastic dynamics converge to a stationary distribution at exponential rates, creating predictable mean-reverting behavior. Traders can exploit this convergence by identifying when assets deviate from their long-term equilibrium distribution and positioning for reversion.

nodes.name: tail-based mispricing detection
nodes.description: Extreme tail behavior of the stationary distribution reveals when assets are significantly mispriced relative to their long-term stochastic equilibrium. By estimating finite exponential moments of the distribution, traders identify assets in the tails that are likely to revert toward the center.

nodes.name: rank-based relative value arbitrage
nodes.description: In systems of competing assets with rank-dependent dynamics, relative performance rankings are mean-reverting due to the reflected Brownian motion structure. Traders exploit predictable reversals in rank orderings by taking positions in assets ranked at extremes.

nodes.title: A Bismut-Elworthy-Li Formula for Singular SDE's Driven by a Fractional Brownian Motion and Applications to Rough Volatility Modeling
Varadhan Estimates for rough differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motions

nodes.name: long-range dependence exploitation
nodes.description: Fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter H > 1/2 exhibits self-similarity and long-range dependence in price paths. This creates exploitable patterns where past price movements inform future direction with non-zero correlation, enabling profitable trading strategies that would be impossible in standard random walk models.

nodes.name: volatility clustering prediction
nodes.description: Fractional Brownian motion dynamics capture volatility clustering—periods of high volatility tend to be followed by high volatility. Exploiting this clustering structure improves risk management and price prediction in non-standard stochastic environments.

nodes.name: multi-level order flow imbalance
nodes.description: Order flow imbalance at price levels deeper into the limit order book (beyond the best quotes) incrementally improves price prediction. Deep LOB order flow reveals latent demand/supply that influences subsequent price formation, with cumulative predictive power increasing as more price levels are included.

nodes.name: limit order arrival and cancellation impact
nodes.description: Limit order submissions and cancellations at all price levels, not just market orders, materially affect price formation. The inclusion of limit order flow (arrivals and cancellations) alongside market orders provides superior price predictability compared to trade imbalance alone.

nodes.title: Marked point processes and intensity ratios for limit order book modeling

nodes.name: order flow imbalance pressure on trade direction
nodes.description: The signed imbalance between quantities available at best bid versus best ask predicts whether the next market order will be aggressive (move price) or passive, and whether it will hit the bid or ask side. Imbalance creates directional pressure on order flow.

nodes.name: spread-state modulation of aggressiveness
nodes.description: When the spread is wide (relative to median), orders become more or less aggressive depending on the sign of the last trade. Wide spreads interact with recent order direction to determine whether new orders will move the price.

nodes.name: hawkes clustering of order flow
nodes.description: Market orders cluster in time: recent aggressive (or non-aggressive) orders on the same side increase the intensity of future orders of that type on that side. This self-exciting behavior captures momentum in order submission.

nodes.title: Point Processes and spatial statistics in time-frequency analysis

nodes.name: self-exciting clustering
nodes.description: When a jump occurs in the point process, the intensity increases, making subsequent jumps more likely. The intensity then decays over time in the absence of new jumps, creating clustering of events.

nodes.name: mean-reversion to stable fixed points
nodes.description: The process exhibits long-run convergence to stable equilibrium intensities determined by the fixed points of the intensity function λ(x). Multiple stable fixed points can exist, with the process converging to one depending on initial conditions and stochastic shocks.

nodes.name: stochasticity-to-dynamics transition
nodes.description: Short-term behavior is dominated by stochastic jumps (which can push the process away from deterministic equilibria), while long-term behavior is governed by the deterministic dynamical system. Jump sizes decay over time (proportional to 1/(t+1)), allowing the dynamical system to dominate asymptotically.

nodes.name: self-exciting clustering in order flow
nodes.description: Market events (trades, orders) exhibit self-exciting behavior where past events increase the intensity of future events in localized space-time regions. By modeling this clustering via Hawkes processes, traders can predict elevated event intensity and adjust execution timing accordingly.

nodes.name: information flow intensity in price discovery
nodes.description: Variations in the rate of mid-price change arrivals (durations) reflect the underlying intensity and timing of information flow entering the market. Faster arrival rates signal more active price discovery and information incorporation.

nodes.name: duration-dependent volatility coupling
nodes.description: Price-change durations are mechanically linked to realized volatility: shorter durations between mid-price moves imply higher frequency of price changes and thus higher volatility. Duration forecasting directly improves volatility and liquidity prediction.

nodes.title: The Importance of Low Latency to Order Book Imbalance Trading Strategies

nodes.name: order book imbalance signal exploitation
nodes.description: Liquidity traders profit by detecting directional price movements from imbalances in bid/ask volume near the spread. When order book imbalance exceeds a threshold, it signals informed traders' directional activity that will move prices, allowing faster traders to front-run this movement.

nodes.name: latency rank competition for informed order flow
nodes.description: Among traders pursuing the same order book imbalance strategy, relative latency rank—not absolute latency magnitude—determines profit allocation. Faster traders capture the signal before slower competitors, creating a zero-sum competition where only the fastest benefit significantly.

nodes.name: informed trader inventory dissipation
nodes.description: Informed traders place directional orders to profit from fundamental value deviations, creating observable order flow patterns. Liquidity traders exploit the temporary inventory imbalances these informed orders create before prices revert to fundamental value.

nodes.title: Queue-based Resampling for Online Class Imbalance Learning

nodes.name: concept drift adaptation
nodes.description: Market regimes and class distributions shift over time; models trained on stale data suffer degraded predictive accuracy. Selective resampling of historical examples allows the model to adapt to changing market conditions while retaining relevant past information, improving trading signal quality.

nodes.name: class imbalance correction
nodes.description: Financial data streams exhibit skewed distributions (e.g., rare events like large moves or reversals are underrepresented). Queue-based resampling balances the training set by selectively including minority-class examples, preventing the model from ignoring predictive signals in tail events.

nodes.name: self-exciting intensity feedback
nodes.description: Jump events increase the intensity process, which raises the probability of subsequent jumps, creating clusters of high activity. The intensity then mean-reverts in the absence of further shocks, generating periods of low activity.

nodes.name: intensity-dependent jump sizing
nodes.description: The size of each jump is drawn from a distribution that depends on the current intensity level before the jump occurs. Higher intensity can lead to larger jumps, which in turn excite the intensity further, amplifying clustering behavior.

nodes.title: Estimation of an Order Book Dependent Hawkes Process for Large Datasets

nodes.name: self-exciting trade arrival clustering
nodes.description: Trade arrivals exhibit endogenous clustering: past trades increase the intensity of future trades through a Hawkes process mechanism with exponential decay kernels, capturing the self-reinforcing nature of high-frequency market activity independent of order book state.

nodes.name: order book state modulation of trade intensity
nodes.description: The order book environment (volume imbalances, spreads, queue depths) nonlinearly modulates the baseline intensity of trade arrivals; richer order book information adds predictive value beyond the self-exciting component alone, with effects that can be captured through high-dimensional nonlinear mappings.

nodes.name: duration-dependent intensity mean reversion
nodes.description: Trade durations inversely affect current trade intensity: longer times since the last trade reduce the intensity of the next trade arrival, reflecting a mean-reverting pattern where market activity gravitates toward typical inter-trade intervals.

nodes.name: default clustering via self-exciting jumps
nodes.description: Credit events arrive in clusters because each jump in the intensity process triggers future jumps with higher probability, creating contagion effects where defaults amplify subsequent default risk rather than being independent arrivals.

nodes.name: firm resistance to default accumulation
nodes.description: Firms do not default on the first adverse event but accumulate resistance that degrades with each shock; default occurs only after sufficient accumulated adverse events exceed the firm's resilience threshold, measured by parameter d_i.

nodes.name: systematic vs idiosyncratic shock decomposition
nodes.description: Portfolio default risk decomposes into common macroeconomic shocks affecting all firms jointly and firm-specific shocks; the common component creates correlated default risk while idiosyncratic components remain independent conditional on the systematic factor.

nodes.name: self-exciting feedback exploitation
nodes.description: Market movements exhibit self-reinforcing dynamics where past price changes increase the intensity of future price changes. By applying stochastic optimal control to capture these non-Markovian temporal dependencies, traders can time entries and exits more responsively to exploit the feedback loops inherent in market microstructure.

nodes.name: non-Markovian temporal dependency capture
nodes.description: Traditional Markovian models assume price movements depend only on current state, but markets exhibit memory effects where the full history of past shocks influences future dynamics. Exploiting these temporal dependencies through stochastic maximum principle optimization allows adaptive trading decisions that standard models miss.

nodes.name: order flow imbalance price discovery
nodes.description: Order flow imbalance (OFI) — the net accumulation of buy versus sell orders at all price levels — is a more sensitive real-time indicator of price discovery than price changes themselves, because OFI fluctuates much faster than prices and incorporates information about queue buildups and depletions deep in the limit order book.

nodes.name: stochastic intensity clustering
nodes.description: The intensity of informative events (order arrivals) is irregular and non-stationary, driven by external information flows; this clustering of event intensity produces heavy-tailed and leptokurtic return distributions that appear as subordinated Wiener processes at macro scales.

nodes.name: queue depletion toxicity
nodes.description: Order flow imbalance can be used to track the toxicity of order flows by monitoring the buildup and depletion of bid and ask queues; toxic flows deplete queues on one side, signaling adverse selection pressure.

nodes.name: probability distortion-driven exit timing
nodes.description: Traders exploit nonlinear probability weighting (overweighting tail events, underweighting middle probabilities) to determine optimal liquidation times for assets following geometric Brownian motion, generating alpha through time-inconsistent stopping decisions that deviate from rational expectations.

nodes.name: loss-aversion-driven stop-loss placement
nodes.description: Traders set asymmetric exit thresholds reflecting loss aversion—cutting losses more aggressively than taking profits—by optimizing the stopping distribution under probability distortion, rationalizing the widespread 'cut loss or take profit' trading heuristic.

nodes.name: reference-point-dependent profit-taking
nodes.description: Traders anchor exit decisions to historical highs or entry prices (reference points) rather than forward-looking fundamentals, using distorted probability beliefs to justify 'sell on percentage of historical high' and 'let profit run' strategies that exploit their own behavioral biases.

nodes.name: no unbounded profit with bounded risk constraint
nodes.description: The NUPBR condition prevents sequences of admissible portfolios from generating unbounded profits with bounded risk, even when arbitrage exists. This constraint ensures that while cheap arbitrage opportunities ('cheap thrills') are available, wealth must remain positive and cannot be scaled without limit.

nodes.name: quantile hedging under incomplete markets
nodes.description: When equivalent martingale measures do not exist, investors can still achieve probabilistic outperformance targets by optimally selecting which states of the world to hedge. The minimum capital required depends on the joint distribution of the deflator and payoff, allowing trade-offs between certainty and capital efficiency.

nodes.name: adverse fill mechanical execution
nodes.description: When a limit order is posted at a price level and the asset price moves through that level, execution becomes mechanically guaranteed at a worse price. This deterministic adverse selection occurs because the order is 'picked off' by incoming market orders after an unfavorable price move, causing immediate marked-to-market losses.

nodes.name: non-adverse fill probability reduction
nodes.description: The probability that a passive market maker's limit order executes at a favorable price (or at least not immediately disadvantageous) depends on queue position, available liquidity at the price level, and the arrival rate of incoming market orders. Lower fill probabilities make limit order posting less attractive, requiring higher expected continuation values to justify posting.

nodes.name: order flow predictability of short-term drift
nodes.description: Incoming market order flow (buy vs. sell) generates predictable short-term price movements in the direction of the flow. Buy market orders push prices upward while sell market orders push prices downward, creating a zero-mean-reverting alpha signal that market makers can exploit through optimal posting decisions.

nodes.description: The imbalance between bid and ask queue sizes at the best limits predicts short-term price movements in the direction of the smaller queue, because that queue will be consumed first and push price in its direction. Market participants exploit this signal to time limit order placement.

nodes.name: adverse selection avoidance via imbalance monitoring
nodes.description: Traders strategically place limit orders when orderbook imbalance signals favor their position, reducing the probability of being filled at unfavorable prices. By monitoring liquidity imbalance, agents can delay order submission to avoid adverse selection costs when the microprice (expected future price given imbalance) is moving against them.

nodes.name: latency erosion of imbalance value
nodes.description: The informational advantage from predicting liquidity flows via imbalance is diminished by latency. If a trader cannot quickly cancel and reinsert limit orders in response to changing imbalance, the value of the imbalance signal decays, creating a rationale for market makers to invest in speed to reduce adverse selection costs.

nodes.name: participant-class imbalance timing heterogeneity
nodes.description: Different market participant classes (institutional brokers, global banks, high-frequency traders) accept limit order executions at systematically different orderbook imbalance states, reflecting their heterogeneous information processing, urgency constraints, and technology investment. Sophisticated participants trade at more favorable imbalances, while less sophisticated ones suffer greater adverse selection.

nodes.description: Extreme parameter configurations appear optimal in-sample but are fragile; small perturbations cause sharp performance degradation or drawdown spikes, leading to out-of-sample failure. Strategies should prioritize stable plateaus over thin peaks.

nodes.name: stability region plateau selection
nodes.description: Near-optimal parameter configurations within a stable region (90% of best in-sample Sharpe) are more robust to regime shifts and execution friction than single-point optima. Plateau regions retain thickness and resist small perturbations.

nodes.description: For stateful strategies (grid, trailing, inventory), naive train-test splitting allows position state and indicator lookback overlap to bleed across window boundaries, making forward tests less blind and producing optimistic evaluations. Purge gaps and state normalization mitigate this.

nodes.name: purged walk-forward validation
nodes.description: Rolling train-test windows with explicit purge gaps between training and forward test periods, combined with state reset, reduce information leakage and serial-dependence effects for path-dependent strategies, enabling more realistic sequential adaptability assessment.

nodes.name: market systemic event hedging alpha
nodes.description: Portfolio managers can generate positive alpha by developing hedging strategies against predictable market systemic events (e.g., crashes). Since systemic events occur almost surely in finite time when volatility is positive, managers who hedge these events capture a risk premium that constitutes measurable alpha.

nodes.name: interest rate risk swaption alpha
nodes.description: Positive alpha exists when portfolio managers exploit implied interest rate risk embedded in perpetual event swaps through swaption strategies. The trivariate relationship between the riskless rate, factor sensitivity exposure, and constant risk premium creates exploitable interest rate exposure that generates alpha.

nodes.name: brownian bridge mean reversion of alpha
nodes.description: Jensen's alpha behaves as a Brownian bridge that reverts toward zero, creating predictable patterns in alpha dynamics. This mean reversion structure, combined with the fact that perfect tracking (zero alpha) has measure zero probability, implies market disequilibrium and arbitrage opportunities almost surely exist.

nodes.title: Mixtures of compound Poisson processes as models of tick-by-tick financial data

nodes.name: tick-by-tick distribution mispricing
nodes.description: Price movements follow a mixture of compound Poisson processes rather than standard distributions; traders can exploit mispricings by recognizing when observed tick-by-tick patterns deviate from the true underlying distribution, allowing prediction of mean-reverting or momentum price changes.

nodes.title: No Tick-Size Too Small: A General Method for Modelling Small Tick Limit Order Books

nodes.name: multi-tick price moves in sparse LOBs
nodes.description: Small-tick assets exhibit sparse limit order books where mid-price changes occur in multiple ticks rather than half-tick increments. This sparsity arises because the relative tick-size is small relative to price, making single-tick moves economically insignificant and causing order clustering at wider intervals.

nodes.name: order clustering at economically meaningful price levels
nodes.description: Market participants cluster limit orders at price levels that represent economically meaningful increments relative to the asset price. In small-tick assets, this clustering is sparse because single ticks are negligible relative to price, forcing orders to cluster at wider intervals and creating multi-level LOB gaps.

nodes.title: A Tick-by-Tick Solution for Concentrated Liquidity Provisioning

nodes.name: fee-chasing concentration
nodes.description: Liquidity providers concentrate capital in price ranges with lower existing liquidity to capture a larger pro-rata share of swap fees, even when those ranges are away from the current price. As more capital is allocated, provisions pile more quickly into liquidity 'wells' with better fee-per-unit returns.

nodes.name: reserves loss-avoidance
nodes.description: Liquidity providers avoid concentrating capital at the current price because reserves there experience the greatest expected depreciation under price movement. This effect scales linearly with total capital and creates a bi-modal distribution of optimal provisions, pushing liquidity away from the current tick.

nodes.name: pro-rata fee dilution penalty
nodes.description: Ticks already saturated with existing liquidity offer lower return on investment for new capital because earned fees are distributed pro-rata among all liquidity providers. This creates an incentive to provision capital to less-crowded ticks regardless of their proximity to current price.

nodes.title: Large tick assets: implicit spread and optimal tick size

nodes.name: uncertainty zone price stickiness
nodes.description: Market takers only execute trades when the efficient price crosses outside an uncertainty zone around the current bid-ask quotes, creating price stickiness and mean reversion. The width of this zone (2ηα) determines how far the efficient price must move before a new transaction occurs.

nodes.name: implicit spread as microstructure intensity
nodes.description: The implicit spread (2ηα) quantifies the intensity of microstructure effects in large-tick assets by measuring the tolerance zone where both buy and sell orders can occur. It replaces the conventional spread (which is artificially bounded at one tick) as the relevant measure of liquidity provision costs.

nodes.name: spread-volatility proportionality for large tick assets
nodes.description: The implicit spread is proportional to volatility per trade (S ~ cσ_tr), extending the Madhavan et al. and Wyart et al. relationships from small-tick to large-tick assets. This relationship reflects market makers' compensation for inventory and volatility risk.

nodes.name: self-exciting order flow contagion
nodes.description: Buy and sell orders arrive as self-exciting Hawkes processes, where past order arrivals increase the intensity of future orders of the same type. This models herd behavior and contagion: when agents observe order flow in one direction, they become more likely to place orders in that same direction, creating clustering of order arrivals.

nodes.name: asymmetric excitation of downward orders
nodes.description: Downward price movements (sell orders) have greater excitatory power on future order intensity than upward movements (buy orders), parameterized by β≥1. Investors react more strongly to price decreases than increases, creating an asymmetry in how order flow responds to price direction.

nodes.name: saturation in order intensity response
nodes.description: The intensity of new orders depends nonlinearly (via a concave function f) on aggregated past order flow, not linearly. This saturation effect means that larger accumulated order imbalances produce diminishing marginal increases in order intensity, preventing explosive feedback.

nodes.name: critical endogeneity and superlinear volatility mean reversion
nodes.description: When market parameters sit at criticality (α = f'(0)(1+βγ)), the aggregated price process exhibits volatility with superlinear (quadratic) mean reversion rather than linear. This arises from the nonlinear order intensity response and mean-field interactions, and is linked to multifractal scaling properties observed in real asset prices.

nodes.title: On bid and ask side-specific tick sizes

nodes.name: tick size impact on market order arrival
nodes.description: Smaller tick sizes increase market taker confidence and willingness to submit market orders, because market makers have greater flexibility to adjust quotes. The intensity of incoming market orders decreases with tick size squared.

nodes.name: inventory risk asymmetry mitigation
nodes.description: Market makers face asymmetric costs for short versus long inventory due to regulatory constraints and overnight repo rates. Side-specific tick sizes can offset these asymmetries, allowing the market maker to trigger more alternations in order flow direction, which improves both spread capture and inventory management.

nodes.name: discrete price grid constraint on quoting
nodes.description: Transaction prices must lie on discrete tick grids. Market makers adjust their fair bid and ask prices only when the continuous efficient price crosses uncertainty zones around tick grid values, creating discrete jumps in quoted prices rather than continuous adjustments.

nodes.title: Optimal liquidation in a Level-I limit order book for large tick stocks

nodes.name: queue depletion execution risk
nodes.description: Limit orders posted at the best ask price face execution risk because they have low time priority and may never execute if the queue depletes before reaching them. This creates a trade-off: posting limit orders saves on market impact costs but risks non-execution, while market orders guarantee execution but incur immediate bid-ask spread costs.

nodes.name: inventory-dependent execution timing
nodes.description: An agent's optimal choice between market and limit orders depends on her remaining inventory position and time to maturity. With large remaining inventory and short time horizon, the agent must accept worse execution prices (market orders) to ensure liquidation; with small inventory or long horizon, she can afford to wait in the queue with limit orders.

nodes.title: How to predict the consequences of a tick value change? Evidence from the Tokyo Stock Exchange pilot program

nodes.name: tick size impact on order execution costs
nodes.description: Larger tick sizes increase the minimum price increment, which raises both market order execution costs (wider effective spreads) and limit order placement costs (larger minimum price improvements required), affecting overall trading microstructure efficiency.

nodes.name: tick size optimization for trading efficiency
nodes.description: There exists an optimal tick size for each asset that minimizes total trading costs; tick sizes that are too large or too small relative to an asset's liquidity and volatility create inefficiencies that can be exploited by identifying mispriced stocks sensitive to tick value changes.

nodes.name: high-frequency trading mitigation via tick design
nodes.description: Adjusting tick values serves as a market design tool to reduce adverse effects from high-frequency trading by changing the granularity of price competition and order placement incentives.

nodes.title: A Tale of Two Consequences: Intended and Unintended Outcomes of the Japan TOPIX Tick Size Changes

nodes.name: tick size reduction decreases quoted spread but reduces depth
nodes.description: Smaller tick sizes allow tighter bid-ask spreads, improving liquidity for small orders. However, this reduces the profitability and increases the risk of liquidity provision, causing market makers to reduce order depth, which harms large institutional traders who face higher execution costs.

nodes.name: execution cost increase from reduced order book depth
nodes.description: When tick size reductions lower the profitability of market making, liquidity providers reduce their depth across the entire order book. Large institutional orders then face difficulty sourcing liquidity and experience higher implementation shortfall and execution costs despite tighter spreads.

nodes.name: high-frequency order cancellation noise without volume increase
nodes.description: Increases in trading speed lead to dramatic increases in message flow driven primarily by order cancellations rather than actual executed trades. This generates noise that does not improve price formation or market depth, and forces low-frequency traders to subsidize high-frequency traders.

nodes.name: market structure uncertainty reduces participation
nodes.description: Ambiguity about how markets operate and how asset prices are formed causes traders to focus on worst-case outcomes, leading risk-averse participants to avoid market participation entirely. Reducing this ambiguity through clearer microstructure features increases overall market participation and liquidity.

nodes.title: The Price Impact of Generalized Order Flow Imbalance

nodes.name: multi-level order flow pressure
nodes.description: Order flow imbalance across multiple price levels in the limit order book—not just at the best bid-ask—affects price formation. Orders queuing at deeper levels signal sustained directional pressure when best-level orders are exhausted.

nodes.name: order book depth saturation
nodes.description: When order quantity at a given price level exceeds a depth threshold, new orders accumulate at the next price level, causing the best execution price to jump by more than one tick. This multi-tick movement is not captured by standard OFI models that assume single-tick moves.

nodes.title: Tick: a Python library for statistical learning, with a particular emphasis on time-dependent modelling
Forecasting High Frequency Order Flow Imbalance

nodes.name: order flow imbalance predictability
nodes.description: Order flow imbalance (OFI)—the asymmetry between bid and offer arrival rates—exhibits predictable near-term dynamics due to lagged dependence between bid and offer events. Forecasting this imbalance using Hawkes processes allows traders to anticipate price movements before the market fully incorporates the order flow signal.

nodes.name: asymmetric order arrival dependence
nodes.description: Bid and offer events are not independent; they exhibit asymmetric and lagged dependence structures. The quantum and direction of this asymmetry correlate with traded price movements, creating exploitable patterns when properly modeled with self-exciting point processes.

nodes.title: Automatic Detection and Classification of Tick-borne Skin Lesions using Deep Learning
Modeling the coupled return-spread high frequency dynamics of large tick assets

nodes.name: volatility clustering in spread-constrained assets
nodes.description: In large tick assets, past squared returns predict future price movement probability through a latent Markov process. High volatility periods cluster because the spread regime (which is coupled to price dynamics) persists, creating predictable transitions between high and low volatility states.

nodes.name: spread-return coupling
nodes.description: Price changes and bid-ask spreads are strongly coupled in large tick assets because the spread is almost always exactly one tick. The latent Markov process governing spread transitions directly determines the conditional distribution of price movements, allowing spread observations to predict price dynamics.

nodes.name: kurtosis reduction through regime switching
nodes.description: The anomalous decrease in return kurtosis at different time aggregations arises because returns are generated by a mixture of regimes (high and low spread states). Mixing distributions with different volatility levels reduces the tail weight of the aggregate return distribution relative to a single-regime model.

nodes.title: Analysis of aggregated tick returns: evidence for anomalous diffusion

nodes.name: tick return size autocorrelation
nodes.description: Individual trade returns (tick returns) exhibit long-range positive autocorrelation in tick time (power-law decay ~Δi^-0.16), causing intervals to cluster periods of large or small tick returns. This autocorrelation allows the mean tick return size to characterize entire intervals and drive non-Gaussian aggregate return distributions.

nodes.name: order book gap volatility
nodes.description: The size of price gaps between best bid and ask prices (reflected in tick return magnitudes) varies over time. While large individual gaps do not dominate extreme aggregate returns (they cancel bidirectionally), the mean gap size across an interval increases by 2x during extreme return periods, contributing to non-Gaussian tails when combined with order flow imbalance.

nodes.title: Optimal Execution with Dynamic Order Flow Imbalance

nodes.name: order flow imbalance adverse selection
nodes.description: Trading in unbalanced markets (one-sided order flow) increases adverse selection costs because market makers widen spreads and adjust liquidity provision in response to toxic order flow. A trader's execution program creates informational footprint by displacing orders and signaling information, which pushes the order imbalance process away from equilibrium and increases execution costs.

nodes.name: information leakage footprint
nodes.description: A trader's execution activity leaves a temporal informational footprint on the order flow ticker that other market participants observe and react to. This leaked information about the trader's activity causes other participants to adjust their statistical views of order flow and expectations, creating transient adverse selection costs that decay over time as the market mean-reverts.

nodes.name: dynamic execution horizon optimization
nodes.description: The optimal execution horizon should be endogenously determined based on current market conditions rather than fixed exogenously. When informational costs are high (order flow imbalance is large), trading should slow down and extend the horizon; when informational costs are low, trading should accelerate to exit sooner. This creates adaptive execution strategies that respond to order flow dynamics.

nodes.name: price impact from order consumption
nodes.description: Executed market orders consume standing limit orders on the bid side of the limit order book, shortening the queue depth and moving the best-bid price. This instantaneous price impact is a convex function of the execution rate, incentivizing traders to split large orders into smaller pieces to minimize liquidity costs.

nodes.title: TICKing All the Boxes: Generated Checklists Improve LLM Evaluation and Generation
Stochastic Price Dynamics in Response to Order Flow Imbalance: Evidence from CSI 300 Index Futures

nodes.name: mean reversion in price response
nodes.description: Price changes following order flow imbalance shocks exhibit mean-reverting dynamics rather than persistent trends. The drift term in price evolution is modeled as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process driven by jump-type Lévy processes, causing prices to gradually revert toward equilibrium after the initial shock.

nodes.name: horizon-dependent metric efficacy
nodes.description: The predictive power of microstructure metrics (OFI, TI, Lambda) varies significantly across different forecast horizons. A metric effective at one time scale may be ineffective or even negatively correlated at another, requiring careful matching of indicator window length to prediction horizon.

nodes.name: regime-dependent indicator stability
nodes.description: Market microstructure metrics exhibit time-varying efficacy across different market regimes (efficient vs. inefficient periods). Robust metrics show only quantitative variation across regimes, while weak metrics display qualitative changes, indicating that market efficiency modulates the strength of microstructure-based price predictability.

nodes.title: When is cross impact relevant?

nodes.name: transient price impact decay
nodes.description: Price impacts from large trades are temporary rather than permanent; the market reverts toward fundamental value as the transient effect dissipates, allowing optimal execution strategies to exploit this mean reversion by spacing orders to minimize cumulative impact.

nodes.name: cross-asset order flow spillover
nodes.description: Trading pressure (order flow imbalance) in one asset transmits to and moves prices of correlated assets. This cross-impact is constrained by the minimum trading frequency of the receiving asset—information flows into less-liquid assets only as fast as they trade, creating a velocity limit on price formation.

nodes.name: liquidity-driven price formation hierarchy
nodes.description: Highly liquid assets (e.g., 10-year bond futures) endogenously form prices through their own order flow, then act as liquidity reservoirs that drive prices in less-liquid correlated products (e.g., cash bonds). The direction of causality runs from liquid to illiquid assets, not from fundamentals to all assets simultaneously.

nodes.name: minimal trading frequency constraint on information velocity
nodes.description: The speed at which price information transmits across correlated assets is bounded by the minimum trading frequency of the receiving asset. Even when order flow imbalances are large, illiquid assets cannot incorporate that information faster than their natural trading rate allows.

nodes.title: CME Iceberg Order Detection and Prediction

nodes.name: hidden liquidity detection via trade-volume discrepancy
nodes.description: Native iceberg orders reveal their hidden volume when trades execute larger than the displayed resting volume, allowing detection of the total order size through the gap between trade size and visible quantity.

nodes.name: iceberg tranche refresh pattern recognition
nodes.description: After a trade consumes the visible tranche of an iceberg order, the order is refreshed (modified) with a new visible quantity, creating a detectable sequence of trade-modify-delete actions that reveals the peak size and total volume structure.

nodes.name: synthetic iceberg detection via order arrival clustering
nodes.description: Synthetic icebergs managed by external vendors are detected by observing new limit orders arriving within a short time window after a trade at the same price level, revealing the ISV's tranche refill pattern despite orders being indistinguishable from regular limit orders.

nodes.title: How does latent liquidity get revealed in the limit order book?

nodes.name: latent liquidity revelation lag
nodes.description: Latent orders are revealed to the limit order book only gradually as they approach the trade price, with a time lag inversely related to the revelation rate ω. This delayed conversion creates a gap between observable and true available liquidity, potentially triggering liquidity crises when the conversion rate is too slow.

nodes.name: price impact nonlinearity
nodes.description: Large metaorders exhibit concave (square-root) price impact because they must draw on latent liquidity that is revealed progressively. The nonlinearity arises from the interaction between order flow and the gradual conversion of latent to revealed liquidity, with impact scaling as Q^θ where θ < 1.

nodes.name: order book depth instability
nodes.description: The revealed order book depth becomes unstable when the latent liquidity overlap parameter kℓℓ exceeds a critical threshold ζc. Beyond this threshold, the incentive to reveal liquidity (controlled by distance-dependent function Γ) becomes insufficient relative to the revelation rate, causing liquidity to vanish and creating holes in the order book.

nodes.name: distance-dependent revelation incentive
nodes.description: Traders reveal latent orders with higher probability as orders approach the trade price, modeled through a conversion probability function Γ(kξ) that increases with decreasing distance ξ from the mid-price. This incentive structure reflects the tradeoff between information leakage and execution probability.
