Byzantine-Resilient High-Dimensional Federated Learning
Learning from Reward-Free Offline Data: A Case for Planning with Latent Dynamics Models

nodes.name: latent dynamics model generalization
nodes.description: Learning a reconstruction-free latent dynamics model via self-supervised learning (JEPA) enables better generalization to unseen environment layouts and new tasks because the learned representations capture task-agnostic structure that transfers across spatial and task variations, unlike policy-based methods that overfit to training data distribution.

nodes.name: trajectory stitching via planning
nodes.description: Model-based planning can compose short suboptimal offline trajectories into long-horizon solutions by learning forward dynamics and searching over action sequences at test time, whereas policy-based methods fail when training trajectories are shorter than the required horizon because goals become out-of-distribution.

nodes.name: in-distribution regularization via uncertainty
nodes.description: Penalizing model predictions with high ensemble variance during planning prevents the agent from committing to state-action transitions that deviate from the training data distribution, maintaining robustness to suboptimal offline data similar to how expectile regression constrains policy-based methods.

nodes.name: sample efficiency from explicit dynamics learning
nodes.description: Learning an explicit forward dynamics model allows agents to extract more information per transition than model-free methods because planning can reuse the learned model across multiple action sequences, making model-based approaches more data-efficient on small datasets.

nodes.title: Consistent Pricing of VIX and Equity Derivatives with the 4/2 Stochastic Volatility Plus Jumps Model

nodes.name: stochastic volatility mispricing
nodes.description: Traditional derivative pricing models (Heston, 3/2) fail to capture the true dynamics of volatility evolution, particularly the dual-regime behavior of instantaneous volatility. The 4/2 model's more flexible volatility specification (a√V_t + b/√V_t) better matches realized volatility dynamics, creating exploitable mispricings in equity and VIX derivatives.

nodes.name: jump risk mispricing
nodes.description: Models that omit or inadequately specify jump components in asset price dynamics systematically misprice derivatives, particularly those sensitive to tail risk. The 4/2 model's explicit jump component captures discontinuous price movements that simpler models miss, allowing traders to exploit pricing discrepancies in options and variance derivatives.

nodes.name: context-specific anomaly detection
nodes.description: Market anomalies that appear globally rare may be normal within specific market contexts (e.g., different regimes, asset classes, or time periods). By learning conditional distributions P(Y|C) rather than global distributions, the model identifies truly abnormal deviations within their proper context, enabling detection of profitable mispricings that global models miss.

nodes.name: lead-lag synchronization via local extrema timing
nodes.description: One market's price reversals (local extrema) systematically precede another's by a consistent phase shift, allowing the leading market to be used as a predictive indicator for the lagging market's future price movements.

nodes.title: Emergence of statistically validated financial intraday lead-lag relationships

nodes.name: information spillover across equities
nodes.description: Price movements in one stock lead to correlated price movements in other stocks at short intraday timescales (below 30 minutes), reflecting the time it takes for information to propagate across the market and for traders to react to cross-asset price signals.

nodes.name: statistical power from high-frequency sampling
nodes.description: Shorter sampling horizons (h < 30 minutes) generate longer time series, increasing statistical power to detect genuine lead-lag relationships that would be obscured by noise at longer horizons, revealing the true timescale of information spillover.

nodes.name: increased market efficiency over time
nodes.description: The decline in validated lead-lag links from 2002–2003 to 2011–2012 (despite higher algorithmic trading penetration) suggests markets have become more efficient at incorporating information, reducing exploitable lagged correlation patterns between stocks.

nodes.title: From Data Acquisition to Lag Modeling: Quantitative Exploration of A-Share Market with Low-Coupling System Design

nodes.name: information diffusion delay across coupled stocks
nodes.description: Price information from economically linked stocks (those with high long-term coupling) propagates with measurable time delays at intraday frequencies, causing leader stocks to exhibit predictive power over follower stocks' returns. This reflects asynchronous price adjustment despite fundamental economic relationships.

nodes.name: industry-driven information cascade
nodes.description: Information disseminates first within industry groups before spreading to economically linked sectors, with large-cap industry leaders influencing smaller peers. This creates multi-stage cascades (e.g., stock A → stock B → stock C) where information flows through the industrial chain.

nodes.name: retail investor heterogeneous information response
nodes.description: The A-share market's dominance by retail investors creates heterogeneity in how quickly different stocks respond to information, causing slower-responding stocks to lag faster-responding ones. This generates exploitable lead-lag patterns at short time horizons.

nodes.name: price limit constraint delay
nodes.description: China's price limit trading system (daily price movement caps) prevents full and immediate reflection of information in prices, causing information to propagate gradually across coupled stocks rather than instantaneously, particularly visible at intraday frequencies.

nodes.title: Information-theoretic approach to lead-lag effect on financial markets

nodes.name: lead-lag information diffusion
nodes.description: Certain stocks or groups of stocks process new information earlier than others, causing their price movements to predictively lead the price movements of lagging stocks. This temporal structure in information dissemination creates exploitable lead-lag relationships across the market.

nodes.name: non-linear return dependencies
nodes.description: Stock returns exhibit non-linear relationships that linear correlation misses. These non-linear dependencies capture complex market dynamics and interdependencies that are economically meaningful but invisible to Pearson correlation analysis.

nodes.name: intraday-daily frequency arbitrage gap
nodes.description: Lead-lag effects are substantially stronger at intraday frequencies than daily frequencies because intraday markets have slower information incorporation and higher microstructure noise, while daily prices reflect more complete information aggregation.

nodes.title: Collaborative Information Bottleneck
Returns and Order Flow Imbalances: Intraday Dynamics and Macroeconomic News Effects

nodes.name: macroeconomic news liquidity shock
nodes.description: Macroeconomic announcements cause sharp, transient shifts in market microstructure: price impact rises while flow impact declines, creating temporary inefficiencies as the market reprices public information and liquidity provision adjusts.

nodes.name: order flow price impact asymmetry
nodes.description: Price responds asymmetrically to order flow imbalances depending on market state: in normal periods, both price and flow impacts are significant at high frequency, but macroeconomic news events alter this relationship by increasing price sensitivity while reducing flow sensitivity.

nodes.name: high-frequency shock dissipation
nodes.description: Order flow shocks and their price impacts dissipate almost entirely within one second, indicating rapid price discovery and mean reversion at ultra-high frequencies that can be exploited before information fully incorporates.

nodes.title: Order Book Queue Hawkes-Markovian Modeling

nodes.name: cross-exciting order flow contagion
nodes.description: The arrival of one order type stimulates the arrival of different order types through mutual excitation. For example, trades at one price level can trigger insertions or cancellations at other levels. The cross-Hawkes kernels φji(t) (where j≠i) capture how events of type j increase the intensity of events of type i.

nodes.name: liquidity state dependent intensity modulation
nodes.description: The baseline intensity of order arrivals depends on the current liquidity state of the order book—specifically queue depths at relevant price levels and bid-ask spreads. Thinner queues or wider spreads modulate the rate at which new orders arrive, reflecting how market participants respond to current liquidity conditions.

nodes.name: intraday time-of-day intensity clustering
nodes.description: Order arrival intensities exhibit systematic intraday patterns, with elevated activity at market open and close (last 30 minutes) and lower activity during midday hours. This time-clustering effect is captured through the Θi(t) component of the baseline intensity, reflecting behavioral and institutional trading patterns.

nodes.title: Conditional Information Inequalities for Entropic and Almost Entropic Points
Optimal Order Execution in Intraday Markets: Minimizing Costs in Trade Trajectories

nodes.name: order book depth impact on execution costs
nodes.description: Trading costs (measured by bid-ask spread) increase non-linearly with order size because larger volumes must be filled at progressively worse price levels deeper in the order book. The spread widens as cumulative volume increases across price levels.

nodes.name: time-to-delivery liquidity variation
nodes.description: Market liquidity and spreads change discontinuously at specific times before delivery (60 and 30 minutes) due to market coupling/decoupling events (XBID coupling changes, local trading initiation). Traders face different execution costs depending on when they trade relative to these structural market events.

nodes.name: market impact from own trading activity
nodes.description: A trader's own execution activity temporarily moves prices against them—buying pushes prices up, selling pushes prices down. This temporary price movement is a cost that must be minimized through optimal order slicing and timing decisions.

nodes.title: No arbitrage and lead-lag relationships

nodes.name: lead-lag correlation across assets
nodes.description: Time-lagged cross-correlations between returns of paired assets create apparent arbitrage opportunities in frictionless markets, but these opportunities are eliminated when market frictions (minimal waiting times or transaction costs) are introduced.

nodes.name: minimal waiting time friction
nodes.description: Imposing a constant minimum time interval between successive transactions prevents arbitrage exploitation of lead-lag relationships by restricting the frequency at which traders can rebalance positions.

nodes.name: proportional transaction costs friction
nodes.description: Constant proportional transaction costs eliminate arbitrage opportunities in markets with lead-lag relationships by making frequent rebalancing economically infeasible, even when price paths have predictable cross-asset correlations.

nodes.title: IT formulae for gamma target: mutual information and relative entropy
Wavelet-based methods for high-frequency lead-lag analysis

nodes.name: multi-scale lead-lag effect
nodes.description: Different market participants with different investment horizons and information sources create lead-lag relationships between assets that vary across time scales. A leader asset's price movements predict a lagging asset's movements at scale-dependent intervals, reflecting the heterogeneous market structure.

nodes.name: scale-dependent information propagation
nodes.description: Information diffuses across financial markets at different rates depending on the time scale of observation. High-frequency traders and low-frequency investors process the same information at different speeds, creating predictable cross-asset correlations that are strongest at specific scales.

nodes.title: HLOB -- Information Persistence and Structure in Limit Order Books

nodes.name: information persistence degradation across LOB depth
nodes.description: Information encoded in the spatial structure of limit order book volume levels decays over increasing prediction horizons. The velocity of this degradation depends on stocks' microstructural properties (tick size classification), with small-tick stocks experiencing faster information decay due to sparser LOB structures.

nodes.name: microstructural heterogeneity in LOB spatial distribution
nodes.description: Heterogeneous spatial separation between consecutive price levels in limit order books reduces deep learning models' ability to capture dependencies, with the effect exacerbated in small-tick stocks that have sparse LOB structures versus large-tick stocks with compact structures.

nodes.name: higher-order volume level dependencies
nodes.description: Non-trivial causal relationships exist among volume levels beyond consecutive price levels in the LOB. These deeper dependencies among up to four variables per clique can be exploited for mid-price prediction when properly structured through topological filtering.

nodes.title: Lead-lag Relationships in Foreign Exchange Markets

nodes.name: Delayed information diffusion across currency pairs
nodes.description: Market information does not spread instantaneously across foreign exchange pairs; slower-moving assets (stock market indexes) lead faster-moving assets (currency pairs) by approximately one minute, contradicting the efficient market hypothesis at high frequency.

nodes.name: Predictive power of lagged returns
nodes.description: Past returns of a leader asset improve prediction of future returns of a lagging asset beyond what the lagger's own past returns provide, as measured by Granger causality and reduction in regression residual variance.

nodes.name: Statistical arbitrage opportunity from lead-lag correlation
nodes.description: Statistically significant lagged correlations between leader and lagger returns create potential arbitrage opportunities where observing a leader's return allows positioning in the lagger before its directional change, though transaction costs may eliminate profitability.

nodes.title: Can Information Flows Suggest Targets for Interventions in Neural Circuits?
On lead-lag estimation of non-synchronously observed point processes

nodes.name: order arrival lead-lag effect
nodes.description: One asset's order arrivals lead another asset's order arrivals by a detectable time lag, revealing information flow and price discovery dynamics between markets. This lead-lag relationship persists even at millisecond timescales and can be exploited if accurately estimated.

nodes.title: A Decadal Analysis of the Lead-Lag Effect in the NYSE

nodes.name: lead-lag price momentum spillover
nodes.description: When a leader stock's price moves beyond a threshold, the lagging stock's price follows predictably within a fixed time lag. This allows traders to profit by buying the lagger after observing the leader's move, exploiting the delayed price discovery between connected stocks.

nodes.name: low out-degree concentration effect
nodes.description: Stocks with fewer outgoing lead-lag connections (low out-degree) receive stronger and more concentrated signals from their few leaders, making their price movements more predictable and tradeable. This network topology effect amplifies the exploitability of the lead-lag relationship.

nodes.name: market regime-dependent signal strength
nodes.description: The lead-lag effect's profitability and optimal trading parameters vary systematically between bull and bear markets. Bull markets reward lower buy thresholds (more aggressive entry), while bear markets require higher thresholds (conservative entry), suggesting the underlying price momentum mechanism strengthens or weakens with market direction.

nodes.title: MillGNN: Learning Multi-Scale Lead-Lag Dependencies for Multi-Variate Time Series Forecasting

nodes.name: lead-lag dependency propagation
nodes.description: Time series segments of one variate (leading) causally affect another variate (lagging) after a time lag. This asynchronous influence propagates through the system at multiple hierarchical scales—both between individual variates and between groups of variates—with different lag structures and decay rates at each scale.

nodes.name: multi-scale decay dynamics
nodes.description: Lead-lag effects weaken over time through two competing mechanisms: rapid dissipation when variates are weakly related, and periodic revival from cyclical or seasonal patterns. The strength of decay varies across grouping scales—fine-grained scales exhibit rapid, sensitive decay while coarse-grained scales show more stable, robust patterns.

nodes.title: NAPLES;Mining the lead-lag Relationship from Non-synchronous and High-frequency Data

nodes.name: lead-lag price discovery delay
nodes.description: One asset's price movements lead another asset's price movements by a measurable lag, allowing profitable trading strategies that exploit the delayed response. This occurs because information or liquidity shocks propagate asynchronously across correlated assets.

nodes.name: macroeconomic announcement-induced lead-lag volatility
nodes.description: Lead-lag relationships between correlated assets become time-varying and more pronounced around significant macroeconomic announcements, as market participants process information at different speeds and adjust positions sequentially.

nodes.title: Robust Detection of Lead-Lag Relationships in Lagged Multi-Factor Models

nodes.name: lead-lag cross-asset propagation
nodes.description: Price movements in one asset lead movements in related assets with a time delay, reflecting incomplete or asynchronous information diffusion across correlated securities. This temporal ordering can be exploited for predictive trading.

nodes.title: The importance of emotional intelligence in leadership for building an effective team
Avellaneda-Stoikov and Cartea-Jaimungal as One Framework: A Forced Uniqueness Theorem for Inventory Market Making

nodes.name: liquidation cost convexity
nodes.description: Larger inventory positions are disproportionately more expensive to unwind due to market impact and bid-ask spreads, creating a convex cost function that forces the market maker to penalize inventory accumulation nonlinearly. This convexity of L(q) drives the terminal penalty coefficient α = ½L''(0).

nodes.name: volatility-adjusted inventory penalty
nodes.description: The running inventory penalty must scale with the price process's quadratic variation (σ²_t) rather than wall-clock time to maintain time-consistency across varying volatility regimes. This forces the relation φ = γσ²/2 and ensures the risk-aversion parameter remains invariant to the volatility clock.

nodes.title: Inventory Management with Partially Observed Nonstationary Demand

nodes.name: demand censoring information loss
nodes.description: When inventory is insufficient to meet an order, the true demand size becomes unobservable (censored), forcing the manager to infer the hidden demand state from only the filled portion. This creates a partial information problem where the manager must learn the true demand regime while simultaneously managing inventory under uncertainty.

nodes.name: regime-switching demand learning
nodes.description: The true economic environment (demand regime) is unobserved and must be inferred through Bayesian updating as orders arrive. The manager updates beliefs about which regime is active based on observed order patterns, then adjusts inventory policy in anticipation of future demand distribution changes.

nodes.name: inventory-dependent order observation
nodes.description: The observable order flow is mechanically determined by both the true demand and current inventory level. Low inventory truncates observed demand, creating a feedback loop where control decisions directly affect what information becomes available for future learning and decision-making.

nodes.title: Next Generation Models for Portfolio Risk Management: An Approach Using Financial Big Data

nodes.name: out-of-target-portfolio information incorporation
nodes.description: Portfolio risk can be better estimated by incorporating information from assets outside the immediate target portfolio, rather than relying solely on within-portfolio correlations. This captures systemic risk signals that traditional VaR approaches miss.

nodes.name: curse-of-dimensionality mitigation
nodes.description: As the number of assets in a portfolio increases, traditional risk models degrade due to estimation error in high-dimensional covariance matrices. Financial big data techniques can overcome this by identifying true risk factors among noise, improving accuracy in large portfolios.

nodes.name: incomplete market measure selection under risk aversion
nodes.description: In incomplete markets with multiple equivalent martingale measures, a risk-averse investor's optimal portfolio strategy is determined by the market's antagonistic selection of probability measure. The investor's wealth allocation and the market's measure choice form a saddle-point equilibrium where the minimal martingale measure emerges as the equilibrium measure.

nodes.name: no-regret strategy under minimal martingale measure
nodes.description: When the factor process evolves under the Föllmer-Schweizer minimal martingale measure and short-selling is prohibited, the investor's optimal strategy collapses to holding only the riskless asset. This occurs because the minimal martingale measure eliminates profitable deviations from the risk-free rate.

nodes.name: factor-stock noise independence constraint on optimal allocation
nodes.description: When the factor process and stock price process have independent noise sources, the optimal investor strategy is the no-regret strategy (riskless asset only) regardless of whether short-selling is allowed. The independence structure prevents the investor from exploiting factor-driven returns.

nodes.title: Logarithmic regret in the ergodic Avellaneda-Stoikov market making model

nodes.name: price sensitivity learning under order flow uncertainty
nodes.description: Market makers must learn the price sensitivity parameter κ (how liquidity takers respond to quoted spreads) online while trading, because offline estimates become inaccurate when other market makers react to the additional volume. The regret from misestimating κ compounds over time, creating a learning-exploitation tradeoff.

nodes.name: inventory risk penalty mechanism
nodes.description: Market makers face a quadratic penalty on inventory holdings to incentivize continuous rebalancing toward zero position, minimizing directional exposure to adverse price movements in volatile markets. This running cost creates a tension between capturing spread profits and managing inventory risk.

nodes.name: order arrival intensity estimation
nodes.description: Market makers can learn the arrival rates λ± of buy and sell market orders offline without participation, since their own small market share does not materially affect aggregate order flow. This allows separation of the learning problem into observable (arrival rates) and unobservable (price sensitivity κ) components.

nodes.title: Liquidity Stress Testing in Asset Management -- Part 3. Managing the Asset-Liability Liquidity Risk

nodes.name: redemption-driven portfolio distortion
nodes.description: When investors redeem shares, asset managers must liquidate positions, which distorts the remaining portfolio's weights away from the original allocation. Non-proportional liquidation rules amplify this effect, forcing remaining investors to bear unintended exposure changes and potential tracking error.

nodes.name: negative externality from strategic redemptions
nodes.description: Redeeming investors impose costs on remaining investors through forced asset sales in illiquid markets, creating payoff complementarities where redemption incentives amplify when other investors also redeem. This financial fragility mechanism can trigger cascading redemptions and systemic liquidity stress.

nodes.name: asset-liability liquidity mismatch
nodes.description: Funds face a timing mismatch between liability obligations (redemptions) and asset liquidity constraints (time to liquidate). When redemption shocks exceed liquid assets available within acceptable time horizons, funds incur liquidity shortfalls and must sell illiquid assets at fire-sale prices, crystallizing losses.

nodes.title: Implementing portfolio risk management and hedging in practice
Value-Based Inventory Management

nodes.name: opportunity cost of capital tied in inventory
nodes.description: Holding inventory requires capital that could be deployed elsewhere, creating an opportunity cost proportional to the cost of capital (WACC). This cost should reduce optimal order quantities below the traditional EOQ level to maximize firm value.

nodes.name: cash flow drag from working capital expansion
nodes.description: Increases in inventory levels expand net working capital, which ties up cash and reduces free cash flows available for discounting. This reduces firm value through the FCFF valuation channel, incentivizing lower inventory holdings than cost-minimization models suggest.

nodes.name: production capacity constraint premium
nodes.description: When production capacity exceeds market demand, firms face a trade-off between setup costs and inventory holding costs. Reducing production order quantities below the POQ optimum decreases inventory levels and working capital drag, creating value despite higher per-unit ordering costs.

nodes.title: Liquidity Stress Testing in Asset Management -- Part 2. Modeling the Asset Liquidity Risk

nodes.name: price impact from participation rate
nodes.description: Large trades incur nonlinear price impact costs that scale with the participation rate (trade size relative to daily volume). The impact follows a power-law relationship where the exponent γ determines whether impact is concave (γ < 1, e.g., square-root) or linear (γ = 1), with larger trades facing disproportionately higher costs.

nodes.name: bid-ask spread component
nodes.description: A fixed spread cost s (half the bid-ask spread) is incurred on all trades regardless of size, representing the cost of immediacy in the market. This component is invariant to trade size and participation rate.

nodes.name: two-regime market impact
nodes.description: Market impact exhibits different regimes depending on trade size: small trades (below threshold x̃) experience lower impact with exponent γ₁, while larger trades (above x̃) face steeper impact with exponent γ₂. This regime-switching reflects qualitatively different market microstructure at different order sizes.

nodes.name: trading limit constraint
nodes.description: Asset managers face a maximum trading limit x⁺ (typically 10% of daily volume) beyond which transaction costs become prohibitive or infinite. This constraint forces liquidation to occur over multiple periods, creating a time-to-liquidation dimension and potential portfolio distortion.

nodes.title: Risk Concentration and Diversification: Second-Order Properties

nodes.name: slow convergence to asymptotic diversification benefit
nodes.description: In heavy-tailed loss distributions, the risk concentration ratio C(α) converges to its theoretical limit nξ−1 arbitrarily slowly as α→1, meaning that at practical confidence levels (95%-99.97%), the first-order approximation severely underestimates concentration and overstates diversification benefits.

nodes.name: second-order regular variation dominance
nodes.description: When the second-order parameter ρ > −(1∧ξ), the tail quantile function's slowly-varying component dominates the convergence rate, causing C(α) to approach its limit with a decay rate governed by a(1/(1−α)) where a is the auxiliary function, leading to potentially very slow convergence.

nodes.name: second-order subexponentiality dominance
nodes.description: When ρ < −(1∧ξ), the convolution tail behavior dominates, and C(α) converges faster via the function b(F←(α)) which decays more rapidly; however, this regime still exhibits sensitivity to small changes in α near 1, potentially flipping from diversification to non-diversification.

nodes.name: regime switch from diversification to non-diversification
nodes.description: Due to slow convergence in heavy-tailed models, risk aggregation can exhibit a sharp transition from positive diversification benefit (C(α)<1) to negative diversification or superadditivity (C(α)>1) at extreme confidence levels, meaning regulatory capital requirements can increase rather than decrease when combining risks.

nodes.title: Combining Reinforcement Learning and Barrier Functions for Adaptive Risk Management in Portfolio Optimization

nodes.name: adaptive risk control under volatility
nodes.description: A barrier function dynamically adjusts portfolio positions in response to increasing market volatility, preventing large losses during downturns by constraining aggressive return-seeking behavior. This adaptive mechanism allows the strategy to shift from offensive to defensive positioning as market conditions deteriorate.

nodes.name: return-risk tradeoff optimization
nodes.description: Reinforcement learning pursues profitable trading opportunities while barrier functions simultaneously enforce risk constraints, creating a dynamic balance that prevents the strategy from over-concentrating in high-risk positions. The dual mechanism allows aggressive alpha generation without catastrophic loss exposure.

nodes.title: Measuring and Managing Carbon Risk in Investment Portfolios

nodes.name: transition risk pricing via carbon beta
nodes.description: Stock prices incorporate systematic risk exposure to unexpected shifts toward a low-carbon economy. Firms with high carbon footprints (brown firms) have positive carbon betas and underperform when climate transition accelerates, while green firms with negative carbon betas outperform.

nodes.name: carbon factor mimicking portfolio construction
nodes.description: A brown-minus-green (BMG) risk factor is constructed by longing brown firms and shorting green firms, sorted by fundamental carbon risk scores across three dimensions (value chain, public perception, adaptability). This factor captures the systematic carbon risk priced by markets.

nodes.name: size-carbon risk confounding
nodes.description: The BMG factor exhibits positive correlation with the SMB (size) factor because green firms tend to have larger market capitalizations. When large firms outperform small firms, both SMB and BMG factor returns decline together, conflating size effects with carbon risk.

nodes.title: On Fairness of Systemic Risk Measures
High-frequency market-making with inventory constraints and directional bets

nodes.name: directional bet adjustment
nodes.description: Market-makers place asymmetric bid-ask quotes to exploit expected price movements. When the market-maker expects prices to rise, she widens the ask spread and tightens the bid spread to encourage selling (reducing long inventory); conversely, she tightens the ask and widens the bid when expecting price declines. The indifference price shifts from the current mid-price toward the expected future price.

nodes.name: adverse selection cost
nodes.description: Market-makers lose money to informed traders who trade when the market-maker's quotes are mispriced relative to true fundamental value. Market-makers recover these losses by charging uninformed traders the bid-ask spread, effectively making noise traders subsidize informed trading.

nodes.title: A new approach for scenario generation in Risk management
Pricing and Risk Management with High-Dimensional Quasi Monte Carlo and Global Sensitivity Analysis
Impacts of National Cultures on Managerial Decisions of Engaging in Core Earnings Management

nodes.name: individualism-driven earnings inflation
nodes.description: Managers in high-individualism cultures inflate reported earnings to signal personal achievement and meet performance targets, as individual success and material rewards are culturally emphasized.

nodes.name: uncertainty-avoidance-driven earnings smoothing
nodes.description: Managers in high-uncertainty-avoidance cultures engage in discretionary accruals and earnings smoothing to reduce income volatility and minimize perceived risk of future performance fluctuations.

nodes.name: masculinity-deterred earnings management
nodes.description: Risk-taking attributes and performance-based incentives in masculine cultures paradoxically reduce core earnings management, as managers pursue real operational improvements rather than accounting manipulation.

nodes.title: A risk management approach to capital allocation
Game-theoretic approach to risk-sensitive benchmarked asset management

nodes.name: risk-sensitive active return optimization
nodes.description: An investor optimizes portfolio allocation to maximize risk-adjusted excess returns over a stochastic benchmark, where risk aversion is parameterized by a sensitivity coefficient that penalizes deviations from expected active returns.

nodes.name: adversarial benchmark setting
nodes.description: The market acts as an antagonistic player that modulates a stochastic benchmark to minimize the investor's expected payoff, creating a game-theoretic equilibrium where the investor's optimal strategy must account for worst-case benchmark dynamics.

nodes.name: macroeconomic factor modulation of returns
nodes.description: Security returns and volatility are driven by latent macroeconomic factors (GDP, inflation, market index) whose dynamics are correlated with price processes, allowing the optimization problem to incorporate systematic economic risk into portfolio selection.

nodes.title: Generative AI Enhanced Financial Risk Management Information Retrieval
A machine learning approach to portfolio pricing and risk management for high-dimensional problems
Conditional Generative Modeling for Enhanced Credit Risk Management in Supply Chain Finance
Options as Silver Bullets: Valuation of Term Loans, Inventory Management, Emissions Trading and Insurance Risk Mitigation using Option Theory

nodes.name: inventory availability optionality
nodes.description: Term loan rates embed optionality because share availability fluctuates stochastically (modeled as GBM), forcing intermediaries to price the risk that they cannot fulfill guaranteed loan quantities. Borrowers have the option to take fewer shares than guaranteed, creating asymmetric payoff structures.

nodes.name: short-sale constraint hedging cost
nodes.description: When shares are hard to borrow, options market makers face elevated hedging costs because they cannot easily short the underlying stock and must instead fail-to-deliver or source expensive inventory. This dislocation between synthetic and actual short prices increases the value of term loan guarantees.

nodes.name: rate-lock strategic value
nodes.description: Short sellers with multi-month trading strategies benefit from locking in fixed borrow rates via term loans rather than facing daily rate fluctuations. This willingness to pay a premium for rate certainty creates a term structure of loan fees that reflects future uncertainty in share availability.

nodes.title: Inventory Management for High-Frequency Trading with Imperfect Competition

nodes.name: inventory-averse position unwinding
nodes.description: HFTs with risk-averse preferences optimally reduce their inventory positions faster than risk-neutral traders would, creating mean-reverting inventory dynamics. This causes prices to adjust downward (for long positions) or upward (for short positions) as HFTs unwind, independent of fundamental value changes.

nodes.name: competitive excess trading
nodes.description: Under Nash competition, each HFT internalizes only her own price impact costs but not the negative externalities imposed on other HFTs. This causes HFTs to trade more aggressively than a cooperative (social planner) solution would, increasing market depth but also increasing total trading volume and transaction costs.

nodes.name: information signal exploitation with rapid decay
nodes.description: HFTs exploit short-lived informational advantages (one-period ahead knowledge of value increments) by trading aggressively when signals are fresh, then rapidly unwinding positions as the signal becomes public. The optimal trade size is linear in the signal strength and inversely related to inventory levels.

nodes.title: Theoretical Sensitivity Analysis for Quantitative Operational Risk Management
A Personal data Value at Risk Approach
Analysis of the Driving Factors of Implementing Green Supply Chain Management in SME in the City of Semarang
LLM-based policy generation for intent-based management of applications
Market Making and Transient Impact in Spot FX

nodes.name: inventory risk premium via quote skewing
nodes.description: Market makers widen spreads and skew quotes away from their inventory position to manage inventory risk. Larger inventory positions trigger larger quote adjustments, compensating the dealer for carrying directional risk.

nodes.name: transient impact from client order flow
nodes.description: When a client trades with a dealer, the mid-price jumps instantaneously but then relaxes exponentially back toward its initial level as the dealer's inventory position normalizes through subsequent client flow. This creates a temporary price deviation that decays with the dealer's risk relaxation timescale.

nodes.name: hedging impact resilience interaction
nodes.description: When dealers hedge large inventory positions in the interbank market, their hedging trades create market impact that decays exponentially. The optimal hedging decision depends on the current resilient impact state—if impact is already elevated, the dealer delays hedging to avoid compounding costs; if impact is decaying, hedging becomes more attractive.

nodes.name: internalization zone contraction under elevated impact
nodes.description: The threshold inventory level beyond which a dealer must hedge (rather than internalize) shrinks when the resilient impact state is elevated. High existing market impact makes external hedging more costly, so dealers tolerate larger internal positions before executing.

nodes.title: Transient impact from the Nash equilibrium of a permanent market impact game

nodes.name: arbitrageur predatory trading response
nodes.description: An arbitrageur observing a directional trader's liquidation schedule exploits the predictable order flow by executing a round-trip strategy (buying early, selling late), which generates transient price reversals even when the underlying market impact is permanent.

nodes.name: strategic execution fragmentation
nodes.description: A directional trader fragments their liquidation into a U-shaped schedule (front-loaded and back-loaded trades) to minimize exploitation by arbitrageurs, which creates correlated order flow patterns that induce observed transient impact despite permanent underlying impact.

nodes.name: implied transient impact from partial order flow observation
nodes.description: An external observer who estimates market impact by regressing price changes on only the directional trader's order flow (ignoring the arbitrageur's offsetting trades) infers a transient decay kernel, even though the true underlying impact is permanent and fixed.

nodes.title: Market Impact of Small Orders

nodes.name: liquidity depletion at best level
nodes.description: When an aggressive order exhausts the volume available at the best bid/ask level, the next level must be accessed, requiring a discrete price step of one tick. The impact is proportional to how many best-level liquidity pools must be consumed, creating the observed linear or concave volume-impact relationship.

nodes.name: informed trader execution scheduling
nodes.description: Informed traders breaking large metaorders into small slices follow execution schedules (TWAP, VWAP, PoV) that force other market participants to cross the spread to meet their own time/volume constraints. This creates predictable order flow that moves prices linearly with cumulative volume executed.

nodes.title: Nash equilibrium for risk-averse investors in a market impact game with transient price impact

nodes.name: predatory trading oscillations
nodes.description: Competing risk-averse agents oscillate between buy and sell orders to protect against being exploited by competitors' execution timing. These oscillations emerge from strategic interaction in a market with transient price impact, where agents must balance liquidation urgency against the risk of being front-run.

nodes.name: transaction cost dampening
nodes.description: Quadratic transaction costs (modeling slippage or transaction taxes) eliminate predatory trading oscillations above a critical threshold. The critical threshold depends on the number of competing agents for synchronized positions, but depends on risk aversion for zero-sum positions.

nodes.name: latency execution cost
nodes.description: When multiple agents trade at the same time, each agent incurs additional costs proportional to the product of their order size and competitors' order sizes, because on average 50% of the time a competitor's order executes first. This creates an incentive to time trades strategically relative to competitors.

nodes.title: Market Inefficiency in Cryptoasset Markets

nodes.name: Impeded capital reallocation across yield strategies
nodes.description: Capital fails to flow freely among direct staking, ETH lending, and liquid staking strategies despite yield differentials that should trigger arbitrage. When one strategy becomes more attractive (higher yield spread), capital does not reallocate to restore equilibrium yields, indicating frictions prevent efficient capital deployment.

nodes.name: StETH lending yield insensitivity to staking yield spread
nodes.description: The stETH lending yield fails to respond to changes in the spread between protocol staking yield (γ_ETH) and Lido's pass-through yield (γ_stETH). Theory predicts a one-for-one relationship, but empirically the coefficient is negative (-0.228), suggesting investors do not arbitrage away the yield differential between direct and liquid staking.

nodes.name: StETH lending yield insensitivity to ETH lending yield
nodes.description: The stETH lending yield shows almost no response to changes in the ETH lending yield (ψ_ETH), despite theory predicting a one-for-one adjustment. The estimated coefficient is only 0.017 instead of 1.0, indicating investors fail to arbitrage between lending ETH directly and pursuing the liquid staking strategy.

nodes.title: A market impact game under transient price impact

nodes.name: predatory trading protection via oscillatory strategies
nodes.description: High-frequency traders engage in rapid buy-sell oscillations (hot-potato game) to protect against predatory exploitation of their price impact. When transaction costs are low, competitors can profit by trading in the opposite direction after observing an agent's trades, so agents preemptively oscillate positions to avoid leaving exploitable drift.

nodes.name: hot-potato game / Flash Crash volume inflation
transaction cost suppression of oscillations
nodes.description: Quadratic transaction costs above a critical threshold θ* eliminate oscillatory equilibrium strategies, forcing traders into monotonic buy-only or sell-only strategies. Transaction costs penalize rapid position reversals, making predatory-trading protection via oscillation economically infeasible.

nodes.name: transient price impact decay exploitation
nodes.description: Traders exploit the time-decay of price impact from competitors' trades. The decay kernel G(t) determines how quickly impact dissipates; traders can profit by trading opposite to competitors when impact has partially decayed, creating incentive for predatory strategies and defensive oscillations.

nodes.title: A theory of passive market impact

nodes.name: order book queue resistance
nodes.description: The price impact of a market order depends on the available volume in the limit order book on that side. When queue depth is larger, it is harder for the price to move in that direction because the price resistance coefficient κ decreases with available volume.

nodes.name: market order intensity response to queue depletion
nodes.description: The arrival intensity of market orders increases when the available volume at the best bid or ask price becomes depleted. Nearly empty piles attract market orders with very high probability, provoking price changes.

nodes.name: limit order passive market impact via queue dynamics
nodes.description: Limit orders create price impact by altering the limit order book state, which affects the price resistance coefficient for subsequent market orders. The impact depends on how the metaorder's presence changes queue mean-reversion and the sensitivity of price stickiness to volume changes.

nodes.title: Optimal Execution in Intraday Energy Markets under Hawkes Processes with Transient Impact

nodes.name: self-exciting order flow momentum
nodes.description: Market orders cluster in time due to self-exciting dynamics captured by Hawkes processes; past order flow increases the intensity of future orders, creating predictable momentum in execution demand that can be exploited to time trades more efficiently.

nodes.title: Deterministic Control of Stochastic Reaction-Diffusion Equations

Fundamental Limits of Controlled Stochastic Dynamical Systems: An Information-Theoretic Approach
Stochastic control on the half-line and applications to the optimal dividend/consumption problem

nodes.name: optimal stopping barrier timing
nodes.description: Returns can be enhanced by dynamically optimizing the timing of capital allocation decisions (dividend payouts, consumption) relative to a stochastic barrier. The mechanism exploits the solution to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation to identify when to execute these decisions, generating alpha through superior timing compared to static strategies.

nodes.name: dynamic capital allocation efficiency
nodes.description: More efficient capital allocation and risk management can be achieved by solving the stochastic control problem to determine optimal dividend and consumption amounts dynamically, rather than using fixed or ad-hoc allocation rules. This efficiency gain translates into enhanced risk-adjusted returns.

nodes.title: Convex Chance-Constrained Stochastic Control under Uncertain Specifications with Application to Learning-Based Hybrid Powertrain Control
