Shrinking Horizon Model Predictive Control with Signal Temporal Logic Constraints under Stochastic Disturbances
Stochastic temporal data upscaling using the generalized k-nearest neighbor algorithm
A stochastic diffusion process for the Dirichlet distribution
A Weak Dynamic Programming Principle for Zero-Sum Stochastic Differential Games with Unbounded Controls
Stochastic inequalities for single-server loss queueing systems
Learning Minimum-Energy Controls from Heterogeneous Data
Cooperative Path Integral Control for Stochastic Multi-Agent Systems
Stochastic Optimal Control with Measurable Coefficients and Applications

nodes.name: optimal control feedback trading
nodes.description: Alpha generation through stochastic optimal control theory that identifies optimal decision-making strategies in uncertain market environments by solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, thereby improving resource allocation efficiency and expected returns relative to traditional approaches.

nodes.title: Zero-sum stochastic differential game in finite horizon involving impulse controls

nodes.name: strategic impulse control exploitation
nodes.description: Alpha generation through solving optimal impulse control strategies in a two-player zero-sum game framework, where traders identify and exploit the timing and magnitude of discrete trading actions that capitalize on strategic interactions with competing market participants.

nodes.title: Optimal order placement in limit order markets

nodes.name: order book queue position premium
nodes.description: Traders can improve execution by strategically placing limit orders in the queue ahead of other orders, capturing better prices by avoiding the adverse selection costs of market orders. The position in the limit order book queue directly affects the probability of execution and the effective price received.

nodes.name: fee structure optimization
nodes.description: Optimal order placement depends on the interplay between transaction fees and rebates across exchanges; traders can exploit fee asymmetries by routing limit orders to exchanges offering rebates and market orders to exchanges with lower fees, thereby reducing net execution costs.

nodes.name: order flow imbalance routing
nodes.description: Real-time order flow characteristics and queue sizes across multiple exchanges inform the optimal split between limit and market orders; traders can exploit temporary imbalances in order flow by routing orders to exchanges with favorable queue conditions and order flow patterns.

nodes.title: Neural Contraction Metrics for Robust Estimation and Control: A Convex Optimization Approach
A general stochastic maximum principle for mixed relaxed-singular control problems
Stabilizing Queuing Networks with Model Data-Independent Control
A Stochastic LQR Model for Child Order Placement in Algorithmic Trading

nodes.name: information leakage from aggressive orders
nodes.description: Aggressive market orders reveal trading intent to other participants, causing them to update beliefs about true market value and reduce willingness to fill passive limit orders at the near touch, thereby reducing the effective fill rate of passive orders.

nodes.name: passive-aggressive order tradeoff
nodes.description: Passive limit orders at the near touch gain a half-spread if filled but face fill uncertainty and completion risk, while aggressive market orders fill immediately but pay the half-spread and incur information leakage costs; optimal execution requires balancing these competing objectives.

nodes.name: delay cost from market drift
nodes.description: Passive limit orders that remain unfilled face a chasing cost when the market mid-price drifts away from the order placement level, penalizing delayed execution and creating urgency to complete orders.

nodes.title: Probabilistic Safety Guarantee for Stochastic Control Systems Using Average Reward MDPs
Stability Bounds for Learning-Based Adaptive Control of Discrete-Time Multi-Dimensional Stochastic Linear Systems with Input Constraints
Deep Learning for Limit Order Books

nodes.name: local spatial structure in order book depth
nodes.description: Price movements depend on local spatial patterns in the limit order book at multiple depth levels beyond the best bid-ask, not just the top-of-book. Information from deeper levels has predictive power for future price changes because order book state exhibits local spatial dependencies.

nodes.name: nonlinear order book dynamics
nodes.description: The relationship between current limit order book state and future price movements is fundamentally nonlinear, meaning simple linear models cannot capture the full conditional distribution of future bid-ask prices. Complex interactions between order sizes, price levels, and order flow create nonlinear predictive patterns.

nodes.title: Conservation Laws in a Limit Order Book

nodes.name: adverse selection avoidance through queue position migration
nodes.description: Market makers avoid posting liquidity at crowded price levels to reduce adverse selection risk. Orders migrate from full levels toward empty levels, with mobility increasing toward the back of the queue, creating pressure gradients that drive order book recovery.

nodes.name: order book recovery self-similarity
nodes.description: After aggressive liquidity taking depletes order book levels, the order book recovers through a self-similar pressure wave that propagates according to a t^(1/3) scaling law, with order density and spread width both expanding at this characteristic rate until constrained by the opposite side.

nodes.name: queue priority competition pressure buildup
nodes.description: Orders several layers behind the touch compete to improve queue position by migrating toward the touch, generating high pressure concentration near the touch level and negative pressure in the vacated deep book regions. This pressure imbalance drives touch advancement.

nodes.title: Optimal Portfolio Choice with Cross-Impact Propagators

nodes.name: transient cross-impact propagation
nodes.description: Trading in one asset creates a time-decaying price distortion in correlated assets through a Volterra propagator kernel. This transient cross-impact persists with power-law or exponential decay, affecting optimal execution timing and inventory management across the portfolio.

nodes.name: alpha decay interplay with cross-impact
nodes.description: When assets have different alpha signal decay rates, cross-impact creates a strategic arbitrage: selling the asset with fastest alpha decay induces cross-impact that depresses the price of the correlated asset with slower alpha decay, allowing the investor to profit from the more persistent signal while leveraging the impact effect.

nodes.name: transaction-triggered round-trip inventory cycling
nodes.description: In the absence of predictive signals, cross-impact induces the investor to build and unwind positions in non-target assets (round trips) as a side effect of liquidating the primary asset. This mechanism forces more aggressive trading in both assets to minimize the adverse price distortion from cross-impact.

nodes.title: Deep Limit Order Book Forecasting

nodes.name: information richness effect
nodes.description: Stocks with higher activity and event frequency at the best bid-ask levels (more information-rich stocks) exhibit greater predictability of mid-price movements because the LOB state contains more signal relative to noise. Stocks with sparse order activity at best levels are harder to forecast.

nodes.name: liquidity depth volatility
nodes.description: Variations in bid-ask spread and depth at best price levels create microstructural conditions that affect the reliability of mid-price forecasts. Stocks with stable, deep liquidity are more predictable than those with volatile spread and shallow depth.

nodes.title: Diffusion Limit of Poisson Limit-Order Book Models

nodes.name: order queue depletion and spread widening
nodes.description: When limit orders at the best bid or ask are exhausted (bracketing queues vanish), the spread widens as the system transitions to a new price level. The depletion of queued orders at interior price ticks forces the essential bid and ask to move apart, creating temporary liquidity gaps.

nodes.name: two-speed price diffusion
nodes.description: Price changes occur at different rates depending on the configuration of buy and sell order queues at different price levels. When interior queues are depleted, the price exhibits faster diffusion; when interior queues are present, price movement is constrained by the queue dynamics, creating asymmetric volatility.

nodes.name: cancellation-driven order flow imbalance
nodes.description: Orders far from the best bid-ask spread are subject to cancellation at rates proportional to 1/√n, creating a time-varying imbalance between buy and sell order flow. This imbalance drives the directional bias of price changes and the probability of upward versus downward price movements.

nodes.title: A diffusion approximation for limit order book models

nodes.name: order arrival and cancellation imbalance
nodes.description: Price dynamics emerge from the imbalance between order placements and cancellations at different price levels. When cancellations and placements are asymmetric across the order book, they create directional pressure on the best bid price through the state-dependent conditional distribution of order events.

nodes.name: price impact from volume density distribution
nodes.description: The drift and volatility of the best bid price depend on the spatial distribution of standing volumes across price levels. The conditional probability of price moves (up vs. down) is determined by the cumulated volume density function, creating feedback between order book shape and price dynamics.

nodes.name: state-dependent order intensity
nodes.description: The rate at which orders arrive and are cancelled depends on the current state of the order book (best bid price and volume distribution). This creates endogenous clustering of order flow, where the probability of price-changing events scales with the volatility function of standing volumes.

nodes.title: Scaling limit of a limit order book model via the regenerative characterization of Lévy trees

nodes.name: order book depth mean reversion
nodes.description: The limit order book depth follows a mean-reverting process (reflected Brownian motion) where orders are continuously added and removed at constant rates. This mean reversion in depth creates predictable liquidity conditions that traders can exploit for order placement optimization.

nodes.name: order flow dynamics anticipation
nodes.description: By modeling the point process of order arrivals and cancellations as a Markovian dynamic, traders can anticipate price movements based on statistical properties of order flow. Understanding the regenerative structure of order flow enables prediction of future liquidity and optimal timing of trades.

nodes.title: Algorithmic trading in a microstructural limit order book model

nodes.name: queue position execution risk
nodes.description: Market maker's limit orders have execution probability that depends on their position in the FIFO queue at each price level. Orders deeper in the queue face lower execution risk, affecting the optimal placement strategy and bid-ask spread setting.

nodes.name: inventory risk management
nodes.description: Market maker must balance the profit from bid-ask spread capture against the risk of holding inventory. Inventory accumulation is penalized in the objective function, forcing the market maker to adjust order placement and cancellation to control position size.

nodes.name: order flow intensity response
nodes.description: The arrival intensities of market orders, limit orders, and cancellations depend on the current state of the order book (depth at each level). Market makers exploit this state-dependence by adjusting their quotes and positions in response to changing order book conditions.

nodes.title: Limit order books, diffusion approximations and reflected SPDEs: from microscopic to macroscopic models

nodes.name: order repositioning smoothing
nodes.description: Traders frequently cancel and quickly resubmit limit orders at adjacent price levels (a random walk of orders across the book). This repositioning behavior smooths the order book profile and moderates the impact of individual order arrivals on price dynamics.

nodes.name: residual order-cancellation imbalance
nodes.description: At each price level, a residual imbalance between the rate of limit order arrivals and the rate of cancellations/market order executions creates lower-frequency directional pressure on the order book depth, independent of the high-frequency matching dynamics.

nodes.title: Optimal incentives in a limit order book: a SPDE control approach

nodes.name: incentive-driven order submission response
nodes.description: Liquidity providers increase their order submission rates at specific price levels in response to exchange-offered incentives (rebates), with the effect being stronger closer to the mid-price where execution probability is higher.

nodes.name: order book depth concentration
nodes.description: Exchange incentive structures that penalize costs less at the first limits than at deeper levels cause liquidity to concentrate disproportionately near the mid-price, creating a non-uniform order book shape.

nodes.name: make-take fee liquidity provision effect
nodes.description: Asymmetric fee structures (rebates for limit orders, charges for market orders) alter the relative attractiveness of liquidity provision versus consumption, shifting the composition and depth of the order book.

nodes.title: Order Flows and Limit Order Book Resiliency on the Meso-Scale

nodes.name: limit order book resilience via liquidity provision
nodes.description: When market orders arrive on one side of the book, the price impact depends on whether limit order providers replenish the depleted queue or withdraw liquidity through cancellations. Strong resilience (new limit orders added) dampens price moves, while weak resilience (net cancellations) amplifies them.

nodes.name: scarce liquidity effect
nodes.description: When limit order supply becomes depleted (net cancellations exceed new submissions), the book exhibits reduced depth and higher execution costs. This scarcity amplifies the price impact of subsequent market orders and increases the slippage faced by traders executing large orders.

nodes.name: asymmetric bid-ask queue dynamics
nodes.description: The relationship between trade imbalance and one-sided limit order flows exhibits a hockey-stick (threshold) nonlinearity, with different sensitivities on the active versus passive sides of the book. Aggressive orders on one side trigger asymmetric responses in limit order submissions and cancellations on that same side.

nodes.title: Cointegration in high frequency data

nodes.name: non-ergodic volatility distortion of cointegration tests
nodes.description: Time-varying variance that is non-ergodic (e.g., regime shifts or jumps in long-term equilibrium variance) causes spurious cointegration signals and distorts the size of standard residual-based cointegration tests, because the tests assume ergodic variance.

nodes.name: price jump impact on cointegration test power
nodes.description: Random-sized, random-timed price jumps (frequent at high frequency, ~10+ per year) deteriorate the statistical power of standard Dickey-Fuller and Phillips-Perron cointegration tests by introducing non-standard behavior in residual-based unit root tests.

nodes.title: Long memory, fractional integration and cointegration analysis of real convergence in Spain
Fractional Cointegration of Geometric Functionals
No-arbitrage conditions and absolutely continuous changes of measure
Asymptotic proportion of arbitrage points in fractional binary markets
Statistical Inference for the Population Landscape via Moment Adjusted Stochastic Gradients
Statistical Arbitrage in Rank Space

nodes.name: enhanced mean-reversion in rank space
nodes.description: Residual returns exhibit stronger mean-reverting properties when stocks are indexed by market-cap rank rather than by company name, because rank space provides a more stable market structure driven by a single dominant factor rather than multiple factors. This enhanced mean-reversion creates more exploitable statistical arbitrage opportunities.

nodes.name: market-neutral portfolio construction
nodes.description: By decomposing returns into factor-driven and residual components via PCA, the strategy constructs portfolios that isolate residual returns while eliminating exposure to systematic market factors. These market-neutral portfolios profit from mean-reverting mispricings without bearing systematic risk.

nodes.name: rank-switching driven rebalancing necessity
nodes.description: Rank positions of stocks change frequently at intraday frequencies, causing divergence between rank-space returns (which track the stock at a given rank position) and name-space returns (which track a specific company). Intraday rebalancing is required to capture the rank-space mean-reversion advantage rather than defaulting to name-space dynamics.

nodes.title: Critical transaction costs and 1-step asymptotic arbitrage in fractional binary markets

nodes.name: path-dependent mean reversion under friction
nodes.description: In fractional binary markets, when price takes repeated steps in one direction (down or up) for a proportional number of times, the process exhibits predictable mean reversion at subsequent steps. Traders can exploit this by taking opposite positions, but transaction costs erode profits; critical transaction costs must exceed a threshold to eliminate this arbitrage.

nodes.name: transaction cost threshold for arbitrage elimination
nodes.description: Arbitrage opportunities in fractional binary markets persist when transaction costs are below a critical level λ_c that depends on market structure. The critical transaction cost converges to 1 (not 0) as the market becomes finer, meaning proportionally larger frictions are needed to eliminate arbitrage in the limit, despite the frictionless fractional Black-Scholes being arbitrage-free under arbitrarily small costs.

nodes.title: Online Learning Algorithms for Statistical Arbitrage

nodes.name: mean reversion in correlated pairs
nodes.description: When two historically correlated stocks diverge in price, they are expected to converge back toward their historical relationship. This exploits the assumption that temporary deviations from correlation are temporary mispricings that will correct.

nodes.name: z-score mean reversion
nodes.description: Stocks trading at extreme deviations from their mean (measured in standard deviations) are expected to revert toward the mean. Extreme positive z-scores signal overshooting and suggest selling; extreme negative z-scores suggest buying.

nodes.title: Strong asymptotic arbitrage in the large fractional binary market

nodes.name: fractional memory in price increments
nodes.description: The fractional Brownian motion (Hurst parameter H > 1/2) driving asset prices exhibits long-range dependence, creating predictable patterns in price changes that allow profitable trading strategies to exploit the non-martingale structure of returns.

nodes.name: dependent random variable accumulation in portfolio value
nodes.description: The portfolio value process decomposes into sums of dependent random variables (particularly through the Yk−1Yk term) rather than independent increments. This dependence structure, characterized via mixingale theory, allows the law of large numbers to generate strictly positive expected profits that grow with the number of trading periods.

nodes.name: transaction cost convergence rate arbitrage
nodes.description: When transaction costs decay at a sufficiently fast rate (o(√log N / N^(2H−1/2)∧(H+1/2))), the cumulative drag from trading costs vanishes faster than the profits from exploiting fractional memory, enabling strong asymptotic arbitrage despite frictions.

nodes.title: Low Volatility Stock Portfolio Through High Dimensional Bayesian Cointegration

nodes.name: volatility clustering reduction
nodes.description: By constructing portfolios from cointegrated stocks with sparse relationships, idiosyncratic volatility is diversified away more effectively, reducing portfolio volatility and improving risk-adjusted returns especially during market stress periods.

nodes.title: Statistical Arbitrage Risk Premium by Machine Learning

nodes.name: idiosyncratic factor exposure premium
nodes.description: Stocks with low co-movement with peers (high idiosyncratic/residual factor risk) command higher expected returns because they cannot be easily hedged using other stocks' returns. The factor risks unique to these stocks are priced.

nodes.name: peer replication hedging effectiveness
nodes.description: Stocks whose returns can be well-replicated by a portfolio of peer stocks (high R-squared) have lower expected returns because their factor risks are easily hedgeable. Stocks with poor peer replication (low R-squared, high SAR) have higher SARP because their factor exposures cannot be efficiently hedged away.

nodes.title: Arbitrage free cointegrated models in gas and oil future markets

nodes.name: long-term cointegration mean reversion
nodes.description: Gas and oil forward prices are linked by a long-term equilibrium relationship through structural indexation (gas contracts indexed to oil prices). Deviations from this equilibrium are mean-reverting, captured by the cointegrating vector in the VECM, causing prices to revert to their common long-term tendency.

nodes.name: market price of risk adjustment
nodes.description: The market price of risk (λt) is specified to encode the long-term cointegration relationship between gas and oil, bridging the gap between historical (physical) probability dynamics and risk-neutral pricing. This adjustment ensures forward prices remain arbitrage-free while respecting the empirical cointegration observed in the data.

nodes.name: volatility term structure factor decomposition
nodes.description: Forward price returns are driven by three orthogonal volatility factors (level, slope, curvature) with different characteristic decay times. Short-term shocks to gas dissipate faster (0.736 years) than to oil (3.761 years), creating predictable mean reversion patterns at different maturities.

nodes.title: Asymptotics of Cointegration Tests for High-Dimensional VAR($k$)
Statistical Arbitrage in the Black-Scholes Framework

nodes.name: risk-free rate mispricing relative to stock drift
nodes.description: Stock prices drift above or below the risk-free borrowing rate, creating a statistical arbitrage opportunity when the stock's expected return violates the no-arbitrage Sharpe ratio constraint. A trader can exploit this by borrowing at the risk-free rate and taking a long position until the stock reaches a barrier level where the mispricing is corrected.

nodes.title: Rough volatility: evidence from range volatility estimators

nodes.name: microstructure noise masking
nodes.description: High-frequency return data can obscure the true rough volatility structure through microstructure noise. Range-based volatility estimators filter out this noise, revealing the underlying fractional volatility dynamics that traditional realized volatility measurements may mischaracterize.

nodes.title: Volatility is rough

nodes.name: order splitting microstructure roughness
nodes.description: High-frequency traders and market participants split large orders over time to minimize market impact, creating a fractal pattern of order flow that induces rough (non-smooth) volatility dynamics at all time scales rather than smooth mean-reverting volatility.

nodes.name: volatility roughness persistence
nodes.description: Log-volatility follows fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent H≈0.1 (H<0.5), making volatility rough and non-smooth across time scales, which classical statistical tests mistakenly identify as long-memory persistence even though true long-memory is absent.

nodes.title: Efficient Integrated Volatility Estimation in the Presence of Infinite Variation Jumps via Debiased Truncated Realized Variations
Detecting Rough Volatility: A Filtering Approach

nodes.name: rough volatility state dynamics
nodes.description: Volatility follows a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent H < 0.5, exhibiting rough (non-smooth) behavior rather than the standard semimartingale assumption. This roughness in the hidden state process drives the observed intensity of price jumps and affects volatility estimation from high-frequency data.

nodes.name: intensity-driven jump clustering
nodes.description: Asset prices change only at random discrete times modeled as jump times of a doubly-stochastic Poisson process, where the intensity λ(X_t) = b·exp(X_t) is driven by an unobservable hidden state process. This creates time-varying clustering of trades and price movements correlated with the latent volatility signal.

nodes.title: Subleading correction to the Asian options volatility in the Black-Scholes model
A GMM approach to estimate the roughness of stochastic volatility

nodes.name: measurement error in realized volatility
nodes.description: High-frequency sampling introduces noise into realized volatility estimates that biases the estimated Hurst exponent toward spuriously high roughness (illusive roughness), masking the true underlying volatility process roughness.

nodes.name: fractional volatility roughness
nodes.description: Stochastic volatility is driven by fractional Brownian motion with a low Hurst exponent (around 0.05), indicating rough, non-smooth volatility paths that exhibit long-memory dependence and mean-reverting behavior.

nodes.title: Rough volatility: evidence from option prices

nodes.name: implied volatility smoothing bias
nodes.description: Option-implied volatility estimates of spot volatility appear less rough (higher Hurst parameter ~0.3) than realized volatility estimates due to time-decay smoothing effects in short-maturity options, creating a measurement artifact that masks the true roughness of underlying spot volatility.

nodes.title: Multiscaling and rough volatility: an empirical investigation

nodes.name: volatility roughness constraint on price multiscaling
nodes.description: Low Hurst exponents in volatility dynamics (rough volatility) mechanically induce multiscaling in price time series. The rough Bergomi model generates price multiscaling only when volatility roughness (H < 0.3) is imposed, suggesting volatility's fractal structure propagates to price increments across multiple moments.

nodes.name: negative interplay between volatility roughness and price multiscaling
nodes.description: Real market data exhibit the opposite dependency structure from rough volatility models: as volatility becomes rougher (lower H), price multiscaling actually decreases rather than increases. This mismatch indicates rough volatility models misspecify how volatility dynamics couple with price scaling properties.

nodes.title: The Fourier Transform Method for Volatility Functional Inference by Asynchronous Observations
Multifractality in Bitcoin Realised Volatility: Implications for Rough Volatility Modelling

nodes.name: multifractal scaling heterogeneity
nodes.description: Bitcoin volatility exhibits scale-dependent local Hölder exponents that vary across time and moment orders, violating the homogeneous scaling assumption required for monofractal roughness estimation. This heterogeneity precludes the existence of a single global roughness index.

nodes.name: failure of rough volatility model applicability
nodes.description: The normalized p-variation estimator systematically fails to produce a zero-crossing in log W(L,K,p) for Bitcoin realized volatility, indicating structural incompatibility between Bitcoin's volatility dynamics and the rough volatility paradigm that succeeds in equity and FX markets.

nodes.name: cryptocurrency market microstructure fragmentation
nodes.description: Bitcoin's fragmented liquidity across exchanges, frequent discontinuities from jumps, and regime-switching volatility create structural features that disrupt the global scaling regularity assumed by rough volatility models, making roughness estimation theoretically ill-posed.

nodes.title: Are low frequency macroeconomic variables important for high frequency electricity prices?

nodes.name: macroeconomic demand signal incorporation
nodes.description: Industrial production and PMI surveys contain forward-looking information about aggregate demand that causally influences electricity prices through expected consumption patterns. Electricity prices respond to these low-frequency macroeconomic signals because they predict future demand for power.

nodes.name: survey-based soft information premium
nodes.description: Purchasing Managers' Index surveys provide qualitative forward-looking sentiment about economic activity that improves electricity price forecasts beyond hard industrial production data alone, suggesting markets incorporate soft information with a lag or incompletely.

nodes.name: frequency mismatch underreaction
nodes.description: Daily electricity prices underreact to monthly macroeconomic releases in the short term because the mismatch in observation frequency creates a lag in information incorporation; this effect is stronger at short horizons than medium horizons.

nodes.title: Macroeconomic Effects of Inflation Targeting: A Survey of the Empirical Literature
Classification of Imbalanced Credit scoring data sets Based on Ensemble Method with the Weighted-Hybrid-Sampling
On the macroeconomic fundamentals of long-term volatilities and dynamic correlations in COMEX copper futures

nodes.name: macroeconomic fundamentals volatility transmission
nodes.description: Low-frequency macroeconomic variables (interest rates, industrial production, PPI, dollar index, consumer sentiment) drive high-frequency copper futures volatility through changes in real economic conditions and inflation expectations.

nodes.name: realized volatility feedback
nodes.description: Recent realized volatility in crude oil futures predicts future volatility through persistence in market microstructure frictions and inventory costs. High past volatility signals elevated uncertainty that persists at medium frequencies.

nodes.name: inflation expectations pricing
nodes.description: Producer price index (PPI) and its volatility are the most efficient macroeconomic channels through which inflation expectations affect copper futures returns and their correlation with equities, reflecting commodity sensitivity to real purchasing power.

nodes.title: Discovering State Variables Hidden in Experimental Data
Macroeconomic forecasting with LSTM and mixed frequency time series data
Mixed Data Clustering Survey and Challenges
Stock Volatility Prediction Based on Transformer Model Using Mixed-Frequency Data

nodes.name: macroeconomic sentiment effect on volatility
nodes.description: Macroeconomic indicators and aggregate economic conditions causally influence stock volatility through changes in investor expectations and risk premia. The paper treats these as objective factors that systematically predict volatility movements.

nodes.name: retail attention-driven volatility
nodes.description: Retail investor attention, as measured by search engine query volume (Baidu search indices), causally affects stock volatility by influencing trading behavior and sentiment. Spikes in public interest in topics correlate with increased volatility.

nodes.title: Lower Bounds of Uncertainty of Observations of Macroeconomic Variables and Upper Limits on the Accuracy of Their Forecasts

nodes.name: trade volume uncertainty propagation
nodes.description: Macroeconomic variable observations have irreducible uncertainty that stems from the random values and volumes of underlying market trades. This fundamental uncertainty in trade volumes creates a lower bound on how accurately any macroeconomic variable can be observed or forecasted.

nodes.name: trade value uncertainty propagation
nodes.description: The random values of market trades introduce fundamental uncertainty into macroeconomic observations. Since macroeconomic variables depend on aggregated trade values, uncertainty in individual trade prices creates an irreducible lower bound on macroeconomic measurement accuracy.

nodes.name: statistical moment limitation on forecast accuracy
nodes.description: Forecast accuracy for macroeconomic variables, prices, and returns is fundamentally limited by the number of statistical moments that can be reliably predicted. Economic constraints restrict practical forecasting to the first two moments (mean and variance), creating an upper limit on achievable forecast precision that cannot be exceeded even with perfect models.

nodes.title: Mid-Long Term Daily Electricity Consumption Forecasting Based on Piecewise Linear Regression and Dilated Causal CNN
Hybrid Density- and Partition-based Clustering Algorithm for Data with Mixed-type Variables
PretopoMD: Pretopology-based Mixed Data Hierarchical Clustering
Predictive regressions for macroeconomic data

nodes.name: dividend-price ratio predictability
nodes.description: Stock returns are predictable from the log dividend-price ratio, which captures the relative cheapness of equities and their expected future payouts. When the dividend-price ratio is high, subsequent returns tend to be higher as the market reprices undervalued dividend streams.

nodes.name: earnings-price ratio predictability
nodes.description: Stock returns are predictable from the log earnings-price ratio, which reflects the earnings yield available to investors. Higher earnings-price ratios signal undervaluation and predict stronger subsequent returns as the market corrects the mispricing.

nodes.title: The Knowledge Graph for Macroeconomic Analysis with Alternative Big Data
Relationships between different Macroeconomic Variables using VECM
The role of global economic policy uncertainty in predicting crude oil futures volatility: Evidence from a two-factor GARCH-MIDAS model

nodes.name: policy uncertainty volatility spillover
nodes.description: Changes in global economic policy uncertainty transmit to crude oil futures volatility through shifts in market expectations and risk premia. Uncertainty shocks cause traders to widen bid-ask spreads and reduce position sizes, increasing realized volatility.

nodes.name: policy uncertainty level vs. change asymmetry
nodes.description: The level of policy uncertainty has weaker predictive power for oil volatility than changes in uncertainty. Absolute uncertainty levels are priced in steadily, but surprise shifts in uncertainty regimes trigger volatility spikes as agents reprrice risk exposures.

nodes.title: Econophysics Macroeconomic Model

nodes.name: macroeconomic wave propagation with amplitude growth
nodes.description: Perturbations in macroeconomic variables (demand, investment, interest rates) propagate as waves across economic space with exponentially growing amplitude, causing irregular time fluctuations and potential economic crises.

nodes.name: agent transaction-driven variable evolution
nodes.description: Financial and economic transactions between agents at similar risk-rating coordinates drive the evolution of macroeconomic aggregates (investment, assets, demand, credits), creating local interactions that propagate through the economic system.

nodes.title: A Random Matrix Approach to Dynamic Factors in macroeconomic data
Econophysics of Macroeconomics: "Action-at-a-Distance" and Waves

nodes.name: non-local transaction propagation
nodes.description: Buy-sell transactions between economic agents at different risk-rating coordinates propagate shocks across the economic space non-locally, causing assets at one location to respond to investment decisions at distant locations without direct spatial proximity.

nodes.name: economic field wave dynamics
nodes.description: Aggregated transactions between economic agents create macroeconomic field waves that propagate across economic space (ordered by risk ratings). These waves can exhibit exponential amplitude growth, destabilizing equilibrium and creating predictable wave-like patterns in macroeconomic variables.

nodes.title: Nowcasting in a Pandemic using Non-Parametric Mixed Frequency VARs
Macroeconomic Forecasting and Machine Learning
Macroeconomic factors and Stock exchange return: A Statistical Analysis

nodes.name: exchange rate pass-through to equity valuations
nodes.description: Currency depreciation increases the domestic currency value of foreign earnings and reduces competitiveness, creating volatility in stock returns. Exchange rate fluctuations have a significant positive association with DSE returns in the long run.

nodes.name: monetary expansion demand effect
nodes.description: Increases in money supply raise aggregate demand for equities and boost stock market returns. Money supply growth has a strong positive long-term cointegrating relationship with stock exchange returns.

nodes.name: inflation erosion of real returns
nodes.description: Rising inflation reduces purchasing power and real returns on equity investments, creating negative pressure on stock valuations. Consumer price index inflation has a significant negative association with stock exchange returns.

nodes.title: How is Machine Learning Useful for Macroeconomic Forecasting?

nodes.name: nonlinear regime shifts under macroeconomic uncertainty
nodes.description: Macroeconomic relationships exhibit nonlinearities that become pronounced during periods of high uncertainty, financial stress, and structural breaks (like housing bubbles). Linear models fail to capture these regime-dependent dynamics, while nonlinear ML methods exploit them for superior forecasts.

nodes.name: financial friction amplification
nodes.description: During financial stress periods, the transmission mechanisms between macroeconomic variables become nonlinear due to credit constraints, risk premia adjustments, and deleveraging dynamics. ML methods capture these friction-induced nonlinearities that standard linear macroeconometric models miss.

nodes.title: Macroeconomic Predictions using Payments Data and Machine Learning

nodes.name: payments data nonlinearity during crises
nodes.description: Real-time payments data (retail and wholesale) exhibits nonlinear predictive power for macroeconomic indicators during crisis periods and extreme growth regimes, whereas the relationship is small and linear during normal times. This suggests that payment flow patterns contain regime-dependent information about economic stress that linear models miss.

nodes.name: asymmetric growth regime sensitivity
nodes.description: The contribution of payments data to macroeconomic predictions is asymmetrical across growth regimes: large and nonlinear during strong negative or positive growth periods, but small and linear during low and normal growth periods. This indicates that economic agents' payment behavior changes structurally depending on whether the economy is in expansion, contraction, or crisis.

nodes.title: Macroeconomic Data Transformations Matter

nodes.name: regularization sensitivity to data transformation
nodes.description: Machine learning forecasting algorithms embed implicit or explicit regularization that responds to how predictors are transformed or combined. Different data transformations alter the effective regularization penalty, changing which features are selected and how strongly they are weighted, thereby improving forecast accuracy.

nodes.name: moving average rotation informativeness
nodes.description: Lagged moving averages and rotations of macroeconomic data contain information that linear models cannot exploit but nonlinear or regularized models can. These transformations interact with shrinkage mechanisms to improve forecasts of various macroeconomic targets.

nodes.name: multi-horizon forecast aggregation advantage
nodes.description: When using regularized or nonlinear forecasting methods, averaging separate single-horizon forecasts substantially outperforms directly predicting the multi-period average growth rate, because the regularization applied at each horizon compounds differently than when applied to a single direct forecast.

nodes.title: Copula-Based Trading of Cointegrated Cryptocurrency Pairs

nodes.name: copula-based mispricing detection
nodes.description: Non-linear dependence structures between cointegrated pairs, captured via copula families, reveal mispricing that linear correlation measures miss; the copula-derived mispricing index signals when pairs are sufficiently dislocated to trade profitably.

nodes.title: Evaluation of Dynamic Cointegration-Based Pairs Trading Strategy in the Cryptocurrency Market

nodes.name: mean reversion in cointegrated pairs
nodes.description: Two assets that move together in the long run (cointegrated) will experience temporary deviations from their equilibrium relationship. When the spread widens, it reverts to the mean, creating a profitable trading signal to short the outperformer and long the underperformer.

nodes.name: optimal look-back window selection
nodes.description: The half-life of mean reversion (calibrated via Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) varies over time. Dynamically adjusting the look-back window for cointegration estimation to match current mean-reversion speed improves signal quality and reduces false positives compared to fixed windows.

nodes.name: market microstructure execution friction
nodes.description: Bid-ask spreads and order execution delays create real costs that erode theoretical profits. Accounting for realistic execution constraints (only trading when size is available at quoted prices) reduces slippage and improves net returns versus naive backtests.

nodes.title: Stochastic Spread Pairs Trading in the Indian Commodity Market
Designing Efficient Pair-Trading Strategies Using Cointegration for the Indian Stock Market

nodes.name: mean reversion in cointegrated price ratios
nodes.description: Pairs of stocks that exhibit long-term cointegration tend to have their price ratios revert to historical means in the short term. When the ratio diverges beyond standard deviation thresholds, the spread is expected to compress back to equilibrium, enabling profitable long/short positioning.

nodes.name: spread-based trading signal generation
nodes.description: Standardized Z-scores of price ratios between cointegrated pairs trigger entry and exit signals. When Z-scores exceed ±1 (upper/lower limits), the overvalued asset is shorted and the undervalued asset is longed, exploiting temporary divergences from equilibrium.

nodes.title: Hong Kong -- Shanghai Connect / Hong Kong -- Beijing Disconnect (?): Scaling the Great Wall of Chinese Securities Trading Costs

nodes.name: cross-listing arbitrage demand pressure
nodes.description: Opening of Hong Kong-Shanghai Connect creates sudden demand surge to gain exposure to Chinese securities through Hong Kong listings, temporarily elevating trading costs in Shanghai as the market absorbs this new flow.

nodes.name: market microstructure adjustment to linkage
nodes.description: When two previously segmented markets become connected, trading costs may increase temporarily as market makers and liquidity providers adjust inventory management and pricing strategies to the new coupled equilibrium.

nodes.title: Modeling of Volatility with Non-linear Time Series Model

nodes.name: asymmetric volatility response to shocks
nodes.description: Negative price shocks trigger larger increases in volatility than positive shocks of equal magnitude, a phenomenon captured by EGARCH models through their leverage effect term. This asymmetry reflects market participants' differential risk perception and hedging behavior in response to downside versus upside moves.

nodes.name: regime-dependent volatility clustering
nodes.description: Financial time series exhibit distinct regimes (e.g., pre- and post-crisis) with different volatility dynamics and persistence; volatility clusters within regimes but the clustering behavior changes discontinuously at threshold crossings.

nodes.title: Bitcoin Forecasting with Classical Time Series Models on Prices and Volatility

nodes.name: mean-reverting price dynamics
nodes.description: Bitcoin log-prices exhibit short-run mean reversion, where deviations from trend tend to reverse within days or weeks, allowing ARIMA models to generate predictive power despite the asset's high volatility. This suggests temporary supply-demand imbalances or liquidity constraints that are gradually corrected.

nodes.description: Market shocks arrive as a Poisson process, causing volatility to spike and then decay according to a power law with exponent D. This generates volatility clustering and multi-scaling of moments, which in turn produces a pronounced implied volatility smile even without price jumps.

nodes.name: heavy-tailed return distribution emergence
nodes.description: The superlinear mean reversion of volatility (γ > 2) combined with Poisson shock arrivals creates heavy tails in the small-time return distribution. These heavy tails are responsible for the divergence of out-of-the-money implied volatility at short maturities, producing a steep volatility smile.

nodes.name: time-scale dependent tail risk pricing
nodes.description: The implied volatility surface exhibits different regimes depending on the ratio of log-strike to maturity (κ/t). At very short maturities, tail risk is priced differently across strike levels because the probability of extreme moves transitions from Brownian (polynomial decay) to shock-driven (power-law decay), creating a non-monotonic smile structure.

nodes.name: leverage effect via score-driven volatility feedback
nodes.description: Volatility responds asymmetrically to positive versus negative returns through score-driven dynamics, creating correlation between price innovations and volatility innovations. This endogenous feedback mechanism captures the empirical leverage effect where volatility rises more sharply following negative returns.

nodes.name: asymmetric innovation distribution in volatility estimation
nodes.description: When the distribution of driving innovations differs from the distribution used to compute the score function, and at least one exhibits asymmetry, the model generates non-degenerate correlation between price and volatility shocks. This distributional mismatch is necessary for capturing realistic volatility-return dependence.

Multiple time scales in volatility and leverage correlations: An stochastic volatility model

nodes.name: long-memory volatility clustering
nodes.description: Volatility exhibits multi-year autocorrelations due to a stochastic mean-reverting level that itself reverts slowly, creating persistent clustering of high and low volatility regimes across extended periods.

nodes.title: Dynamic Linear Coregionalization for Realistic Synthetic Multivariate Time Series

nodes.name: correlation drift
nodes.description: Inter-channel correlations evolve smoothly over time via autoregressive processes rather than remaining static. Models pretrained on static correlations develop rigid relational priors that fail to adapt to real-world nonstationary dependency structures.

nodes.name: regime-switching correlations
nodes.description: Cross-channel relationships shift discretely between K latent regimes with distinct correlation structures, governed by a Hidden Markov Model. This captures structural breaks and regime-dependent relationships common in financial and environmental data.

nodes.name: lagged cross-channel dependencies
nodes.description: Observed channels depend on lagged values of latent factors with variable delays (lead-lag effects), not just instantaneous correlations. This captures temporal offsets between related signals that static correlation models cannot represent.

nodes.description: Order arrivals exhibit self-exciting behavior where past order flow increases the intensity of future orders, captured through multivariate Hawkes processes. This clustering in order flow dynamics affects the conditional distribution of price changes and volatility.

nodes.name: order flow volatility coupling
nodes.description: The intensity and clustering of order flow in the limit order book directly drives realized volatility. Higher order flow clustering (measured via Hawkes intensity) leads to higher conditional volatility, establishing a causal link between LOB microstructure and price volatility.

nodes.description: Price jumps in multiple assets are self-reinforcing through mutual excitation: a jump in one asset increases the probability of simultaneous jumps in correlated assets, creating clusters of coordinated price movements across the market.

nodes.name: volatility clustering via self-exciting feedback
nodes.description: Past price jumps increase the intensity of future jumps through endogenous feedback mechanisms, generating power-law distributed volatility clusters rather than constant volatility, as captured by the quadratic kernel structure.

nodes.description: Price jumps in financial assets exhibit temporal clustering due to self-exciting dynamics, where the occurrence of one jump increases the probability of subsequent jumps in the near term. This clustering is driven by common systemic shocks that propagate through the market.

nodes.name: cross-asset jump synchronization
nodes.description: Multiple assets experience synchronized price jumps during systemic events, indicating that jumps are not idiosyncratic but driven by common factors affecting the entire market. This high-frequency cojump phenomenon reflects the transmission of shocks across correlated assets.

nodes.name: self-excitation and cross-excitation clustering
nodes.description: Events in one asset or market component trigger cascading events in the same and other components through self- and cross-exciting dynamics, creating observable clustering patterns in event arrival times. The branching ratio (integral of kernel functions) quantifies the average number of events directly triggered by a single event.

nodes.name: causal network structure shift
nodes.description: The underlying causal influence structure between market components (captured by the kernel matrix and its integral, the branching ratio matrix) changes over time in response to market shocks or regime changes. Detecting shifts in this causal network topology reveals when the endogenous propagation mechanisms between assets fundamentally alter.

nodes.name: volatility contagion through event intensity
nodes.description: Market shocks propagate across cryptocurrency assets by increasing the intensity (frequency and magnitude) of price-movement events in connected assets, as measured by changes in the background rate and excitation parameters of the multivariate Hawkes process.

nodes.name: trade sign cross-correlation memory decay

nodes.name: fat-tailed return distribution effect on network topology

nodes.name: nonlinear long-term correlation effect on network topology
nodes.description: Persistent nonlinear dependencies in returns over long horizons alter the visibility graph structure, causing deviations from random walk behavior. These correlations create non-universal scaling patterns that differ across spanning tree types.

nodes.name: coupling between fat-tailedness and correlation
nodes.description: The joint interaction between fat-tailed returns and nonlinear long-term correlations produces nonuniversal allometric scaling behaviors in maximal and random spanning trees, whereas minimal spanning trees exhibit universal scaling independent of these factors.

nodes.name: short-term momentum underreaction
nodes.description: Stock prices underreact to recent price trends in the short run, causing past winners to continue outperforming and past losers to continue underperforming. This creates exploitable momentum in time series returns over short look-back and holding periods.

nodes.name: long-term mean reversion overreaction
nodes.description: Stock prices overreact to sustained trends over longer horizons, causing extended price movements to reverse as the market corrects its excessive extrapolation of past performance. This creates contrarian profits over longer look-back and holding periods.

nodes.name: market development scaling heterogeneity

nodes.description: Investors underreact to the semantic content and sentiment expressed by CEOs in earnings calls, creating a predictable lag between the qualitative signal in the call and full market price discovery. The market gradually incorporates the nuanced language cues that professional analysts miss.

nodes.name: analyst recommendation disconnect
nodes.description: Professional analysts' pre-earnings buy/sell/hold recommendations have low predictive power for post-earnings stock movements, suggesting that traditional analyst forecasts fail to capture information that is embedded in the qualitative narrative of earnings calls.

nodes.name: soft data informativeness premium
nodes.description: Semantic features of earnings call transcripts contain more predictive information about future stock returns than traditional hard quantitative metrics (sales, EPS), implying markets systematically underweight qualitative narrative relative to its true information content.

nodes.title: Structured Event Representation and Stock Return Predictability

nodes.name: news sentiment underreaction
nodes.description: Market participants underreact to the nuanced sentiment and event features embedded in news articles, allowing LLM-extracted event representations to predict subsequent stock returns as the market gradually incorporates the full information content of news.

nodes.name: structured event feature extraction
nodes.description: Large language models extract rich, structured event features from news text that capture multidimensional aspects of corporate events (e.g., sentiment, entity relationships, event type) more accurately than traditional bag-of-words approaches, enabling better prediction of market reactions.

nodes.title: A Quantum Approach to Stock Price Fluctuations

nodes.name: stable distribution mean reversion
nodes.description: Over short time intervals (minutes to days), stock returns follow a shape-stable Lévy distribution with power-law tails rather than Gaussian. This stability allows predictable mean reversion patterns that can be exploited for alpha generation without model parameter fitting.

nodes.name: market sentiment wave number signal
nodes.description: The Fourier wave number conjugate to returns serves as a quantitative measure of market sentiment. Extreme wave numbers (large |q|) indicate tail events and sentiment extremes that predict short-term price reversals and trading opportunities.

nodes.name: power law tail exploitation
nodes.description: The decay rate γ(q) ∝ |q| for large wave numbers captures fat tails in return distributions. These power-law tails persist over short horizons and can be systematically exploited to identify extreme price movements before mean reversion occurs.

nodes.title: Maximum Entropy Production Principle for Stock Returns

nodes.name: entropy-driven predictability exploitation
nodes.description: Stock returns exhibit measurable structural complexity (Shannon entropy rate) that contains exploitable predictability overlooked by standard algorithms. By identifying periods of low entropy (high structure/predictability) via the Maximum Entropy Production Principle, traders can generate alpha from inherent non-random patterns in price formation.

nodes.name: algorithmic inefficiency in complexity utilization
nodes.description: Standard trading algorithms fail to extract profit from the structural complexity present in stock return time series, despite this complexity being measurable and correlated with trading profitability. This creates an opportunity gap where entropy-aware strategies can outperform conventional approaches.

nodes.title: Portfolio Volatility Estimation Relative to Stock Market Cross-Sectional Intrinsic Entropy

nodes.name: cross-sectional entropy risk decomposition
nodes.description: Portfolio volatility can be estimated by decomposing cross-sectional dispersion (entropy) of stock returns rather than relying solely on time-series volatility. This allows identification of stocks with low correlation to overall market volatility, enabling alpha generation through better risk-adjusted selection.

nodes.name: low-correlation stock selection
nodes.description: Stocks that exhibit lower correlation with market-wide volatility can outperform market indices while maintaining equal or lower portfolio risk. This mechanism exploits the fact that cross-sectional entropy reveals stocks decoupled from systematic volatility movements.

nodes.title: Cross-sectional topological anomaly scores and intraday return predictability in the S&P 500: A BallMapper, decoder-conditional VAE, and Function-on-Function regression approach

nodes.name: topological latent structure anomaly
nodes.description: Stocks exhibit statistically unusual patterns in the latent topological structure of their intraday return curves (detected via delay embedding and graph topology) that deviate from their market-level peer context. These deviations are predictive because they represent persistent misalignments in co-movement structure that gradually resolve.

nodes.name: market regime-dependent reversal timing
nodes.description: The timing of when topological anomalies reverse direction is conditional on the current market regime. Different regimes exhibit different speeds of mean reversion, causing the same anomaly score to have regime-dependent predictive content for intraday returns.

nodes.name: gradual return impact accumulation
nodes.description: Topological anomalies accumulate their predictive impact on returns gradually over time rather than being immediately priced in. Recent anomaly history carries disproportionate weight in predicting future returns, suggesting slow incorporation of latent structural information.

nodes.title: Modelling stock correlations with expected returns from investors

nodes.name: cross-stock expectation correlation
nodes.description: Agents form expected returns for one stock based on historical returns of another stock. When agents' expectations for stock A correlate positively with historical returns of stock B, this creates positive correlation in actual returns between the two stocks, and vice versa for negative correlation.

nodes.name: heterogeneous agent expectation formation
nodes.description: Agents with heterogeneous expected returns (rather than homogeneous expectations) make trading decisions that generate more robust and realistic stock correlation patterns. The diversity in agent expectations creates richer dynamics in how information dissemination and historical returns translate into correlated price movements.

nodes.name: information dissemination lag in expectation formation
nodes.description: Agents incorporate information dissemination delays when forming expected returns based on other stocks' historical returns. This lag between information arrival and agent decision-making creates predictable patterns in stock correlations that can be exploited for alpha generation.

nodes.title: The $κ$-generalised Distribution for Stock Returns

nodes.name: heavy-tailed return distribution mispricing
nodes.description: Traditional normal distribution assumptions cause systematic mispricing of assets with extreme tail risk. The κ-generalised distribution better captures heavy tails and kurtosis, allowing identification of underpriced or overpriced securities whose true risk profile is misestimated by Gaussian models.

nodes.name: extreme movement prediction via tail modeling
nodes.description: The κ-generalised distribution's asymptotic power-law behavior for large deviations enables better prediction of extreme market movements and tail events. This allows traders to anticipate and position ahead of large price swings that standard models systematically underestimate.

nodes.title: Value matters: Predictability of Stock Index Returns

nodes.name: mean reversion to fundamental valuation
nodes.description: Stock prices deviate from fundamental values (proxied by CAPE ratio) due to random disturbances and sentiment-driven momentum, but revert to their fundamental reference level over long horizons, generating predictable excess returns.

nodes.name: momentum-driven short-term mispricing
nodes.description: Agents' belief that expected returns are higher in bullish markets than bearish ones creates a momentum component that drives prices away from fundamentals in the short and medium run, generating bubbles and crashes before mean reversion occurs.

nodes.name: CAPE-based fundamental anchoring
nodes.description: The cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio provides a stable long-run reference growth level for returns; initial CAPE values linearly predict long-horizon expected returns, allowing exploitation of the gap between current prices and this fundamental anchor.

nodes.title: Against the Norm: Modeling Daily Stock Returns with the Laplace Distribution

nodes.name: tail risk mispricing from distribution model misspecification
nodes.description: Investors and models using normal distributions systematically underestimate the probability and magnitude of extreme returns, leading to mispricing of tail risk. By correctly modeling returns with a Laplace distribution that better captures fat tails, one can identify and exploit assets where tail risk is underpriced.

nodes.title: Multidimensional Analysis of Monthly Stock Market Returns

nodes.name: seasonal reversal after positive returns
nodes.description: Following a positive April return, Turkish stocks experience a negative May effect, suggesting mean reversion or profit-taking behavior at seasonal turning points rather than momentum continuation.

nodes.name: December seasonal bullishness
nodes.description: Both Turkish and American stock markets exhibit abnormally positive returns in December, potentially driven by year-end portfolio rebalancing, tax-loss harvesting reversals, or increased liquidity demand.

nodes.title: Distributions of Historic Market Data - Stock Returns

nodes.name: volatility mean reversion mispricing
nodes.description: Short-term returns exhibit predictable tail probabilities due to mean-reverting volatility with long memory that is not fully priced by the market. Traders can exploit the statistical properties of volatility dynamics, particularly in high-volatility regimes, to generate alpha over short time frames.

nodes.name: variance-horizon linear relationship
nodes.description: The mean realized variance of stock returns exhibits a linear relationship with the time horizon over which returns are calculated. This predictable scaling pattern, independent of volatility stochasticity, can be exploited as a trading signal when market prices deviate from this relationship.

nodes.title: What Does ChatGPT Make of Historical Stock Returns? Extrapolation and Miscalibration in LLM Stock Return Forecasts

nodes.name: LLM momentum extrapolation bias
nodes.description: Large language models over-extrapolate recent stock performance when forecasting returns, placing excessive weight on recent trends similar to human behavioral biases. This causes LLMs to generate optimistic return forecasts that exceed both historical averages and future realized returns.

nodes.name: LLM risk miscalibration
nodes.description: LLMs systematically underestimate tail risk and outlier events when constructing confidence intervals, generating pessimistic assessments of extreme outcomes. This creates skewed forecast distributions where the model is overconfident about central tendencies but underestimates downside risk.

nodes.name: LLM forecast overvaluation premium
nodes.description: Stocks that LLMs forecast to perform well based on recent trends become overvalued relative to their true expected returns, creating a short-selling opportunity by exploiting the gap between LLM predictions and actual market outcomes.

nodes.title: The Impact of Credit Risk and Implied Volatility on Stock Returns

nodes.name: credit risk premium exposure
nodes.description: Stock returns, particularly for distressed firms, are driven by fluctuations in credit risk premia extracted from CDS markets. Stocks with higher sensitivity to credit risk movements command a risk premium that explains cross-sectional return variation.

nodes.name: implied volatility risk premium
nodes.description: Equity option-implied volatility contains a risk premium that explains stock returns. Stocks with higher sensitivity to changes in implied volatility earn differential returns, reflecting compensation for volatility exposure.

nodes.name: derivative market information leakage
nodes.description: Credit and volatility derivatives price risks ahead of or more efficiently than equity markets, allowing derivative-implied risk premia to forecast stock returns. This reflects slower information incorporation in equity prices relative to derivative markets.

nodes.title: Vector-Quantized Discrete Latent Factors Meet Financial Priors: Dynamic Cross-Sectional Stock Ranking Prediction for Portfolio Construction

nodes.name: noise suppression through information bottleneck
nodes.description: Vector quantization acts as an information bottleneck that filters out noise from cross-sectional stock data while preserving robust market structure, improving signal-to-noise ratio in return prediction.

nodes.name: regime-adaptive factor loading
nodes.description: Time-varying factor loadings generated through a structure-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts allow the model to adapt to changing market regimes, with discrete vector-quantized codes routing to specialized experts for different market conditions.

nodes.name: cross-sectional structure exploitation
nodes.description: Discrete latent factors learned from the cross-sectional structure of stock returns capture persistent patterns in relative stock performance that classical factor models miss due to their inflexibility.

nodes.title: Statistical Properties of Statistical Ensembles of Stock Returns

nodes.name: statistical moment mean reversion
nodes.description: Stock return distributions deviate from their expected statistical properties (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis) in predictable ways. Traders can exploit these temporary deviations in the first four central moments by identifying when they are out of equilibrium and trading on their reversion to normal levels.

nodes.name: cross-sectional moment correlation
nodes.description: The statistical moments of returns across different stocks in an ensemble exhibit correlated fluctuations. By identifying these correlations in the probability density functions and temporal properties of moments, traders can predict relative performance and exploit mispricings between stocks with similar or divergent moment structures.

nodes.title: An explanation for the distribution characteristics of stock returns

nodes.name: underreaction to minor information
nodes.description: Financial markets systematically underreact to events or information with minor impacts, leading to predictable price adjustments over time as the market gradually incorporates the full information content.

nodes.name: overreaction to significant information
nodes.description: Financial markets systematically overreact to events or information with relatively significant impacts, causing prices to move beyond their fundamental values and subsequently mean-revert as the market corrects the excessive reaction.

nodes.name: positive information bias
nodes.description: Markets exhibit asymmetric reactions to information, responding more strongly to positive events or information than to negative ones of comparable magnitude, creating directional mispricings.

nodes.title: Nonuniversal distributions of stock returns in an emerging market

nodes.name: tail exponent mispricing by market capitalization
nodes.description: Stocks with different market capitalizations exhibit systematically different return distribution tail exponents, creating mispricings when markets fail to account for these nonuniversal tail properties. Larger-cap stocks have heavier tails (higher exponents) than smaller-cap stocks, suggesting differential risk pricing.

nodes.name: tail exponent mispricing by turnover rate
nodes.description: High-turnover stocks exhibit lighter tails (lower exponents) than low-turnover stocks, reflecting how trading intensity shapes return distributions. This nonuniversal relationship creates exploitable mispricings when investors fail to adjust risk models for turnover-dependent tail behavior.

nodes.title: Principal Component Analysis and Hidden Markov Model for Forecasting Stock Returns

nodes.name: regime-shift predictability
nodes.description: Market returns exhibit distinct regimes with different statistical properties and transition probabilities. By identifying these hidden regimes through HMM, one can forecast future factor returns more accurately than assuming a single stationary distribution, generating alpha from regime-aware positioning.

nodes.name: factor structure exploitation
nodes.description: Stock returns are driven by a lower-dimensional set of common factors (principal components of the return covariance matrix). Forecasting these latent factors and reconstructing individual stock returns from factor forecasts captures systematic return patterns that simple buy-and-hold strategies miss.

nodes.title: A Model for Stock Returns and Volatility

nodes.name: volatility mean reversion exploitation
nodes.description: Brown noise patterns in VIX/VXO time series exhibit predictable mean-reversion dynamics that allow traders to anticipate volatility shifts before they occur, enabling profitable positioning in options or equities ahead of volatility regime changes.

nodes.name: volatility distribution mispricing
nodes.description: Market participants misprice options and equities because they use inadequate volatility models; the generalized inverse gamma distribution more accurately captures true volatility dynamics than standard measures, creating exploitable mispricings.

nodes.title: Skewness Dispersion and Stock Market Returns

nodes.name: delayed macro news incorporation
nodes.description: Market gradually incorporates macroeconomic news (especially monetary policy announcements) into prices with a lag, creating predictable return patterns. High cross-sectional dispersion in firm-level skewness signals incomplete price adjustment to macro shocks.

nodes.name: aggregate risk repricing
nodes.description: Variation in aggregate risk and valuation adjustments across firms, reflected in skewness dispersion, drives the delayed incorporation of macroeconomic information into market prices and future returns.

nodes.title: Continuous Cash-Overlay Filters for a Static Growth--Defensive Risk Sleeve: Slow-Tail Compensation, V-Shape Crash Brakes, Walk-Forward Validation, and Max-Cash Combination

nodes.name: slow-tail compensation state detection
nodes.description: Dynamic cash allocation responds to continuous market compensation regimes (rate headwinds, risk-premium compression, rate-path stress) by increasing cash weight during unfavorable states, reducing exposure to deteriorating risk-reward conditions.

nodes.name: V-shape crash brake filter
nodes.description: A fast-reacting mechanism that increases cash allocation during rapid market downturns by monitoring VIX, credit spreads, drawdown depth, and re-entry signals, acting as a drawdown-control tool that exits before severe losses and re-enters after V-shaped recoveries.

nodes.name: cash-rate carry optimization
nodes.description: The cash leg earns the contemporaneous risk-free rate, creating a dynamic return advantage when cash weights are elevated during periods of high rates or poor risky-asset compensation, allowing the overlay to capture rate-driven alpha.

nodes.title: Time-varying return predictability in the Chinese stock market

nodes.name: time-varying market efficiency during turmoil
nodes.description: Market efficiency breaks down during periods of turmoil and volatility, creating predictable return patterns that are absent during calm periods. This time-varying predictability arises from nonlinear dependencies and inefficiencies that intensify when markets are stressed.

nodes.name: nonlinear return dependence
nodes.description: Returns exhibit nonlinear dependencies and higher-order statistical structure beyond linear autocorrelation, which can be exploited for prediction. These nonlinear patterns are particularly pronounced during market turmoil when standard linear models fail.

nodes.title: Multifractal characteristics and return predictability in the Chinese stock markets

nodes.name: multifractal volatility mean reversion
nodes.description: Market returns are predictable from the spectral width (Δα) of the multifractal spectrum, which measures the degree of multifractal scaling in price fluctuations. When multifractal characteristics widen, indicating increased complexity in price dynamics, subsequent returns tend to revert as the market normalizes its volatility structure.

nodes.title: From Index to Equity: Pre-Training Transformers for Stock Return Prediction

nodes.name: index pre-training transfer learning
nodes.description: A transformer model pre-trained on broad market index dynamics (TSX) captures general market trends that transfer to individual stock prediction, reducing prediction error when fine-tuned on specific equities. This leverages the statistical structure of aggregate market movements to improve stock-level forecasting.

nodes.name: intra-day return direction predictability
nodes.description: Intra-day price movements exhibit directional patterns that can be predicted from recent market and stock-level data, suggesting that short-term return reversals or continuations are not purely random and contain exploitable signal.

nodes.title: Return or stock price differences

nodes.name: linear-multiplicative model mismatch
nodes.description: Mispricing arises when analysts apply linear statistical models to tick-by-tick price data that follows a multiplicative (log-normal) process. This model misspecification creates exploitable discrepancies between return-based and price-difference-based analyses.

nodes.name: tick-data analytical framework selection bias
nodes.description: The choice between analyzing returns versus raw price differences on high-frequency tick data produces systematically different conclusions about price movements. Traders can exploit this by identifying which analytical framework correctly captures the true underlying process and trading against those using the wrong framework.

nodes.title: Cash Flow Entropy

nodes.name: cash flow concentration imbalance
nodes.description: Markets misprice securities when cash flows are concentrated among few agents versus dispersed across many agents. Traders can exploit this by identifying when cash flow aggregation or diversification is extreme relative to equilibrium, generating alpha from the relative performance differential between concentration regimes.

nodes.name: cash flow entropy differential constraint
nodes.description: An economy must maintain a balance between cash flow aggregating and diversifying agents; when this constraint is violated (inflow entropy diverges from outflow entropy), the market exhibits predictable mean-reversion as the system rebalances toward equilibrium.

nodes.title: Does the time horizon of the return predictive effect of investor sentiment vary with stock characteristics? A Granger causality analysis in the frequency domain

nodes.name: sentiment-driven mispricing by firm size
nodes.description: Investor sentiment causes predictable price movements in smaller-cap stocks more strongly than larger-cap stocks, because smaller firms have less analyst coverage and higher information asymmetry, making them more susceptible to sentiment-driven mispricing.

nodes.name: sentiment-driven mispricing by valuation
nodes.description: Investor sentiment has stronger predictive power for low book-to-market (growth) stocks than high book-to-market (value) stocks, because growth stocks have more subjective valuations and are more sensitive to shifts in investor mood and expectations.

nodes.name: sentiment-driven mispricing by profitability
nodes.description: Investor sentiment exhibits stronger predictive effects on returns of lower-profitability stocks than higher-profitability stocks, because low-profitability firms have more uncertain cash flows and are more vulnerable to sentiment-driven repricing.

nodes.name: sentiment-driven mispricing by investment intensity
nodes.description: Investor sentiment has long-term predictive power for high-investment stocks but only short-term predictive power for low-investment stocks, because high-investment firms have more uncertain future returns and longer-duration cash flows that are more sensitive to sentiment shifts.

nodes.title: Neuroevolution Neural Architecture Search for Evolving RNNs in Stock Return Prediction and Portfolio Trading

nodes.name: neural architecture search predictive edge
nodes.description: Evolved RNNs via neuroevolution (EXAMM algorithm) discover non-linear patterns in historical returns that traditional models miss, generating alpha through superior out-of-sample return forecasting.

nodes.name: time series memory exploitation
nodes.description: RNNs with augmented memory mechanisms capture temporal dependencies and regime shifts in stock returns that simpler forecasting approaches cannot, enabling systematic outperformance across market conditions (bear and bull markets).

nodes.title: Harnessing Earnings Reports for Stock Predictions: A QLoRA-Enhanced LLM Approach

nodes.name: textual sentiment underreaction
nodes.description: Market participants fail to fully incorporate nuanced sentiment and forward-looking signals embedded in earnings transcripts, allowing LLM-based interpretation of textual data to capture predictive information that traditional models miss.

nodes.name: financial metric integration
nodes.description: Earnings report financial metrics (growth rates, profitability measures) combined with external market factors (analyst grades, index performance) provide complementary signals that improve prediction accuracy beyond what either source alone can deliver.

nodes.title: Time-varying neural network for stock return prediction

nodes.name: time-varying factor importance
nodes.description: The predictive power of different factors (size, momentum, industry indicators) shifts over time as market conditions change. A model that adapts to these shifting dynamics can better predict returns than static factor models.

nodes.name: industry risk concentration during distress
nodes.description: During periods of market distress and heightened risk, industry-level factors become more important for explaining stock returns relative to firm-level characteristics. This suggests investors price in systematic industry risk more heavily when markets are stressed.
